At the end of Chapter 3, we shrank each CTA in gemv's v6 down to a single warp computing 1 row, and it actually ran slower than v5—because concurrent in-flight reads per SM dropped to just ~8.7 KiB (Chapter 3, Section 9). How do we push bytes in flight back up? To see that, we need to look one level deeper inside the SM: the SMSP (SM sub-partition, 4 per SM).

Chapter 3, Section 1 worked out that one SM holds at most 64 resident warps. Split them evenly across the 4 SMSPs, and each SMSP gets 1 warp scheduler and holds at most 16 resident warps. An SMSP scheduler can issue only 1 instruction per cycle, while a memory load waits tens to thousands of cycles—how do we keep that wait from turning straight into total runtime?

In this chapter we follow a single warp through one full pass: what it does while waiting for data, who waits for whom when its 32 threads split across branch paths, and why reducing 32 per-thread partial sums into one number leaves only 1 thread doing the work.

1Only 1 Issue Slot per Cycle: Which Waits Actually Count Toward Total Runtime?

An issue slot sits idle only on cycles when the SMSP has not a single eligible warp; whether those idle cycles add to total runtime depends on whether issue slots are the first resource to saturate.

On every clock cycle (Chapter 2, Section 2), the SMSP's warp scheduler scans the warps resident in its sub-partition (Figure 4-1). Once a warp's next instruction has been fetched and decoded, all of its operands are ready, and the target execution unit is free, that warp is eligible.

Each SMSP has only 1 issue slot per cycle. The scheduler picks 1 eligible warp, issues 1 instruction from it, and marks that warp selected. Switching between warps takes zero time: every resident warp keeps its registers on-chip the whole time (Chapter 3, Section 1), so picking warp A on this cycle and warp B on the next never saves or restores any state. That part works just like hardware multithreading on a CPU. The difference is scale: CPU SMT (simultaneous multithreading) can issue instructions from several threads in the same cycle, but holds only a few thread contexts per core. An SMSP holds up to 16 warp contexts, yet issues only 1 instruction from 1 warp per cycle (fine-grained multithreading).

What about the other resident warps that don't issue on that cycle? They fall into two buckets. Some are not selected—ready to go, just not the warp chosen on this cycle. The rest are stalled, still waiting for data to return, for a barrier to release, or for a busy execution unit to free up. Only when the entire SMSP has zero eligible warps does the cycle count as no eligible, leaving the issue slot idle. Even if 15 warps sit not selected on a cycle, as long as 1 warp issues an instruction, that cycle's issue slot is full.

When a 4-warp CTA lands on an SM, we assume its 4 warps go to the 4 SMSPs, 1 warp per SMSP. (NVIDIA documents only that a warp stays on one SMSP from launch to completion; it doesn't disclose the assignment rule.) You can see this in Mode 1 of Figure 4-1, which is v1 from Primer 3: each 128-thread CTA computes 1 row, and each thread loads one BF16 element (2 B) at a time. One SM holds 16 such CTAs, so each SMSP holds 16 warps—one from each CTA, each reading a different row of WWW. On every iteration, each warp sends 2 loads to the Load/Store Unit (LSU; Chapter 3), one BF16 of WWW and one of xxx, and then quickly stalls waiting for the data to come back (the bytes-in-flight numbers below count only WWW). Once all 16 warps are stuck waiting, most cycles end up no eligible.

2Scoreboards and In-Order Issue: How Does a Warp Keep Moving After Firing a Load?

The scoreboard marks only the pending destination register as not ready, so the warp keeps going until the first instruction that uses it; the more independent instructions you pack in between, the fewer warps you need to keep the issue slot full.

Every GPU warp issues instructions strictly in program order (in-order issue), so it cannot jump ahead of a stalled instruction out of order. So how does it keep moving right after firing a load? With a scoreboard (Figure 4-2). When the warp issues a load, the hardware logs an entry on the scoreboard, and the warp keeps issuing the independent instructions that follow as long as they don't touch the pending result. Only when the warp hits the first instruction that actually uses that result does it wait for the scoreboard to clear, at which point the scheduler switches to another eligible warp. According to public reverse-engineering analyses, the compiler encodes ahead of time in the machine instruction which scoreboard to wait on and before which instruction to stall (NVIDIA's official documentation doesn't disclose this encoding; see Chapter 6, Section 5). When the data arrives and the scoreboard clears is tracked by the hardware at runtime. Global memory loads and shared memory (SMEM) loads use this exact same mechanism; only the number of wait cycles differs.

Now apply Little's Law (Chapter 2, Section 3) to a single SMSP, where the resource we want to keep fed is the 1-instruction-per-cycle issue slot. (Here we count instructions in flight; Section 3 will count bytes in flight.) Suppose a load takes DDD cycles to return, and a warp can issue nnn instructions—including the load itself—between firing the load and first using its result. Since the issue slot wants 1 instruction every cycle, keeping it full takes about D/nD / nD/n warps taking turns:

required resident warps≈⌈Dn⌉\mathrm{required\ resident\ warps} \approx \left\lceil \frac{D}{n} \right\rceilrequired resident warps≈⌈nD​⌉

Take a short-latency load first. A conflict-free SMEM load takes ~23 cycles (Chapter 3, Section 7). If each load is followed by 3 independent instructions (n=4n = 4n=4), then ⌈23/4⌉=6\lceil 23 / 4 \rceil = 6⌈23/4⌉=6 warps taking turns are enough to reach 0 no eligible cycles (Figure 4-2, Mode 4). With only 4 resident warps, they can't cover the whole wait window, and idle cycles show up on the timeline (Mode 3).

Now flip it around: what if the next load's address depends on the value returned by the previous load? Say three tables sit in SMEM and we chain lookups: idx = len[i]; p = table[idx]; v = data[p];. Right after each load issues, the very next instruction needs its result, pinning n=1n = 1n=1 at every step. At about 23 cycles per load, 3 chained loads wait about 69 cycles in total, stalling a single warp on the scoreboard three times in a row (Figure 4-2, Mode 1). A single serial chain can't be split apart on its own. If an outer loop wraps it, though, len[i + 1] in iteration i+1i + 1i+1 doesn't depend on iteration iii. While iteration iii is still waiting on data, the warp can fire off the next iteration's load early and stretch nnn larger (v7 in the next section fires several independent WWW loads ahead in just this way; Chapter 7, Section 6 walks through cross-iteration page-table prefetching in full). The catch is register pressure: every extra pending load ties up another set of destination registers, and using more registers may cut the number of resident warps (Chapter 3, Section 1). We check that trade-off in the next section when we run the numbers for v7.

3When Memory-Bound, Do You Feed the Issue Slot or HBM? (The Mechanism Behind gemv v6 → v7)

A memory-bandwidth-bound kernel needs to saturate SM-wide bytes in flight, not issue slots—and the way to do it is to have each thread fire several independent wide loads before using the first result.

Let's check from throughput which resource hits its ceiling first: the issue slot or HBM bandwidth. In v7 below, each warp executes 1,231 machine instructions in total (1,144 in the main loop) to stream 32×512 B=16,384 B32 \times 512\ \mathrm{B} = 16{,}384\ \mathrm{B}32×512 B=16,384 B of weights WWW, which works out to about 0.075 instructions per byte of WWW (about 0.070 in the main loop). Across all 132 SMs (132×4=528132 \times 4 = 528132×4=528 SMSPs) running at about 1.8 GHz, even at the measured HBM plateau of about 4.54 TB/s (Chapter 2, Section 3), each SMSP receives at most about 4.8 B per cycle; multiplied by about 0.070–0.075 instructions per byte, that demands at most about 0.33–0.36 instructions per cycle—roughly a third of the 1-instruction-per-cycle issue slot (and when v8 reaches 67.1% of peak DRAM bandwidth below, the profiler measures an active issue-cycle share of 28.4%). In gemv, the issue slot never comes close to saturating and sits without an instruction to issue on most cycles.

An under-filled issue slot is harmless here because the resource racing against it is HBM bandwidth: whichever resource hits its ceiling first sets total runtime through its own Little's Law equation. Because gemv streams 37.75 MB of weights and uses each weight for only a single multiply-add, HBM hits its ceiling long before the issue slots do. In our H200 measurement streaming 4 GiB across all 132 SMs, ordinary 16 B loads reach 95% of the bandwidth plateau at about 24–40 KiB/SM in flight in machine code depending on loads per thread, and at 64 KiB/SM every tested configuration reaches at least 98.3% (enough, not the minimum); once HBM is on that plateau, dividing in-flight bytes by bandwidth at 64 KiB/SM puts the estimated upper bound on mean round-trip latency at about 1.9 µs (about 3,400 cycles at about 1.8 GHz; v7's actual loaded round-trip time was not measured), leaving the SMSP issue slot idle on roughly two-thirds to three-quarters of cycles.

Look back at Figure 4-1: both modes spend over 80% of their cycles in no eligible, yet their runtimes are worlds apart because of how many bytes they keep in flight. In Mode 1 (v1 from Primer 3), each thread loads only 1 BF16 of WWW per iteration, so 16 warps on an SMSP hold just 1 KiB in flight at once, or 4 KiB across the SM. In v6, each thread keeps only one 16 B load of WWW outstanding per step, which still comes to only about 8.7 KiB per SM. Mode 2 models 4 warps per SMSP on a simplified 600-cycle unloaded axis with 56 schematic instructions per batch (eight 16 B WWW loads plus 48 compute instructions waiting as a batch, whereas real v7 machine code executes 286 instructions per batch): 8 wide loads per thread put 16 KiB of issued loads in flight on one SMSP and 64 KiB across the 4 SMSPs, which in Mode 2's recurring 8-load batch model already sits in the >98% plateau region of Chapter 2, Section 3 (real v7 instead hits about 69.8 KiB/SM in a one-time opening burst and keeps 3–6 loads per thread, or about 26–52 KiB/SM, in flight afterward; see below). Mode 1 and v6 are slow because they keep too few bytes in flight, not because their issue slots sit empty. Note also that compressing 286 real instructions per batch down to 56 makes Mode 2 show 82% no eligible cycles; in real execution, both the plateau throughput calculation above (about 64%–67% non-issue cycles) and profiler measurements on v8 (71.6% non-active issue cycles, or about 28%–29% active when scaled by instruction count and duration to v7) give fewer non-issue cycles (about 64%–72%) than the toy's 82%, though roughly two-thirds to over 70% of cycles still issue nothing.

That is how v6 → v7 pushes bytes in flight back up: by fully unrolling the loop so each thread fires multiple wide loads ahead of first use. Because a warp stalls as soon as it hits an instruction that consumes a pending load, concurrent bytes in flight per SM at any point equal resident warps × 32 threads per warp × loads currently outstanding per thread × bytes per load. In Chapter 3, Section 9, v6 took K as a runtime argument so its loop stayed un-unrolled: averaging about 17.45 resident warps per SM, each thread issued just one 16 B load of WWW per step before immediately running multiply-adds, leaving only about 8.7 KiB/SM in flight throughout. In v7, we make K = 8192 a compile-time constant and fully unroll all 32 chunks (written in source as groups of BATCH = 8 that stage eight uint4 loads of WWW and xxx before the multiply-adds, together with __launch_bounds__(32), whose standalone effect was not measured). In the compiled machine instructions (SASS; see Chapter 6, Section 5 for how source compiles to SASS), the compiler places 8 loads of WWW and 7 loads of xxx back to back ahead of the very first multiply-add. (In a separate batch-size check on v9 not expanded in this book—keeping full unrolling while setting the batch size to 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16—the compiler hoisted 7–8 loads of WWW in every case, with BATCH = 1 hoisting 7 loads and running in 14.37 µs; from this we infer that full loop unrolling, rather than the manual BATCH = 8 array, is what enables the compiler to hoist those loads.) Counting only WWW, that opening burst lifts concurrent WWW bytes in flight to a one-time peak of about 69.8 KiB/SM during the initial first-byte wait, while across the remaining 24 loads of WWW each thread keeps 3–6 loads outstanding (about 26–52 KiB/SM; on H200, ordinary 16 B loads measured in machine code reach 95% of the bandwidth plateau at about 24–40 KiB/SM depending on loads per thread, with 64 KiB/SM enough rather than the minimum):

17.45×32×8×16 B≈69.8 KiB17.45 \times 32 \times 8 \times 16\ \mathrm{B} \approx 69.8\ \mathrm{KiB}17.45×32×8×16 B≈69.8 KiB

Keep in mind that about 69.8 KiB/SM is a one-time opening peak, not a time average across the kernel. Only the first 8 loads of WWW issue back to back; the remaining 24 loads of WWW sit interleaved with multiply-add instructions, keeping 3–6 loads of WWW per thread outstanding at each later issue (about 26–52 KiB/SM), so time-averaged bytes in flight stay below the opening peak (neither the runtime time average nor v7's actual loaded round-trip time was measured; see Section 6). Even so, under the same static machine-code scan from load issue to first register use, v7 averages 4.06 outstanding WWW loads across its 32 first-use points—above the 3.0 average (peak 4 loads = 32 KiB/SM) of a streaming control kernel whose large-size slope already reaches 4.43 TB/s (about 97.6% of the plateau)—and doubling v7 itself from 2,304 to 4,608 rows (where residency rises to its 20-warp/SM cap) streams the second 37.75 MB at a marginal rate of 4.54 TB/s (with a 4.59 TB/s slope up to 36,864 rows). From these two supports, we infer that v7 at 2,304 rows already comes within a few percent of the HBM plateau in steady state, and is held back mainly by the fixed cost of a short 37.75 MB launch rather than in-flight starvation (the split between first-byte latency and CTA completion skew remains open; see Section 6).

What does v7 pay for those extra loads? Holding all those 128-bit loads in registers (8 groups of WWW plus the in-flight xxx loads) pushes per-thread register usage from 30 up to 83, which rounds up to 88 under the 8-register allocation granularity (Chapter 3, Section 1). Because the register file is split evenly across the 4 SMSPs and allocated per SMSP (⌊16,384/(32×88)⌋=5\lfloor 16{,}384 / (32 \times 88) \rfloor = 5⌊16,384/(32×88)⌋=5 warps per SMSP), each SM can still hold up to 20 single-warp CTAs—still above the 17.45 CTAs per SM assigned by the grid. So we don't lose a single resident warp, and peak bytes in flight scale by the full 8× (see the chart in Section 6 for the measured speedup). If register pressure pushed the residency cap below the 17.45 warps assigned by the grid, resident warps would drop and bytes in flight would no longer scale by 8× (we did not measure such a counterexample on gemv).

4When a Warp Issues One Branch Path at a Time, Who Waits for Whom?

Short conditionals use predication to mask writeback at almost no cost; long divergent branches inside a warp have to run one path after the other, while branches split along whole-warp boundaries never hold each other up.

Inside a warp, the 32 threads are called 32 lanes. Starting with compute capability 7.0 (NVIDIA's version number for a GPU architecture; H200 is 9.0), GPUs use Independent Thread Scheduling: each lane keeps its own program counter, which tracks the next instruction that lane will run. Yet on any given cycle, the warp scheduler still issues only 1 instruction from this warp, and the active lanes sitting at that instruction run it together. This execution model is called SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads; see Figure 4-3).

Every thread has a few 1-bit predicate registers, such as P0. On a short conditional like if (tid == 0) y[row] = sum;, the compiler doesn't emit a branch jump at all. Instead, it attaches a predicate (such as @!P0) to the instruction, issues it across all 32 lanes as usual, and lets the lanes where the condition is false suppress their writeback.

Once a branch body is long enough to need a jump, you get branch divergence. The hardware tracks which lanes take part in the current instruction with a 32-bit active mask. Lanes can split into sub-warp groups and reconverge later, but the warp issues instructions for only one path at a time while lanes on the other path sit idle. In the SASS we inspect, the compiler places a BSSY before a divergent branch to set the reconvergence point (Chapter 10, Section 9), and a BSYNC at the reconvergence point where lanes that finish first wait for the other path. Past BSYNC, the lanes that were active at BSSY run together again—all 32 of them if all 32 were active before the split, while any lanes that have already exited don't come back. If the warp finishes one path before starting the other, you pay the sum of both paths' runtimes, not the longer of the two (see Variant 3 below). Independent Thread Scheduling also means the 32 lanes of a warp are no longer guaranteed to stay in lockstep by default. When code needs them aligned at a specific point, it calls __syncwarp(mask): the lanes in the mask wait for each other there, and their earlier memory writes become visible to one another (we did not measure its standalone cost; Chapter 8, Section 11 uses it so each warp aligns before lane 0 issues a single release).

Figure 4-3 puts three branching variants side by side for warp 0's epilogue right after the CTA barrier (machine instruction counts are in the figure readout):

  • Variant 1 (predicated store): This does no additions and isolates predication when more code follows: only lane 0, where the condition holds, computes the address of y[row] and stores the value already in its register (the compiler places kernel parameters such as y in constant memory, which the SM reads through its read-only constant cache; its read latency was not measured—see Appendix B, Section 4, No. 27), issuing in a single predicated pass with no branch jump.
  • Variant 2 (one-sided branch if (tid == 0) { 128 additions }, v1 epilogue): The other 31 lanes exit right at the branch entry (when no code follows at the end of a kernel, the compiler terminates them immediately with a predicated exit), yet the warp cannot vacate its SMSP slot until lane 0 finishes summing smem[0..127]. A floating-point multiply-add takes about 4 measured cycles before the next dependent instruction can use its result (Chapter 5, Section 1), and we estimate a floating-point addition at the same value. Figure 4-3 shows the ideal fully unrolled bound with the loop limit hardcoded to the constant 128: 128 serial additions take about 512 cycles, plus about 32 cycles for the first 16 B SMEM read using the full-warp measurement from Chapter 3, Section 7 (1-lane 16 B SMEM read latency was not measured; estimating about 26 cycles from the 2-cycle-per-wavefront slope gives about 538 cycles), for at least about 544 cycles with just 1 of the 32 lanes doing useful work. In v1's actual machine code with runtime blockDim.x (231 dynamic post-barrier instructions across 8 loop passes), summing the compiler-encoded issue-stall intervals (Chapter 6, Section 5) and 32-cycle 16 B SMEM waits puts this tail at about 970 cycles (about 923 cycles if 1-lane 16 B reads take about 26 cycles; upper bound not derived, standalone duration not measured).
  • Variant 3 (two-sided branch, illustrative code if (lane < 16) {…} else {…}, 128 additions per branch): The two paths reconverge at BSYNC. If the warp finishes one path before starting the other, the 128 additions of the first 16 lanes and the 128 additions of the last 16 lanes add straight together (~2×5122 \times 5122×512 cycles; we did not measure whether the hardware interleaves the two paths to hide part of each wait), and all 32 lanes turn back on after BSYNC.

By contrast, if you split a branch along whole-warp boundaries—such as if (warp_id == 0)—all 32 lanes in a warp see the exact same condition, so the warp never diverges. That is how Chapter 3, Section 5 separates producer warps from consumer warps; the trade-off is that work can only be handed out in 32-thread chunks, and we did not measure the time cost of that coarser granularity separately. One more rule to keep in mind: __syncthreads() requires every thread in the CTA to reach the exact same barrier instruction, so you can't put it inside a branch taken by only some threads (Chapter 7, Section 7 shows how different branches can meet at a shared barrier).

In v1's SASS, every row uses Variant 2 to sum 128 partial sums (v2–v5 were not determined). By v6 and v7, each CTA is down to a single warp with just 32 partial sums, yet that same one-lane serial reduction still burns several hundred machine-code cycles (about 380 cycles; see the next section and Chapter 6, Section 5)—as we'll price out and replace in the next section.

5Keeping the Reduction Inside One Warp: How Does Warp Shuffle Eliminate Shared Memory and CTA Barriers? (The Mechanism Behind gemv v7 → v8)

A reduction across at most 32 threads can read neighbor registers directly in 5 warp-shuffle steps, bypassing both shared memory and the CTA barrier.

Now replace v7's SMEM epilogue with a warp shuffle (Figure 4-4, Mode 2). In v8, the code calls __shfl_xor_sync(0xffffffff, acc, o), which lets each thread read acc from the register of thread lane XOR o. The first argument is the lane mask: 0xffffffff means all 32 lanes take part, and the instruction itself aligns those lanes at that point. Issued through the Load/Store Unit (LSU; Chapter 3, Section 2), a warp shuffle exchanges values between registers without reading or writing shared memory or global memory. Compared with the SMEM version (Figure 4-4, Mode 1)—which keeps a CTA barrier so all 32 threads finish writing shared memory before thread 0 reads their values—a warp shuffle never touches shared memory, so that barrier goes away too.

The reduction runs log⁡232=5\log_2 32 = 5log2​32=5 halving steps with o = 16, 8, 4, 2, 1: in C++ source semantics, each step performs 1 warp shuffle plus 1 addition so all 32 lanes hold the full sum before lane 0 writes y[row], whereas in v8's compiled machine code all 32 lanes issue the 5th shuffle and lanes 1–31 immediately exit (@P0 EXIT, matching Variant 2 in Section 4) during its wait, leaving lane 0 alone to run the 5th addition and an unpredicated store. Each shuffle result is tracked by the same scoreboard mechanism from Section 2. On Hopper, a 32-bit integer warp sum can use a single redux.sync (compiled to machine instruction REDUX, which reduces 32-bit signed/unsigned integers across active lanes by sum, min/max, or bitwise ops into a warp-wide uniform register whose latency was not measured; see Chapter 7, Section 7 for uniform registers); Hopper (H200, compute capability 9.0), however, has no floating-point redux.sync: single-precision floating-point supports only min/max and requires next-generation Blackwell targets sm_100a (architecture-specific) and sm_100f (family-specific, sm_10x family; see the start of Appendix A), and no target provides floating-point add, so v8 keeps this 5-step shuffle.

Put the two cycle budgets side by side for summing those 32 values:

  • v8 warp shuffle: Each warp shuffle takes about 24 measured cycles before the next dependent instruction can use its result, paired with one about 4-cycle addition, giving a bare dependency chain of 5×(24+4)+1=1415 \times (24 + 4) + 1 = 1415×(24+4)+1=141 cycles; walking v8's actual machine code using its compiler-encoded issue-stall intervals (Chapter 6, Section 5) and 24-cycle shuffle scoreboards (with the read of parameter y overlapped inside the 5th shuffle wait) comes to about 152 cycles, using 0 bytes of SMEM and 0 CTA barriers (standalone epilogue time was not measured).
  • v7 SMEM epilogue: Having all 32 threads write SMEM, cross the CTA barrier, read back the first 4 B value, and complete the 1st addition takes 44.3 measured cycles in our microbenchmark; on a simplified chain-only schematic that models only the addition dependency chain (omitting the 4.30-cycle scalar SMEM read issue interval), thread 0 finishes the remaining 31 serial additions in 31×4=12431 \times 4 = 12431×4=124 cycles plus 1 final store, for about 169 cycles on the schematic axis. Walking v7's actual SASS under the exact same stall-field rule (including reading blockDim.x, loop branch checks, and two loop passes of 16 B SMEM loads) puts the epilogue at at least about 380 cycles (384 cycles using the 32-cycle full-warp LDS.128 latency, or about 372 cycles if 1-lane LDS.128 is estimated at about 26 cycles; constant-cache and taken-branch costs were not measured, the upper bound was not derived, and standalone epilogue time was not measured).

Comparing the two side by side: the simplified chain-only schematic differs by only about 28 cycles (169−141169 - 141169−141, or about 16 ns at about 1.8 GHz), whereas under the same machine-code walk v8 saves at least about 230 cycles per warp epilogue (384−152=232384 - 152 = 232384−152=232 cycles, or about 220 cycles if 1-lane LDS.128 is about 26 cycles—at least about 0.12 µs across 1.80–1.98 GHz, and about 0.13 µs at about 1.8 GHz, with the upper bound not measured). Moreover, starting from v6, all 2,304 single-warp CTAs reside concurrently in a single wave (Chapter 3, Section 9; they do not all finish at the same instant, as Section 6 shows): each warp runs its epilogue once at its own end, so the whole kernel shortens by roughly one epilogue on whichever warp finishes last rather than multiplying across 2,304 rows.

Back in gemv, v8 drops v7's 128 B of SMEM and __syncthreads() and swaps in that 5-step warp shuffle. The immediate benefit is slightly fewer executed machine instructions (1,231 → 1,159) and slightly fewer registers per thread (83 → 78) than v7, while the grid still supplies 17.45 warps per SM on average (the profiler reports 4.38 warps/SMSP, or about 17.5 per SM, alongside 24.8% achieved active occupancy, or about 15.9 active warps/SM).

Two points are worth noting. First, warp shuffle works only within a single warp: a reduction across more than 32 threads (like v1) still shuffles within each warp first and then combines across warps through SMEM and a CTA barrier. Second, in v8 the compiler places only 7 loads of WWW ahead of the first multiply-add, moving the 8th load into the first multiply-add group (why the compiler chose this schedule was not determined). That lowers only the one-time opening burst inside the initial first-byte wait from 8 loads in v7 (about 69.8 KiB/SM) to 7 loads (112 B per thread, or about 17.45×32×7×16 B≈61.1 KiB17.45 \times 32 \times 7 \times 16\ \mathrm{B} \approx 61.1\ \mathrm{KiB}17.45×32×7×16 B≈61.1 KiB per SM); across the remaining 25 loads of WWW, v8 keeps the same 3–6 loads per thread outstanding (about 26–52 KiB/SM; on H200, ordinary 16 B loads measured in machine code reach 95% of the bandwidth plateau at about 24–40 KiB/SM depending on loads per thread, with 64 KiB/SM enough rather than the minimum), and across all 32 loads of WWW its static first-use average (4.12 vs. 4.06 in v7; 3.34 vs. 3.20 instruction-weighted) is no narrower than v7's.

6The gemv Evolution v6 → v7 → v8: Why Does One Step Save So Much and the Next Save So Little?

v7 shortens the memory wait across the main loop; v8's machine-code epilogue saves at least about 230 cycles (at least about 0.12 µs, or about 0.13 µs at about 1.8 GHz; upper bound not measured), beating v7 by 0.42–0.54 µs in paired clean read-flush event runs while essentially tying under write flushing, for reasons not determined.

In the evolution chart below, we use PyTorch's matrix-vector multiplication function torch.mv as our baseline; under the hood, it calls NVIDIA's matrix library cuBLAS.

Look at v6 → v7 first: v7 runs about 1.43× faster than v6 (saving 6.48 µs). Every step of the main loop across the 8,192 columns waits on HBM; once the opening burst climbs to about 69.8 KiB/SM and subsequent steps keep 3–6 loads of WWW per thread outstanding (about 26–52 KiB/SM; on H200, ordinary 16 B loads measured in machine code reach 95% of the bandwidth plateau at about 24–40 KiB/SM depending on loads per thread, with 64 KiB/SM enough rather than the minimum, and runtime time-averaged bytes in flight were not measured—see Section 3), steady-state HBM bandwidth is inferred (Section 3) to climb out of starvation to within at most a few percent of the plateau, shrinking the wait right away. That speedup also puts v7 back ahead of torch.mv (v5 was already faster before v6 slipped behind).

Now look at v7 → v8. By our Section 5 machine-code walk, the epilogue on the last-finishing warp saves at least about 230 cycles (at least about 0.12 µs, or about 0.13 µs at about 1.8 GHz; upper bound not measured); in a memory-bandwidth-bound main loop, executing about 5 fewer instructions (1,144 in v7 vs. 1,139 in v8; the 72-instruction drop per warp sits mainly in the epilogue) does not by itself cut total runtime, and dropping the opening burst from 8 loads to 7 changes only the one-time peak during the initial first-byte wait while keeping the recurring 3–6 loads per thread just as wide. So how do we tell whether a small one-step change is a real speedup or just run-to-run variation (also called measurement noise)? We check two rules. First, across paired runs in the same round, the difference between the two versions must have the same sign every time. Second, that paired difference must exceed the largest gap between the medians of a single version within this set of runs—which we call its span below. Chapter 7, Section 1 gives the alternating paired ABBA setup and parameters, and Chapter 6, Section 8 gives the noise band for the full-graph replay chain.

Under the clean 512 MiB read-flush CUDA-event protocol here (whose SM clock was not recorded), we ran v7 then v8, and then reversed the order (v8 then v7), on each of two machines, for 4 paired runs in total (the chart shows the low and high of each version's 4 medians). Across those 4 runs, v7's own median span is 0.32 µs and v8's is 0.29 µs; both are smaller than the 0.42–0.54 µs by which v8 beats v7 in every paired run (pooled medians 15.15 → 14.74 µs, 1.03×), and all 4 differences share the same sign—so under this clean read-flush event method, the speedup is reproducible. Putting the full measurement record side by side, however: in an earlier event-timing round that flushed L2 with a 512 MiB write, the same kernel pair measured 15.68 vs. 15.62 µs (−0.06 µs, −0.4%, 1.00×—no gain within run spread), and single-launch base-clock profiling in that round recorded 12.54 µs on v7 vs. 13.47 µs on v8, while our unlocked-clock (about 1.96 GHz) follow-up profiler run measured v8 at 11.9 µs without running v7 in the same pass. By Section 5's machine-code walk, the epilogue swap saves at least about 230 cycles on the last-finishing warp (at least about 0.12 µs across 1.80–1.98 GHz, or about 0.13 µs at about 1.8 GHz—roughly 22%–31% of the 0.42–0.54 µs read-flush gain, with the epilogue upper bound not measured); how much of the 0.42–0.54 µs read-flush gain comes from the epilogue versus main-loop scheduling or outside-kernel and L2-flush effects—and why it disappears under the 512 MiB write flush—was not determined.

Even though v8 fires an opening burst of 7 wide loads (about 61.1 KiB/SM) and keeps 3–6 loads per thread outstanding thereafter (about 26–52 KiB/SM; on H200, ordinary 16 B loads measured in machine code reach 95% of the bandwidth plateau at about 24–40 KiB/SM depending on loads per thread, with 64 KiB/SM enough rather than the minimum), its runtime still sits well above the bandwidth floor: inside the GPU kernel body, subtracting the 8.3 µs needed to stream the weights at steady-state bandwidth leaves about 3.6 µs (see the chart above). Four candidates account for that about 3.6 µs: first, first-byte and drain round-trip latency on a short 37.75 MB launch; second, lower post-opening average WWW bytes in flight once later loads sit interleaved with multiply-adds at 3–6 loads per thread (about 26–52 KiB/SM), keeping the time average below the opening peak (inferred from our Sections 3 and 5 steady-state comparisons to give up at most a few percent of plateau bandwidth; not measured separately); third, loading and unpacking the input vector xxx (16 KiB, hitting L1 at about 94%: in an auxiliary v7 check that passed xxx as a kernel argument—removing xxx loads and per-thread xxx unpacking while also letting the compiler hoist 12 loads of WWW instead of 8 and keep 9–12 loads outstanding at later issues instead of 3–6—event time dropped by 0.61 µs and profiler body time by 0.83 µs, so the xxx-only share was not measured and is inferred to apply qualitatively to v8); and fourth, per-CTA completion skew (measured on v7 across all 2,304 CTAs with %globaltimer: cross-SM start timestamps span about 0.16 µs—treated strictly as an estimate because sub-1 µs differences across SMs are uncalibrated; see Chapter 10, Section 5—whereas end timestamps spread from 7.71 µs at the 1st percentile to 12.64 µs at the max under the same cross-SM %globaltimer caveat in Chapter 10, Section 5, with the last 10% of CTAs taking 2.4 µs while DRAM sits under-used for reasons not determined; v8 was not timed per CTA, and how hardware assigns CTAs to SMs is undocumented and not measured). How much each of the four contributes inside v8 was not measured separately.

One last piece of bookkeeping: why is this gap about 2.8 µs when Primer 3, Section 5 quoted 4.6 µs? Because they measure two different things: 4.6 µs is the full event-timed duration of an empty kernel (including the empty kernel's own GPU execution), whereas about 2.8 µs here is v8's event timing minus its profiler kernel-body duration across two separate runs (mostly launch and event-recording overhead, plus an unseparated run-to-run machine and SM-clock difference; see Chapter 10, Section 1 for details).

Takeaway: An issue slot stays busy as long as at least 1 warp is eligible each cycle; a memory-bandwidth-bound kernel needs to saturate SM-wide bytes in flight by having each thread fire several independent wide loads back to back.

Next chapter's question: Once data lands in registers, we still have to unpack it and run multiply-add instructions; as the token count TTT grows from 1 to 8, which execution pipeline fills up first?
