Below 1 full wave, there are not enough bytes in flight to saturate HBM (see Chapter 2, Section 3): at low concurrency (decode 1-request full attention), 128 segments launch 128 CTAs — just 0.24 waves — and measured gather bandwidth crawls at about 1.3 TB/s; splitting into 256 segments (256 CTAs, 0.48 waves) keeps all CTAs within 1 wave while doubling in-flight reads, which makes execution faster.

At high concurrency, the math flips and we must split into fewer segments instead. Take decode 16-request full attention: keeping 128 segments launches 2,048 CTAs, or 3.88 waves; consolidating to 32 segments (512 CTAs, 0.97 waves) pulls the grid inside 1 wave, saving about 3 waves of entry/exit overhead and cutting the partial results read by the merge step to 1/4. Multiplying 3 waves × 6.6 µs predicts a maximum saving of about 20 µs, and the measured saving is about 12 µs; the source of the difference was not measured separately. Decode 32-request full attention and verify 16- and 32-request full attention likewise consolidate their segment counts, running faster by executing fewer waves or reading half as many partial results in the merge step (when the segment count drops to 16, the merge kernel also shrinks its launch from 4 warps to 2 warps; the time saved on each shape is shown in the chart below).

Full-attention verify at this stage uses the single-KV-head split kernel (one CTA computes one KV head, likewise placing 4 CTAs per SM, or 528 CTAs per wave). Consolidating verify 16-request full attention from 32 segments (1,024 CTAs, 1.94 waves) to 16 segments (512 CTAs, 0.97 waves) pulls it inside 1 wave, with most of the saving in the merge step (see the note in the chart below). Conversely, cutting verify 16-request full attention further from 16 segments down to 8 segments (256 CTAs, 0.48 waves) makes it much slower (see the note in the chart below). Our explanation (unverified): once all CTAs already fit within 1 wave, cutting further saves zero waves and only drops co-resident CTAs per SM from about 4 to about 2 — halving in-flight reads — while doubling the number of tiles each CTA processes serially.

Verify 1-request sliding window has a neat boundary quirk of its own: the latest of the 8 new tokens attends to 7 more keys than the earliest, so at most 2,048+7=2,0552{,}048 + 7 = 2{,}0552,048+7=2,055 keys are visible, requiring ⌈2,055/64⌉=33\lceil 2{,}055 / 64 \rceil = 33⌈2,055/64⌉=33 tiles of 64 keys — 1 more than 32. Originally, each KV head was split into 32 segments, forcing 17 CTAs to process 2 tiles serially each. We first switch to 64 segments per KV head: 33 segments process 1 tile each and the remaining 31 empty segments write only lsei=−∞\mathrm{lse}_i = -\inftylsei​=−∞, eliminating the serial wait for a second tile and saving about 1.10 µs (see the chart below). Later steps drop the empty segments to launch 33 single-tile CTAs per KV head (66 in total) and shrink the ring buffer here (see Chapter 3, Section 4) to 1 stage; those two steps were measured separately. The cost is that the merge step reads 33 (oi,lsei)(o_i, \mathrm{lse}_i)(oi​,lsei​) pairs.

Requests in the same batch often have different lengths: in this workload suite, historical lengths lie within ±7.5%\pm 7.5\%±7.5% of the mean, so the longest request is about 16% longer than the shortest (1.075/0.925≈1.161.075 / 0.925 \approx 1.161.075/0.925≈1.16). When segments are divided equally per request, CTAs for the longest request run about 16% longer than those for the shortest, holding up the last SMs at the tail. To fix this, we concatenate the keys of all requests into a single logical strip and partition it evenly across all CTAs by actual key count; the trade-off is that one segment may span two requests, requiring extra work in the merge step (measured results on verify appear in Section 7).

Prefill also needs to balance its tail, using a different kernel: each CTA has 1 producer warpgroup and 3 consumer warpgroups (Chapter 3, Sections 4 and 6). Each consumer warpgroup computes 64 query rows, so one CTA handles 24 tokens × 8\times\ 8× 8 query heads =192= 192=192 query rows for one KV head; its register usage allows only 1 CTA per SM, making 1 wave equal to 132 CTAs. At T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384, the grid launches ⌈16,384/24⌉×2=683×2=1,366\lceil 16{,}384 / 24 \rceil \times 2 = 683 \times 2 = 1{,}366⌈16,384/24⌉×2=683×2=1,366 query-tile CTAs in total.

Each of those 1,366 query-tile CTAs streams all KV entries visible to it from L2: 1,366 CTAs ×\times× an average of about 73,728 visible keys ×\times× 128 B per key per KV head, totaling about 12.9 GB. H200's L2 peak bandwidth is unpublished: at the 7.33 TB/s re-read rate measured in the residency-hint microbenchmark of Chapter 2, Section 4, streaming through once takes about 1.76 ms; using the 16-bit MMA loop of unpooler at T=128T = 128T=128 from Chapter 6 (where 128 CTAs read about 67.11 MB of weights in 16.17 µs at about 4.15 TB/s while re-reading twice that volume of input tiles from L2 into shared memory, for an estimated total of about 12.4 TB/s), it takes about 1.0 ms. Either figure is shorter than the 2.50 ms dense FP8 compute lower bound from Section 1, so prefill remains compute-bound.

We launch the 683 CTAs of each KV head in descending order of work from heaviest to lightest. As explained in Chapter 2, Section 1, CTAs do not switch in lockstep waves — as soon as an SM frees a slot, the next CTA is dispatched; under the causal mask, earlier query tiles attend to fewer keys and do less work, so the last CTAs dispatched onto SMs are the lightest 40 query tiles (40 CTAs). Once the dispatch queue drains, SMs that finish early sit idle waiting for this last batch of CTAs to complete. Splitting each KV head's lightest 40 query tiles into 4 segments along the key dimension (40 and 4 were tuned empirically) expands the grid to (683−40+40×4)×2=1,606(683 - 40 + 40\times 4) \times 2 = 1{,}606(683−40+40×4)×2=1,606 CTAs. We pay the entry/exit and merge overhead of 240 extra CTAs, and in return the final batch of CTAs takes only 1/4 of the original time, letting the tail SMs finish earlier and saving 345 µs at 65K history (see the chart below).

What if we replace static key-count balancing with dynamic claiming, where each CTA claims its next tile from a global counter? In measured runs, that is actually slower (about 23 µs slower on verify 32-request full attention). Every claimed 64-key tile adds a metadata handoff and a 128-thread intra-CTA barrier, raising the measured per-tile cost by about 10% while breaking the pipeline that prefetches the next tile's page-table entries (see Section 6). At the same time, static imbalance is at most about 16% to begin with and is already tiny once we split evenly by key count, so dynamic claiming has very little ceiling left to recover.

With a fixed segment count, short requests or sliding-window boundaries can also produce empty segments (start ≥\ge≥ end). On shapes that enable empty-segment skipping, an empty segment writes only lsei=−∞\mathrm{lse}_i = -\inftylsei​=−∞ and skips writing an all-zero output. Because 2−∞=02^{-\infty} = 02−∞=0, the formula in Section 3 still holds, and when the merge step sees −∞-\infty−∞, it skips that segment directly. We did not measure the time saved by skipping empty segments separately.

No single combination of kernel and split count wins across all shapes, so a1 looks up a per-shape table. At this stage, decode sliding window and verify sliding window both use the single-KV-head mma.sync split kernel (one CTA computes one KV head; register usage sets 3–4 CTAs per SM). Decode full attention uses the two-KV-head split kernel described earlier in this section. Per-shape table lookup cuts the 6-workload geometric mean defined in Section 1 by about 8%; because this version also switched several kernels at the same time, not all 8% comes from table lookup alone (the final kernel assignment for each shape appears at the end of Section 12).

5a1 → a2 (Part 1): When Two KV Heads Share the Same 128 B K Row, How Should the Two Halves Be Read?

Launching the two CTAs that read the two halves of the same row back-to-back saves ~12 µs on 32-request full-attention verification; having a single CTA gather the full 128 B row raises gather bandwidth by 30%–50%+ in an isolated gather microbenchmark.

Because the page table scatters each token into an arbitrary page slot, the kernel sees a stream of random addresses. TMA multidimensional tensor copies cannot follow a page table. That leaves two options: each thread issues 16 B cp.async instructions, or each row gets one 128 B 1D bulk copy, cp.async.bulk (see Chapter 3, Section 3 for the four paths). The decode and verify kernels in this chapter gather row by row with 16 B cp.async. One token's K row is 128 B wide (see Section 1): 8 threads issuing one 16 B cp.async each can gather the full 128 B row at once, whereas the single-KV-head split kernel has only 4 threads issue one instruction each to fetch only the 64 B half-row for its own head. In an isolated gather-only microbenchmark, gathering the full 128 B row at once hits about 4 TB/s of random-row gather bandwidth — about 30% to 50%+ faster than gathering two 64 B half-rows separately (see the chart below).

The lightest fix is to reorder the grid dimensions so that two CTAs with adjacent blockIdx values handle the two KV heads of the same token segment: launching them back-to-back places the reads of the two halves of the same row right next to each other in time (see Chapter 2, Section 2; whether the second read hits L2 was not measured, only the latency). This relies on the measured behavior from Chapter 2, Section 1 — H200 dispatches CTAs in increasing blockIdx order. It takes zero registers and zero shared memory, at the cost of depending on an unspecified dispatch order; even if that dispatch order changes, the numerical result is still right. On verify 32-request full attention, this saves about 12 µs (and leaves verify 16-request full attention unchanged).

In the decode (L=1L = 1L=1) kernel, the two KV heads of one token together have only 2×8=162 \times 8 = 162×8=16 query rows, so a small 4-warp (128-thread) CTA using mma.sync can compute both heads together. Having one CTA gather the full 128 B row into shared memory — applying a 128 B XOR swizzle on write to avoid bank conflicts (see Chapter 3, Section 7) — lets both heads read from the same buffer. Capping each CTA at 128 registers per thread and 48 KiB of shared memory (3 buffer slots ×\times× 8 KiB each for K and V) places 4 CTAs per SM (the same as in Section 4, before the full-row gather); at the cost of an extra shared-memory buffer shared by the two heads, this saves about 16 µs on decode 32-request full attention.

In verify (L=8L = 8L=8), a single KV head already has 64 query rows and must use wgmma. So full-attention verify switches to a 3-warpgroup (384-thread) two-KV-head fusion (merging 2 KV heads per CTA) kernel: 1 producer warpgroup gathers one full K row and one full V row (256 B in total) per token and feeds 2 consumer warpgroups, one per KV head (for warp specialization, see Chapter 3, Section 4). That saves about 5 µs on verify 32-request full attention (see the chart below). Sliding-window verify uses a sliding-window single-KV-head wgmma kernel, where each CTA computes one KV head with 1 producer warpgroup and 1 consumer warpgroup. Replacing the single-KV-head mma.sync split kernel with it makes verify 16- and 32-request sliding window faster (see the note in the chart below). In both wgmma verify kernels, each consumer warpgroup feeds one head at a time to wgmma (K-extent D=64D = 64D=64 FP8 bytes =64= 64=64 B; the two-KV-head fusion kernel stores each 128 B row as two 64 B per-head blocks), so Q and K in shared memory use Hopper's 64 B swizzle mode per head (XORing 16 B chunks by (row÷2) mod 4(\text{row} \div 2) \bmod 4(row÷2)mod4, repeating every 512 B; see Chapter 3, Section 7) and set the matching wgmma descriptor mode, whereas only V converted to 16-bit (128 B per row) keeps the 128 B swizzle. The trade-off of two-KV-head fusion is that the total CTA count is cut in half and each SM holds only 2 CTAs. What if we copy this heavy 384-thread two-KV-head fusion structure over to token-by-token decode (L=1L = 1L=1)? Decode 16- and 32-request full attention run about twice as slow (see the note in the chart below). Our explanation (unverified): the 128-thread small CTA places 4 CTAs per SM whereas the 384-thread heavy structure places only 2, cutting in-flight gather reads per SM in half; at L=1L = 1L=1, 56 of the 64 rows in wgmma are also padding.

The half-row versus full-row bandwidth chart above came from a standalone microbenchmark that only does gather. The gather microbenchmark below copies the structure of the two-KV-head fusion kernel: 2 CTAs per SM, 1 producer warpgroup gathering into a shared-memory ring buffer, and consumer warpgroups that simply return ring slots without doing any compute. When we measure its gather bandwidth with a real page table, even laying out all addresses completely contiguously saves only a little over 10% of the gather time (see the chart below). Next, inside the real verify kernel, we turn off the consumers' matrix multiplies and softmax and leave only the producer gathering KV (which we call the producer-only microbenchmark below): runtime is still 92%–94% of the full kernel, so the kernel really is bottlenecked on gather. This two-KV-head fusion gather microbenchmark achieves lower bandwidth than the standalone microbenchmark; how much of that drop comes from having fewer bytes in flight was not measured separately.

6a1 → a2 (Part 2): When Reading Each KV Page Requires a Three-Hop Pointer Chain First, How Do We Hide That Wait?

Preloading the first 4 page-table tiles before the loop and prefetching 2 iterations ahead with even/odd register pairs to avoid copying pending loads aims to hide the page-table lookup round trip inside the pipeline; issuing sequence-length and page-table loads concurrently at batch size 1 saves a measured ~0.26 µs on decode 1-request full attention.

When each page holds only 1 token, reading a single KV row has to walk a three-hop pointer chain first: Hop 1 reads seq_lens[b], Hop 2 uses the resulting logical page index to read page_table[b, i], and Hop 3 uses the physical page slot to compute addr=base+slot×128\mathrm{addr} = \mathrm{base} + \mathrm{slot} \times 128addr=base+slot×128, fire the first cp.async, and wait for the KV data to land. On the lightly loaded verify 1-request full-attention shape, the measured time from launch until the first tile's data lands is about 2.4 µs (see Figure 7-6 Mode 1 for the duration of each hop); this 2.4 µs is entry latency, distinct from the 6.6 µs full-load overhead in Section 4. Where does that wait land? Right on the integer multiply-add instruction that first computes a memory address from the physical page slot: the profiler shows that warps at this instruction stall mostly on the scoreboard waiting for the page-table load to return (accounting for 37%–42% of stall sampling share, defined in Chapter 10, Section 7; for the scoreboard, see Chapter 4, Section 2). The multi-slot ring buffer from Chapter 3, Section 4 can hide data transfer latency, but it cannot hide address latency — cp.async cannot issue until the address is known.

To pull that per-tile page-table round trip off the critical path, we prefetch page-table entries ahead and separate each load from its use. In global memory, page_table is int32 throughout (64 entries = 256 B per tile). The first revision bundles three changes into one build: first, registers hold two in-flight int32 page-entry vectors instead of precomputed int64 slot offsets plus masks, forming the int64 slot offset only when cp.async issues (compiling with 0 spills, whereas an earlier trial holding three int32 vectors hit 128 registers with 2 spills; how many registers this saved relative to the prior int64 slot + mask form was not measured); second, Tiles 0..3 are preloaded into registers before the wait call with the L1 evict_last hint (ld.global.L1::evict_last, asking L1 to evict these entries last, which PTX treats as a performance hint only); third, loop iteration jjj uses ready page entries to issue cp.async for Tile j+2j+2j+2 (keeping two tiles in flight inside the 3-slot ring buffer; small decode CTAs track cp.async completion by group via commit_group / wait_group, whereas producer-consumer verify rings signal slot readiness via cp.async.mbarrier.arrive, see Chapter 3, Sections 3 and 5) while issuing the page-table load for Tile j+4j+4j+4. In 60-round V1c paired runs, this three-part build saves 0.99–1.58 µs on decode 16-request full attention (individual shares among the three parts were not measured separately; the 0.18–0.26 µs delta on decode 1-request full attention sits inside the 0.4 µs noise band, and decode 32-request full attention is within noise). Yet its 3-way unrolled loop still rotated registers across loop-latch joins by copying pending LDG results: on the version right before the next unroll change, the profiler found on decode 32-request full attention that 20 of the 36 loop-latch copies read pending page-table loads, with the top 3 stall instructions alone accounting for 20.0% of all stalls (the combined share across all 20 copies was not tallied separately, at least 20.0%; the stall share on the first revision itself was not measured), serializing the prefetch again. A follow-up revision unrolls the loop by 6 and alternates the two page-entry register vectors in place on even and odd iterations, eliminating pending-load copies (post-change stall share not measured) and giving page_table for Tile j+4j+4j+4 a full 2-iteration code distance before iteration j+2j+2j+2 consumes it; in 60-round V1c runs, decode 1-request full attention shifts by 0.08–0.16 µs (inside the 0.4 µs noise band), while decode 16- and 32-request full attention save 0.34–0.48 µs and 0.70–0.86 µs (passing the paired gate at margins comparable to identical-code file-copy bias). Other lookahead depths were not measured separately.

For a single request, we can also avoid waiting on the sequence length. The kernel launch parameters already include the page-table column count max_pages (Section 1); at B=1B = 1B=1, this usually equals the request's own page count, though the page table may also be pre-allocated to a larger cap, so seq_lens[0] must still be read. For 1-request decode, the kernel computes the segment range from max_pages first and issues the page-table loads for the first 4 tiles concurrently with seq_lens[0]; once seq_lens[0] returns, it verifies before actual use whether the true range matches (re-reading only on a mismatch; the check itself has zero measured cost). Turning three hops into two saves a measured ~0.26 µs on decode 1-request full attention in high-round S-series paired runs (95% CI [−0.272,−0.240][-0.272, -0.240][−0.272,−0.240] µs, clearing the identical-code replica spread and winning across two independent paired runs; see the chart below), and applies only to B=1B = 1B=1. On verify 1-request full attention there is no gain: starting at Tile 3, the producer must wait for the consumer to free a ring-buffer slot, so the small head start won at entry is absorbed by Tile 3.

Push prefetching past the register limit, however, and it turns into a loss. In the two-KV-head fusion verify kernel of Section 7, the producer has only 32 registers at runtime (setmaxnreg cuts it to 32 in Section 7; see Chapter 3, Section 6 for the mechanism), so it prefetches only the page slots of the next tile (Tile j+1j+1j+1). Increase that prefetch distance, and the extra in-flight page slots no longer fit in registers and spill to local memory (see Chapter 3, Section 1): verify 32-request full attention gets about 2.4%–2.6% slower instead (raw log not verified).

Prefetching across the memory-queue boundary brings no gain either. The preceding prologue kernel writes only q and K/V for the new tokens of this pass. The old historical pages were written earlier and are already ready before the wait call, so we could kick off main-loop prefetching early — yet measured runs show no gain (0.13–0.56 µs slower, paired round count not recorded; see the chart below). The reason is probably queueing delay: those non-critical requests enter the memory request queue first (where along the memory path the bottleneck sits was not measured), ahead of the critical Tile 0 requests, making Tile 0 wait longer.

Prefetching across the L2 residency boundary brings no gain either. Hardware L2 prefetch instructions (cp.async.bulk.prefetch.L2 for a single-thread contiguous byte span, or per-thread cache-line prefetch.global.L2; see Appendix B, Quick Reference 2) only pull data from HBM into L2 without bringing it into the SM. If we issue one before the wait call to prefetch the page table, those prefetched lines may be evicted by KV data streaming through L2 before they are used, forcing a second read from HBM; in 60-round V1c paired runs, this is 0.03–0.53 µs slower (with the 0.03 µs lower end inside the 0.4 µs noise band; see the chart below).

7a2 → a3: Once Multi-Token Attention Enters wgmma, How Do the Producer and Two Consumer Warpgroups Split Registers and Stagger the Pipeline?

Making the producer warpgroup the Gluon warp_specialize default partition (run directly by the 4 launch warps) and computing addresses after role splitting leaves no live variable across setmaxnreg.dec, enabling unmasked loop peeling to compile at zero spills; two named barriers then stagger the two consumer warpgroups by half a step on the Tensor Core.

Inside the "two-KV-head fusion" kernel used for verify, one CTA packs 3 warpgroups totaling 384 threads — 1 producer warpgroup plus 2 four-warp consumer warpgroups; the query tiles Q0, Q1 :  [64,  64]  FP8\shape{Q_0,\ Q_1}{64,\;64}{FP8}Q0​, Q1​:[64,64]FP8 for the two KV heads stay resident in shared memory, and the producer gathers 256 B per token into the ring buffer (see Section 5). At compile time, we allocate 80 registers per thread, so one CTA uses 384×80=30,720384 \times 80 = 30{,}720384×80=30,720 registers and the 65,536 registers of one SM can hold at most 2 CTAs (for residency, see Chapter 3, Section 1); at runtime, setmaxnreg trims the producer to 32 registers per thread and hands the freed registers to the two consumer warpgroups, raising each consumer thread to 104 registers (128×32+256×104=30,720128 \times 32 + 256 \times 104 = 30{,}720128×32+256×104=30,720; see Chapter 3, Section 6).

Register usage sets residency, and residency sets how many CTAs fit in 1 wave: at 2 CTAs per SM, 1 wave is 2×132=2642 \times 132 = 2642×132=264 CTAs. So verify 32-request full attention launches 264 CTAs directly. Following Section 4, it concatenates the key tiles of all requests into one logical strip, inserts 5 virtual tiles between every two adjacent requests to stand for the cost of crossing a request boundary, and splits the strip evenly across the 264 CTAs by tile count to fill 1 wave exactly. This step saves about 3.7 µs (see the chart below). The trade-off is that a segment may span two requests, so the merge step has extra work to do.

Remember from Section 5 that the producer-only microbenchmark accounts for 92%–94% of total runtime, so any slowdown in the producer directly drags down the entire kernel. To avoid register spills in the producer, one invariant has to hold: every value still live when setmaxnreg.dec executes must fit inside the reduced register budget. At this stage the kernel is written in Gluon (see Chapter 6, Section 8), and gl.warp_specialize assigns the warpgroup roles. The default partition runs directly on the 4 launch warps, outside the worker dispatch loop, and takes the remainder of the CTA register pool. The worker partitions sit inside a worker dispatch loop that the compiler generates, each with an explicit register target. Before splitting out the unmasked loop, the shipped baseline made the producer a worker partition (trimmed to 24 registers at runtime by setmaxnreg.dec 24, with 112 and 104 for the two consumers) at 0 spills; yet whenever unmasked loop peeling was added onto that worker-producer layout, the compiler hoisted a loop-invariant producer KV-row address above the worker dispatch loop so it stayed live across setmaxnreg.dec 24, overflowed 24 registers, and spilled 8 B to local memory (see Chapter 3, Section 1), adding a local-memory load wait on each use — so those candidates were rejected. The fix makes the producer the default partition and the two consumer warpgroups worker partitions (104 registers each). The producer now runs outside the dispatch loop and gets the remainder of the register pool: 384×80/128−2×104=32384 \times 80 / 128 - 2 \times 104 = 32384×80/128−2×104=32 registers, i.e., setmaxnreg.dec 32. Segment bounds and addresses are built after role splitting, so no live variable crosses setmaxnreg.dec and the peeled unmasked loop compiles with 0 spills (the later CUDA C++ rewrite likewise keeps this setup inside each role branch):

// Unshipped loop-peel candidate (illustrative): producer is a worker partition (dec 24; unpeeled base has 0 spills), peeling hoists address above dispatch loop, crossing dec 24 and spilling 8 B
if (wg_id > 0) { /* the two warpgroups get 112 and 104 */ consumer_loop(); }
else           { setmaxnreg_dec<24>();  producer_loop(); }

// Shipped fix: producer is the default partition (32 remaining registers, outside the dispatch loop); bounds and addresses are built after role splitting, peeled loop keeps 0 spills
if (wg_id == 0) { setmaxnreg_dec<32>();  producer_loop(); }
else            { setmaxnreg_inc<104>(); consumer_loop(); }

On verify 32-request full attention, comparing this combined "producer as default partition + unmasked loop peel" build against the 0-spill unpeeled baseline keeps local-memory spills at 0 and saves about 15.8 µs (we did not measure the two changes separately). Splitting out the unmasked loop means that key tiles that fall completely inside the visible range run a tight main loop without mask checks, and only the last few tiles run a masked tail loop. We measured that split alone on verify 16-request full attention, in the single-KV-head verify kernel, where it saves about 3.4 µs (see the chart below). The catch: whether the producer spills depends on the compiler's dispatch structure and on which variables stay live across setmaxnreg.dec. Change the partition order or the compiler version, and you must recheck the disassembly.

Inside that same CTA loop, scalars that are identical across all 32 threads of a warp — such as the ring-buffer slot index, phase bit, and matrix descriptor — can live in a uniform register (UR), a scalar register shared across the entire warp (see Figure 7-7 Mode 4, shown on the prefill kernel). A general-purpose vector register stores one copy of the same value per thread, which takes 32 register slots across the warp. A uniform register stores a single copy for the whole warp, and uniform-datapath instructions compute on it. Both forms issue once per instruction; what UR saves is vector register capacity and vector pipeline occupancy. ptxas decides which variables go into UR; source code cannot specify this directly. The limitation is that uniform registers hold only values identical across all 32 lanes of a warp, and the per-warp uniform-register limit bounds them. The latency gain was not measured separately on this kernel.

Now look at what happens inside each loop iteration: a consumer warpgroup first issues the wgmma for Q⋅K⊤Q \cdot K^{\top}Q⋅K⊤, then runs the elementwise softmax operations (on the ALU/FMA and SFU pipelines), and then issues P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V (for P, see Section 3). Because every KV tile starts a fresh score tile from scratch, the first Q⋅K⊤Q \cdot K^{\top}Q⋅K⊤ wgmma passes predicate scale-d = 0 to write D=A⋅BD = A \cdot BD=A⋅B directly without reading old accumulator values (wgmma.fence is still required before the first issue; see Chapter 5, Section 5). If both consumer warpgroups execute the same phase at the same time, they fight over the Tensor Core simultaneously and then leave it idle simultaneously. We stagger them with two named barriers (see Chapter 5, Section 7): each barrier synchronizes the 256 threads of the two consumer warpgroups, while the producer warpgroup in the same CTA does not participate. A named barrier provides two instructions: bar.arrive adds 128 to the arrival count without blocking so the calling warpgroup keeps running, whereas bar.sync adds 128 to the arrival count and blocks until the count reaches 256. Two named barriers (Barrier 0 and Barrier 1) stagger the two consumer warpgroups by half a step in three moves:

  1. Before entering the loop, the 128 threads of Group 1 issue a non-blocking bar.arrive on Barrier 0. Next, the 128 threads of Group 0 execute bar.sync on Barrier 0, bringing the arrival count to 128+128=256128 + 128 = 256128+128=256 so Group 0 passes immediately and starts the first MMA stage [Q⋅K(0)][Q\cdot K(0)][Q⋅K(0)]; meanwhile, the 128 threads of Group 1 execute bar.sync on Barrier 1, where only 128 threads have arrived so far, causing Group 1 to wait at Barrier 1.
  2. Once Group 0 issues its MMA window and waits with wait_group<0> until all matrix multiplications in that window complete, its 128 threads issue a non-blocking bar.arrive on Barrier 1, bringing Barrier 1's arrival count to 256 to release Group 1 before Group 0 moves on to compute softmax.
  3. From then on, the two groups alternate: once the matrix multiplications in its combined MMA window [P⋅V(j), Q⋅K(j+1)][P\cdot V(j),\ Q\cdot K(j+1)][P⋅V(j), Q⋅K(j+1)] complete, each group issues bar.arrive on the other group's barrier to release it and moves on to softmax; before its next MMA window, it executes bar.sync on its own barrier to wait until the other group arrives and brings the count to 256.

We pay one extra 256-thread barrier synchronization per iteration and serialize the MMA issue windows of the two groups; in return, we save about 2.3 µs on verify 32-request full attention (see the chart below). Conversely, locking only the Q⋅KQ \cdot KQ⋅K segment instead of combining [P⋅V(j), Q⋅K(j+1)][P\cdot V(j),\ Q\cdot K(j+1)][P⋅V(j), Q⋅K(j+1)] into a single window adds extra per-iteration waiting that slows verify 32-request full attention by about 4.5–4.8 µs.

8a3 → a4: When the Softmax Between the Two Matrix Multiplications Accounts for Over Half the Instructions, How Do We Lighten It?

After RMSNorm, the base-2 attention scores have a bounded upper limit so BF16 weights cannot overflow, allowing per-tile rescaling to be skipped entirely and row sums to be offloaded onto the idle Tensor Core.

An SMSP can issue only 1 instruction per cycle (see Chapter 4, Section 1). Look at the compiled 64-key loop of the verify kernel: it takes 288 machine instructions in total, and softmax accounts for 58% of them — the intra-tile maximum reduction, ex2 to compute α\alphaα, multiplying every element of OOO by α\alphaα, and the row-sum reduction (from disassembly counts at the time; raw disassembly not kept and not verified). The 4 warps of the producer warpgroup sit across the 4 SMSPs (this book assumes so; NVIDIA documentation does not state how warps map to SMSPs; see Chapter 4, Section 1). So they share each SMSP's 1-instruction-per-cycle issue slot with the warps of the two consumer warpgroups, and every instruction a consumer avoids issuing is one fewer cycle in which a producer cp.async can be blocked from issuing. In Section 5, the producer-only microbenchmark accounted for 92%–94% of total runtime; part of the remaining about 6%–8% is the cost of consumers occupying issue slots and delaying producer cp.async instructions.

Rescaling on every tile in Section 3 existed solely to prevent 2s−m2^{s-m}2s−m from overflowing. After unweighted RMSNorm, each row has a root mean square of 1, so a 64-dimensional vector has Euclidean length 64=8\sqrt{64} = 864​=8; RoPE is a rotation and preserves length. Across all versions in this chapter, the prologue kernel finishes RMSNorm and RoPE in FP32 before casting q and k directly to FP8 E4M3, and historical keys in the cache were written the same way: with a 3-bit mantissa, round-to-nearest has a relative error of at most 2−42^{-4}2−4, which stretches vector length by at most a factor of 1.06251.06251.0625. Because the dot product of two vectors cannot exceed the product of their lengths (the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality), ∣q⋅k∣≤8×8×1.06252=72.25|q\cdot k| \le 8 \times 8 \times 1.0625^2 = 72.25∣q⋅k∣≤8×8×1.06252=72.25; multiplying by 0.6840.6840.684 and then by log⁡2e\log_2 elog2​e gives: ∣s∣≤72.25×0.684×1.4427≈71.3|s| \le 72.25 \times 0.684 \times 1.4427 \approx 71.3∣s∣≤72.25×0.684×1.4427≈71.3 That is a worst-case upper bound, not a statistical estimate. It requires every historical key to have been written by this chapter's prologue, so that each key has a root mean square of exactly 1. FP8 subnormal components with ∣x∣<2−6|x| < 2^{-6}∣x∣<2−6 round with an absolute error of at most 2−102^{-10}2−10, which raises the worst-case bound by about another 0.1. The standalone operator benchmark synthesizes historical keys directly from standard normal random numbers, with no per-key normalization. So on those synthetic inputs the bound is not a strict guarantee, though actual dot products stay far below it.

Like FP32, BF16 has an 8-bit exponent with an upper limit of about 21282^{128}2128. When the weights P are stored in BF16 and we compute p=2min⁡(s, 72)p = 2^{\min(s,\ 72)}p=2min(s, 72) directly, the largest value is only 2722^{72}272. Since 80,000≈216.380{,}000 \approx 2^{16.3}80,000≈216.3, summing across all 80,000 keys reaches at most about 2882^{88}288, which fits in the FP32 denominator; the smallest value, 2−71.32^{-71.3}2−71.3, also sits well above the smallest normal BF16 number (about 2−1262^{-126}2−126). So we do not need a reference maximum at all: the per-tile max reduction, α\alphaα, and the rescaling of OOO all disappear. That saves about 6.7 µs on verify 32-request full attention (see the chart below). The trade-off is that we now depend on the upper bound above: it holds only along the "unweighted RMSNorm + FP8 rounding" path, and must be re-derived if the model or data type changes. Because that bound sits below 72, the clamp at 72 never triggers and acts only as a safety guard. The baseline runs RMSNorm and RoPE inside one prologue kernel, writes BF16 out, and then converts to FP8 in subsequent kernels. What if we used this no-rescaling scheme on that baseline numerical path? On the 46 sliding-window layers that run RoPE, q and k are rounded to BF16 once in registers after RMSNorm and rounded to BF16 a second time when written out after RoPE, adding two extra BF16 roundings that push the upper bound up to about 72.4. At that point, the clamp at 72 may trigger; once it does, the output changes silently. Full-attention layers skip RoPE, so they add only one extra BF16 rounding on writeback, with an upper bound of about 71.9.

Next, we move the row-sum reduction onto the Tensor Core. We first did this in the single-KV-head full-attention verify kernel, where it shipped in one commit with two other changes to save about 2.6 µs on verify 16-request full attention (no standalone number was recorded in the changelog); the sliding-window single-KV-head wgmma kernel copied from it carried this over, whereas the two-KV-head fusion verify kernel still summed in registers at this stage until folding the row sum into a single FP8 wgmma.m64n72k32 instruction in Section 10. Each tile's contribution to the denominator lll is the row sum of P, which equals P×1P \times \mathbf{1}P×1. Doing that sum on the ALU/FMA pipeline takes 38 additions plus 4 warp shuffles (from disassembly counts at the time; raw disassembly not kept and not verified). Why 4 shuffles? Because in the MMA accumulator fragment layout, each row sits across the 4 consecutive lanes of a quad (see Chapter 5, Section 3), so summing within each quad takes 2 XOR shuffles per row across the 2 rows held per thread. Instead, we place a constant all-ones matrix in shared memory and issue 4 wgmma.m64n8k16 instructions (64 keys =4×k16= 4 \times k16=4×k16, FP16 input; see Chapter 5, Section 3), saving a net 38 instructions per tile at the cost of extra Tensor Core cycles and an all-ones block in shared memory. This only works if the Tensor Core has idle cycles: this kernel is bottlenecked on gather and issue slots. Section 9 covers how the FP8 version uses it.

The final version removes the Tensor Core row-sum reduction from both single-KV-head wgmma verify kernels (verify 1-request full attention and verify sliding window, Section 5) and goes back to in-register accumulation. Measured inside the same build as a module-consolidation rewrite, the delta is about 0.26 µs on verify 32-request sliding window and about 0.13 µs on verify 1-request full attention (paired round count and noise band not recorded, and the standalone net gain was not measured separately; see the chart below); on which workloads it would become a loss was not measured. Inferring from the pipeline rules of Chapters 4 and 5, offloading row sums onto the Tensor Core pays off only when the ALU/FMA pipeline saturates first while the Tensor Core still has idle capacity.

One more attempt brings zero gain: using the half-precision paired instruction ex2.approx.f16x2 in hopes of halving SFU time. Because the Hopper SFU executes scalar operations one lane at a time (see Chapter 5, Section 1), the compiler expands this instruction into 2 MUFU.EX2.F16 instructions plus 1 byte-permute PRMT (we read this from the disassembly at the time and did not keep the record; for PTX-to-SASS translation, see Chapter 6, Section 5). That saves zero SFU time and adds 1 extra instruction: zero gain.

9a4 → a5 (Part 1): After Compressing the Weight Matrix P to 1-Byte FP8, How Do We Compute Exponentials Quickly Without Overflowing?

Leaving exponent headroom triggers rescaling via a warp-vote instruction only when a tile exceeds the threshold, and computes E4M3 bytes directly on the FMA/ALU pipelines via the linear approximation 8(y+7)8(y+7)8(y+7).

To run the P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V multiplication in the next section on the FP8 Tensor Core, we first have to store P in E4M3. The catch is that the upper bound of E4M3 is only 448 (see Section 1), and when the exponent field is all zeros its value is (j/8)⋅21−7(j/8)\cdot 2^{1-7}(j/8)⋅21−7 (where jjj is the 3-bit mantissa value) with a minimum positive subnormal value of 2−92^{-9}2−9 (for subnormal numbers, see Chapter 6, Section 3) — so P must be scaled into this narrow range.

Rescaling historical accumulators only when a tile threatens to overflow is called lazy rescaling. Keeping the row maximum of Tile 0 as the reference mrefm_{ref}mref​, we write the weights as P′=2 8−τ⋅2 s−mrefP' = 2^{\,8-\tau}\cdot 2^{\,s-m_{ref}}P′=28−τ⋅2s−mref​ where τ\tauτ is the headroom reserved for lazy rescaling (a base-2 exponent). As long as a new tile's maximum satisfies mtile≤mref+τm_{tile} \le m_{ref} + \taumtile​≤mref​+τ, we have P′≤28−τ⋅2τ=256<448P' \le 2^{8-\tau}\cdot 2^{\tau} = 256 < 448P′≤28−τ⋅2τ=256<448, so it cannot overflow and mrefm_{ref}mref​, OOO, and lll remain untouched. On each iteration, the entire warp executes just one vote instruction: __any_sync(…, m_tile > m_ref + τ). Here __any_sync asks all 32 threads (lanes) of a warp whether the condition holds for any lane; if even one lane is true, every lane receives true. Only when some row exceeds the threshold does the warp update mrefm_{ref}mref​ and multiply by α\alphaα. Because E4M3 has a narrow range and every tile must check whether mtilem_{tile}mtile​ exceeds the threshold, each thread again has to find the maximum of its own scores on every tile; the cross-thread warp-shuffle reduction runs only on Tile 0 and when the vote is true. The other costs are one vote instruction and the occasional rescaling (when no row exceeds the threshold, computing α\alphaα and rescaling OOO are still skipped). At τ=4\tau = 4τ=4, the per-tile trigger rate is only 7%–18%; relaxing it to τ=6\tau = 6τ=6 saves another ~1.4 µs on verify 32-request full attention.

However, the headroom τ\tauτ also has a bound at the other end: the larger τ\tauτ is, the smaller 28−τ2^{8-\tau}28−τ becomes, and the sooner small weights drop below 2−102^{-10}2−10 (half of the smallest subnormal 2−92^{-9}2−9) and round to 0. In the two-KV-head fusion verify kernel, before adopting τ=6\tau = 6τ=6 we tried pushing τ\tauτ directly from 4 to 8: that caused too many small weights to underflow, pushing the output error beyond the numerical tolerance (the maximum error allowed relative to the reference implementation; see Chapter 10, Section 4), so it was rejected (even though it ran about 3.7 µs faster). Yet the same τ=8\tau = 8τ=8 passes inside the sliding-window single-KV-head wgmma kernel (Section 5) and saves about 0.83 µs (see the chart below). One possible explanation is that full-attention layers attend to about 80,000 visible keys (versus at most 2,055 in sliding-window layers), so more small weights get flushed to 0; why one kernel exceeds the tolerance while the other passes was not determined.

In prefill, the bottleneck shifts to the SFU. The SFU accepts only 1 warp instruction every 8 cycles — an issue interval 8× that of FMA (see Chapter 5, Section 1); in the 128-key loop, each consumer warp issues 66 MUFU.EX2 instructions per tile, driving SFU pipeline utilization to 77.3%. Because softmax sits right between the two matrix multiplications, any slowdown on the SFU directly delays the start of the subsequent P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V stage.

How can we offload the exponential from the SFU? Look at the E4M3 byte code of the target weight 2y2^{y}2y: it is approximately a linear function of yyy (see Chapter 6, Section 3 for the bit fields). Write the base-2 exponent yyy as an integer part plus a fractional part, y=n+fy = n + fy=n+f (0≤f<10 \le f < 10≤f<1): the 4-bit exponent field holds n+7n + 7n+7, which shifted left by 3 bits gives 8(n+7)8(n+7)8(n+7); the 3-bit mantissa field uses the linear approximation 2f≈1+f2^{f} \approx 1 + f2f≈1+f to hold 8f8f8f. Combined, the byte code is c≈8(y+7)c \approx 8(y + 7)c≈8(y+7). Let's check one byte by hand: take y=2.5y = 2.5y=2.5 (n=2, f=0.5n = 2,\ f = 0.5n=2, f=0.5), which gives 8(2.5+7)=768(2.5+7) = 768(2.5+7)=76, or 0100 1100 in binary. Here the exponent field is 1001 =9=2+7= 9 = 2 + 7=9=2+7 and the mantissa field is 100 =4=8×0.5= 4 = 8 \times 0.5=4=8×0.5; decoding gives 22×(1+4/8)=62^{2}\times(1 + 4/8) = 622×(1+4/8)=6, compared with the exact value 22.5≈5.662^{2.5} \approx 5.6622.5≈5.66. For normal weights 2y≥2−62^y \ge 2^{-6}2y≥2−6, the worst-case relative error is only about 6% (at f≈0.44f \approx 0.44f≈0.44, 1.441.441.44 versus 1.361.361.36), which is on the same order as the 3-bit mantissa rounding error of E4M3 itself (at most 6.25%); below 2−62^{-6}2−6 the error grows larger, and below 2−72^{-7}2−7 the byte code goes negative and is clamped to 0.

Because c=8(y+7)c = 8(y+7)c=8(y+7) is a linear function, there is no need to queue on the SFU — we can compute the byte directly on the FMA and ALU pipelines. To encode every 4 values, we first use a saturating multiply-add FFMA.SAT (where .SAT clamps the result to [0,1][0, 1][0,1], clamping negative byte codes to 0 right here) to compute the normalized value u=(y+7)/15∈[0,1]u = (y+7)/15 \in [0, 1]u=(y+7)/15∈[0,1]. Next, cvt.rn.f16x2.f32 converts into a half-precision pair (f16x2), and a half-precision multiply-add computes 1024+120u=1024+c1024 + 120u = 1024 + c1024+120u=1024+c. Because half-precision FP16 (bit layout in Section 2) has an exact unit step size of 1 on the interval [1024,2048)[1024, 2048)[1024,2048), the integer c∈[0,120]c \in [0, 120]c∈[0,120] lands directly in the low 8 mantissa bits of the FP16 value. After register moves (MOV), PRMT packs the 4 low bytes into a 32-bit word: every 4 values issue 9 to 10 instructions in total (the exact breakdown by instruction type was not measured). This step cuts MUFU.EX2 instructions per tile from 66 down to 2 (see the Figure 7-9 readout for the change in SFU utilization), and the profiler measures about an 18% latency reduction on the full-attention kernel at 65K prefill history (see the third chart at the end of the chapter). The trade-off is that every 4 weights consume 9–10 issue slots — 5–6 more issue slots than the original 4 MUFU instructions — shifting pressure from the SFU to the issue slots while introducing piecewise-linear approximation error. Because the denominator lll multiplies those exact same bytes by the all-ones matrix (the method from Section 8), the numerator and denominator use the exact same approximated values, so the error does not appear on only one side.

Next, we use the subnormal range of FP16 to drop that half-precision multiply-add step. FP16 has an exponent bias of 15, and its all-zero-exponent subnormal range is evenly spaced: its values are 21−15⋅m/210=m×2−242^{1-15}\cdot m/2^{10} = m \times 2^{-24}21−15⋅m/210=m×2−24 (where mmm is the 10-bit integer mantissa), with a minimum step size of 2−242^{-24}2−24. We multiply the byte code c=8(y+7)c = 8(y+7)c=8(y+7) by 2−242^{-24}2−24, folding the factor 8×2−24=2−218 \times 2^{-24} = 2^{-21}8×2−24=2−21 straight into FFMA.SAT. The lower bound 0 of .SAT handles the negative-bytecode clamp from above (E4M3 could represent down to 2−92^{-9}2−9, but this small range of tiny weights is flushed to 0); meanwhile, the maximum ccc of 120 times 2−242^{-24}2−24 stays far below the upper bound 1. Next, calling cvt.rn.f16x2.f32 converts two values to FP16 at once with round-to-nearest, so the hardware rounds ccc directly into the low 8 mantissa bits of FP16; PRMT then packs the 4 bytes into a 32-bit register. That cuts 4 instructions per 4 values (2 half-precision multiply-adds and 2 MOV instructions) and saves about another 78 µs on the 65K-history full-attention kernel (see the third chart at the end of the chapter).

In the final prefill version of a5, an all-f16x2 formulation replaces the 2−212^{-21}2−21 scaling above: before finding the intra-tile maximum, cvt.rn.f16x2.f32 converts the raw FP32 scores in pairs to f16x2. Because FP16 has a step size of 1 on [1024,2048)[1024, 2048)[1024,2048) and the low 8 mantissa bits of 1024+c1024 + c1024+c equal ccc directly, both the intra-tile maximum reduction and the linear encoding 1024+c1024 + c1024+c (clamping negative values to 1024) execute on f16x2 at two half-precision values per instruction. This saves a net 28 instructions per tile (from disassembly counts at the time; raw disassembly not kept and not verified), at the cost of rounding the scores to FP16 once before finding the maximum. The standalone latency change of this step on the 65K single operator was not measured separately (and is not plotted in the third chart at the end of the chapter); Section 10 next eliminates that initial batch of conversions as well. By contrast, approximating exp2 with an FMA polynomial issues about 7.5 extra instructions for every MUFU instruction it replaces, which runs slower in a loop where issue slots are already tight.

10a4 → a5 (Part 2): How Do the Two Matrix Multiplications Consume Narrower Inputs and Hide the Transpose of V Inside the First Stage's Background Execution Window?

Compute P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V directly with native FP8 wgmma, hiding the 18 byte-transpose instructions for V inside the asynchronous wait window of the first MMA stage.

Originally, we had to convert V to 16-bit in shared memory before running 16-bit wgmma for P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V — which both added a chain of conversion instructions and consumed twice as much shared memory. Once both P and V are in E4M3, we can issue the native FP8 instruction wgmma.m64n64k32.f32.e4m3.e4m3 directly: a 64×6464 \times 6464×64 tile with inner dimension k=32k = 32k=32 per step, E4M3 inputs, and FP32 accumulation (see Chapter 5, Section 3). Per the PTX specification note, FP8 wgmma with .f32 accumulators accumulates internally at higher than half precision but lower than single precision (published papers measure about 13–14 mantissa bits on Hopper and often pair it with two-level accumulation to curb error; a5 in this book passes the numerical tolerance with direct accumulation, and how much further two-level accumulation would reduce error was not measured). In the two-KV-head fusion verify kernel, switching to FP8 P (τ=4\tau = 4τ=4; see Section 9) and FP8 P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V together saves about 8.8 µs on verify 32-request full attention; the sliding-window single-KV-head wgmma kernel (Section 5) switches to FP8 P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V in the same way (see the chart below). Each tile also saves 8–16 KiB of shared memory; the trade-off is that FP8 P introduces the approximation error discussed in Section 9. The final two-KV-head fusion kernel also appends 8 all-ones rows to V⊤V^{\top}V⊤ and issues wgmma.m64n72k32 to compute P⋅VP\cdot VP⋅V and the row sum in a single instruction; the cost is 1 KiB more shared memory per KV head for the all-ones rows and 4 more accumulator registers per thread, and its standalone gain was not measured.

Sixteen-bit wgmma can pass the instruction immediate argument imm-trans-b = 1 to read N-major V directly, whereas FP8 wgmma requires the right-hand matrix in shared memory to be contiguous along the inner-product dimension — bytes from the same feature dimension at different key positions sitting next to each other, called K-major layout (inner-dimension major) (where K is the matrix-multiply inner-product dimension, which in P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V is the key position). In the KV cache, however, V packs the 64 features of a single key contiguously, so every tile needs a software byte transpose. For this we use the shared-memory matrix load instruction ldmatrix: for each 8×88 \times 88×8 sub-tile, 8 consecutive lanes supply the 8 row addresses and each 4-lane quad (see Chapter 5, Section 3) receives one 16 B row. Each tile's transpose takes 2 ldmatrix.x4.trans instructions (transposing 8×88 \times 88×8 sub-tiles of 16-bit elements), 8 byte-permute PRMT instructions (see Chapter 6, Section 2), and 8 shared-memory stores STS, for 18 instructions in total (PTX also offers the in-register transpose movmatrix.m8n8.trans.b16, SASS MOVM, likewise at 16-bit granularity — see Appendix B, Quick Reference 3 — but because V starts in shared memory and must be written back to shared memory for wgmma, ldmatrix.trans combines the shared-memory load and 16-bit transpose in one instruction, so movmatrix is unused). After writing to shared memory, the warpgroup also issues a fence.proxy.async and waits on the named barrier from Section 7 for its turn. Those two steps order the generic shared-memory writes from the warpgroup's 4 warps ahead of the asynchronous reads of wgmma (see Chapter 3, Section 3). Both steps are present before and after the change below, so they do not affect the comparison.

Once issued, wgmma executes asynchronously in the background, and its results are not needed until wait_group (for commit and wait, see Chapter 5, Section 5). Inserting these 18 transpose instructions between the commit point of Q⋅K⊤Q \cdot K^{\top}Q⋅K⊤ and wait_group<0> runs them concurrently with the matrix multiplication. The transpose still issues all 18 instructions, but they hide inside the background execution window of Q⋅K⊤Q \cdot K^{\top}Q⋅K⊤ and no longer sit on the critical path, saving about 1.8 µs on verify 32-request full attention.

In the final two-KV-head fusion kernels for verify 16- and 32-request full attention, we go one step further with cross-iteration overlap: we also remove the wait for P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V at the end of each tile, so Tile jjj's P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V is committed without waiting, crosses the loop back-edge, and stays in flight alongside Tile j+1j+1j+1's Q⋅K⊤Q \cdot K^{\top}Q⋅K⊤ (no wait_group in between); after transposing V on the next tile, a single wait_group<0> retires both together. Each consumer thread still uses 104 registers with zero spills (at the cost of keeping one extra set of 8 in-flight P fragment registers). On verify 16-request full attention, overlapping the transpose with Q⋅K⊤Q \cdot K^{\top}Q⋅K⊤ plus cross-iteration overlap saves about 1.7 µs in total (see the chart below).

In prefill, Q⋅K⊤Q \cdot K^{\top}Q⋅K⊤ can also switch to half-precision (f16x2) accumulation. Because the accumulator holds raw unscaled E4M3 dot products before multiplying by the attention scale (test cache keys are not necessarily normalized per key, and the scale factor can be 1/641/641/64, so Section 8's post-scale 72.25 bound does not apply here), we bound the raw dot product directly: RMS-normalized and E4M3-rounded q has length at most 8×1.0625=8.58 \times 1.0625 = 8.58×1.0625=8.5, and any E4M3 key has components within [−448,448][-448, 448][−448,448] for a length of at most 448×64=3,584448 \times \sqrt{64} = 3{,}584448×64​=3,584, so Cauchy-Schwarz bounds the raw accumulator at 8.5×3,584=30,4648.5 \times 3{,}584 = 30{,}4648.5×3,584=30,464, below the FP16 maximum of 65,504; FP16's 11 significand bits also give enough precision for softmax scores (keeping results within the numerical tolerance). The all-f16x2 approach at the end of Section 9 still wrote 32 cvt.rn.f16x2.f32 calls per tile in source to pack 64 FP32 scores per thread into f16x2; now the accumulator of wgmma.m64n128k32.f16.e4m3.e4m3 produces f16x2 directly, eliminating 32 cvt.rn.f16x2.f32 calls in source (34 conversion instructions in disassembly) and freeing 32 accumulator registers. Applying this only on unmasked full tiles cuts the full-attention prefill kernel runtime by 14.5% at T=753T = 753T=753 and by 16.8% at T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384 with 65K history (see the chart below). We also tested splitting softmax and P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V into a two-stage pipeline or splitting 128 keys into 64-key subtile pipelines, but neither yielded a gain because the compiler scheduled more instructions.

11a5 → a6 (Part 1): Should the Prologue and the Gating Epilogue Each Take a Separate Kernel?

Prefill fuses the prologue into a one-CTA-per-token kernel; decode and single-request verify fuse the prologue into each split-KV CTA and fuse the gating epilogue into the final kernel that writes o_attn.

Remember from Section 1 that our original baseline runs the five steps as about 7 separate kernels, where each additional kernel adds one launch and one "write back to HBM or L2 and read it out again" round trip (see Chapter 1, Section 3). An early fused prologue for prefill split the 20 heads of each token (16 q, 2 k, and 2 v) across 5 CTAs per token (from notes at the time; early source not kept and not verified); a6 consolidates this into 1 CTA per token (3 warps totaling 96 threads): RMSNorm, RoPE, casting q to FP8, and writing the new K/V entries all happen inside this single CTA, with each head's sum of squares reduced in registers via warp shuffles without using shared memory or a CTA barrier. With 4 threads per head, 96 threads cover 24 head slots; because there are only 20 actual heads, the extra 4 head slots leave 16 threads idle (register usage and residency were not measured separately). At T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384, prologue latency drops from about 53 µs to about 31 µs (see the chart below).

For decode and single-request verify, launching a separate prologue kernel just for a few rows of q and the new tokens' K/V isn't worth the boundary cost. Because one KV head has only 8 rows × 64\times\ 64× 64 dimensions per token, each split-KV CTA can read qkv directly to recompute the q rows it needs; each segment whose key range contains the new token positions computes and writes only the K/V entries for the new positions falling inside its own range, crosses a CTA barrier, and then reads them back. Why does this work without any cross-CTA synchronization? Because each segment reads only the keys and values in its own key range: the segment covering the new positions uses the values it just computed, and all other segments read only older historical cache entries that were already written in prior passes. Dropping the prologue kernel eliminates one launch and one dependency edge, saving about 1.8 µs on decode 1-request full attention (see the chart below).

At the other end of the pipeline, the gating epilogue rmsnorm(oraw)⊙σ(gate)\mathrm{rmsnorm}(o_{raw}) \odot \sigma(gate)rmsnorm(oraw​)⊙σ(gate) cannot run until the complete orawo_{raw}oraw​ is ready, and it no longer launches as a separate kernel either. In prefill, unsplit query tiles compute it directly, while for the 40 light query tiles split into 4 segments in Section 4, whichever of the 4 CTAs finishes last merges the segments inside the main kernel and then computes the gating epilogue (using ticket numbers; see the second path in Section 12). Shapes that merge inside the main kernel in Section 12 likewise compute the gating epilogue inside the main kernel before writing out, while shapes that still keep a separate merge kernel compute the gating epilogue at the end of the merge kernel after summing the partial results. The trade-off of fusing the prologue and epilogue is that every split segment recomputes q and the code becomes tightly coupled; the time saved by fusing the epilogue alone and any extra register or shared-memory usage were not measured separately.

Where a separate merge kernel remains (such as decode 1-request full attention), the main kernel hands off to the merge kernel via PDL (see Chapter 1, Section 4 for the mechanism). Comparing the three modes — "no PDL", "trigger after the main loop", and "trigger at function entry" (see the chart below) — shows that placing the trigger at function entry is actually the slowest: the merge-kernel CTAs enter too early, occupy SMs while sitting idle at the wait call for about 7.5 µs, and slow down the main kernel as well, probably because CTAs from both kernels co-reside on the same SMs and contend for slots (unverified). Because every shape with a separate merge kernel behaves this way, this chapter places the trigger after the main loop and before writeback.

12a5 → a6 (Part 2): Without a Separate Merge Kernel, How Are the Partial Results of Each Segment Summed Inside the Main Kernel?

Multiplying each segment's numerator and denominator by 2mi2^{m_i}2mi​ converts them to a common zero reference, so segments can be accumulated directly with atomic adds without waiting for the global denominator; a few paths still merge with per-segment maxima or lse\mathrm{lse}lse weights as in Section 3. Finally, one of three paths, chosen by grid size, finishes the merge.

Why did the merge in Section 3 need lse\mathrm{lse}lse? Because each segment's Oi,liO_i, l_iOi​,li​ were scaled by its own mim_imi​. If each segment outputs Oi2miO_i 2^{m_i}Oi​2mi​ and li2mil_i 2^{m_i}li​2mi​ instead (the true numerator and denominator referenced to 0), segments can accumulate directly with atomic adds, without waiting for the global denominator. The totals are simply ∑iOi2mi\sum_i O_i 2^{m_i}∑i​Oi​2mi​ and ∑ili2mi\sum_i l_i 2^{m_i}∑i​li​2mi​, followed by a single division o=Ototal/ltotalo = O_{total} / l_{total}o=Ototal​/ltotal​ at the end. In Section 8 we derived the upper bound ∣mi∣≤71.3|m_i| \le 71.3∣mi​∣≤71.3, so 2mi2^{m_i}2mi​ stays far below the FP32 upper limit of about 21282^{128}2128. The first path below and the decode shapes on the second path use this approach; light prefill tiles and the third path still follow Section 3 and merge with per-segment maxima or lse\mathrm{lse}lse weights. Below, three in-kernel merge paths split the workload by grid size and segment count per request. Each path notes at the start of its paragraph which shapes it handles, and the list at the end of this section covers the shapes that still use a standalone merge kernel.

The first path is L2 atomic add + grid barrier + per-row normalization epilogue, used only on the verify 16- and 32-request full-attention shapes (264 CTAs). All CTAs atomically add their partial sums into the L2 workspace buffer defined in Section 3, then increment the same arrival counter in L2 and wait until it reaches the total count — this device-wide wait across all CTAs is a grid barrier. Its causal chain has three steps:

  1. Each consumer thread atomically adds its numerator into the L2 workspace buffer using non-fetching vector atomic adds, and likewise for the denominator: verify 32-request full attention uses red.global.add.v4.f32 (adding 4 FP32 values at once) and verify 16-request full attention uses .v2.f32 (adding 2 FP32 values at once); red means write-only without fetching the old value (see Chapter 2, Section 7). Next, the 256 threads of the two consumer warpgroups cross a named barrier; in the memory model, that barrier orders the atomic adds of all threads in both consumer warpgroups before the representative thread's release (without requiring the atomic adds to have already landed in L2).
  2. A single representative thread for the CTA (thread 0 of consumer warpgroup 0) executes one atom.acq_rel.gpu addition on the global arrival counter and then polls it with ld.acquire.gpu until all CTAs have arrived. In CTAs still waiting, that 1 polling warp calls __nanosleep(64) (PTX nanosleep.u32, SASS NANOSLEEP) between polls to sleep briefly and yield issue slots — which the profiler's stall taxonomy (see Chapter 10, Section 7) records under sleeping — while the other 7 consumer warps wait at the next named barrier (the standalone gain of this backoff was not measured).
  3. Once the representative thread observes that all CTAs have arrived, the 256 threads of the two consumer warpgroups cross a second named barrier so that all consumer threads are ordered after that acquire.gpu; the 264 CTAs then partition the rows among themselves: read the accumulated numerators and denominators, divide, apply RMSNorm, multiply by σ(gate)\sigma(gate)σ(gate), write out o_attn, and zero their own slice of the workspace buffer for the next launch. Normal global loads after acquire.gpu observe the results published to L2 by every CTA's release without reading stale L1 lines on the local SM (Chapter 2, Section 6).

Why can a single thread's release represent the entire CTA? Because a release operation publishes all prior writes that the releasing thread has already observed (for cumulativity, see Chapter 2, Section 6) — without that first named barrier, the representative thread's release would not cover the atomic adds issued by the other consumer threads.

Who zeroes the arrival counter for the next launch? Nobody does. The 32-bit counter only ever increments, and the total increment per launch must divide 2322^{32}232 evenly so that launch boundaries stay aligned across wrap-around; because 264 does not divide 2322^{32}232, we set the per-launch total to 65,536 and partition it across the 264 CTAs: 64 CTAs add 249 and 200 CTAs add 248, so the weights sum to 65,536 per launch. Each CTA adds its own weight to the old value returned by its atom and rounds up to the next multiple of 65,536 as the target value to wait for on this launch; using a signed difference for the comparison avoids any need to zero the counter across graph replays.

Why does reusing the same counter across launches never mix two launches? Because the PDL chain enforces a strict handoff invariant: every PDL kernel executes its own wait call before finishing (see Chapter 1, Section 4), and the next kernel that uses this counter touches it only after its own wait call — which guarantees that the previous launch has completely finished and all its writes are visible.

What keeps this spin-wait from deadlocking? Every CTA is guaranteed to see the counter complete only if all 264 CTAs achieve co-residency (simultaneous residency). By resource usage, each SM holds 2 CTAs, and 264=2×132264 = 2 \times 132264=2×132 equals the exact capacity of 1 wave. Formally, CUDA guarantees full-grid co-residency only under cooperative launch (see Chapter 2, Section 6). Here we skip cooperative launch and rely on three prerequisites plus the empirical dispatch behavior observed on hardware (the CUDA specification does not promise to dispatch all 264 CTAs onto SMs at once):

  1. The grid does not exceed the capacity of 1 wave. The host verifies this before launch via an occupancy query and falls back to a separate merge kernel if the grid does not fit.
  2. No other work occupies the SMs for an extended period, including kernels on other streams in the same process (such as cross-GPU communication kernels) and other processes; the preceding PDL kernel does not count — because the current kernel enters only after every CTA of its predecessor has either triggered or exited (Chapter 1, Section 4), all predecessor CTAs are already on SMs, do not wait on us, and will exit.
  3. The main kernel waits until the entire grid has arrived at the barrier before issuing the PDL trigger call to release the next kernel, preventing CTAs of the next kernel from entering SMs early and taking slots.

Within this chapter's isolated Stage 2 benchmark, no other kernel competes for SMs while Stage 2 executes, so Prerequisite 2 is satisfied; when multiple streams or processes share the SMs, you must switch to cooperative launch (see Chapter 2, Section 6). In single-request trials on this operator, cooperative launch added about 1.2–1.8 µs of launch overhead (we did not keep the raw record). Avoiding cooperative launch saves that overhead in exchange for accepting a risk: if Prerequisite 2 or the dispatch behavior above fails to hold, the kernel will hang silently without reporting an error (Chapter 2, Section 6).

Folding this merge step in eliminates the separate merge kernel, saving a net ~3.0 µs on verify 32-request full attention (see the chart and note below).

Because the arrival order of cross-CTA floating-point atomic adds in the first path varies with scheduling, two runs on the exact same input can differ in the last few bits (with a relative difference below 10−410^{-4}10−4, within the numerical tolerance), whereas a separate merge kernel produces bitwise-identical results every run. How this last-bit difference affects the draft acceptance rate (see Primer 1, Section 7) was not measured.

The second path is last-arriver merge, which handles decode 1-, 16-, and 32-request full attention and decode 32-request sliding window in Chapter 9's single-layer pipeline, along with the 40 split light prefill tiles in this chapter. Earlier CTAs never stay behind to spin-wait in place. Across those decode shapes, each segment still adds its 2mi2^{m_i}2mi​-scaled numerator and denominator into the workspace buffer with floating-point atomic adds (for decode 1-request full attention, which has 256 segments, segment sss accumulates into replica s mod 8s \bmod 8smod8 of 8 workspace copies, spreading writes across 8 addresses to sidestep the single-address contention discussed at the end of this section; the standalone gain of that sharding was not measured). All threads in the CTA then cross a first CTA barrier before thread 0 draws a ticket with atom.acq_rel.gpu (using the mechanism from Chapter 2, Sections 6–7): earlier CTAs exit right after drawing their ticket, while the CTA that draws the final ticket crosses a second CTA barrier, reads the accumulated numerator and denominator for the row, resets that row's workspace and ticket counter to 0 with ordinary stores, and runs the division and gating epilogue. Those two CTA barriers play the exact same role as the two named barriers on the first path: the first orders all atomic adds in the CTA before thread 0's release, and the second orders all reads in the CTA after thread 0's acquire. Ordinary stores are enough to zero the state because nothing touches that row again until the next launch, and the PDL invariant above ensures the two launches run strictly one after the other. Because no CTA ever waits on another CTA, this path is deadlock-free even when the grid spans multiple waves; in exchange, cross-CTA floating-point atomic adds execute in schedule-dependent order, so bitwise-identical outputs are not guaranteed by construction. Eliminating the standalone merge kernel means the finishing CTA reads back only the summed numerator and denominator rather than fetching every segment's partial output one by one.

The 40 split light prefill tiles also merge in the last-arriving CTA via ticket numbers (where the final ticket writes 0 back to the counter), but without floating-point atomic adds: the 4 segments each write their own (oi,lsei)(o_i, \mathrm{lse}_i)(oi​,lsei​), and the CTA that receives the final ticket merges them in the fixed segment order 0–3 using the lse\mathrm{lse}lse weights from Section 3 before computing the gating epilogue; that leaves no accumulation workspace buffer to zero and keeps the result bitwise deterministic.

Verify 1-, 16-, and 32-request sliding window and decode 1- and 16-request sliding window take the third path: direct cross-CTA write to remote shared memory (DSMEM) within the same cluster. A thread block cluster declares several CTAs as a group that hardware guarantees to keep co-resident simultaneously. Physically, a GPC (Graphics Processing Cluster) is a group of adjacent SMs on the die wired together by its own inter-SM interconnect, and all CTAs of a cluster must fit inside the same GPC (scattered slots across different GPCs cannot form a cluster). Each GPC is built from TPCs (Texture Processing Clusters, with 2 SMs per TPC): a full GH100 die has 8 GPCs ×\times× 9 TPCs =144= 144=144 SMs, whereas the 132-SM H200 enables 66 TPCs, and how many are enabled in each GPC is not publicly documented. The portable cluster-size limit is 8 CTAs; the 16-CTA clusters used on 1-request sliding window at the end of this section are non-portable and require setting CU_FUNC_ATTRIBUTE_NON_PORTABLE_CLUSTER_SIZE_ALLOWED = 1 (cudaFuncAttributeNonPortableClusterSizeAllowed in the runtime API) before launch. Beyond on-chip merging, clusters can also pair with TMA multicast from Chapter 5, Section 6.

DSMEM (Distributed Shared Memory) lets one CTA in a cluster directly read and write a peer CTA's shared memory: when sender and receiver sit on different SMs, traffic crosses the intra-GPC SM-to-SM interconnect without going through L2, whereas the hardware path when two CTAs of one cluster co-reside on the same SM or when a CTA writes to itself is undocumented. The st.async instruction asynchronously writes a 4–16 B register value into the shared memory of a target CTA in the same cluster (including the executing CTA itself) and records the arrived byte count on the receiver's mbarrier (see Chapter 3, Section 5); as soon as the receiver's expected byte count is reached, it knows all segments have arrived. TMA can also bulk-copy a block directly from local shared memory into a peer CTA's shared memory (cp.async.bulk.shared::cluster.shared::cta, likewise decrementing the peer's mbarrier), which fits forwarding large blocks already sitting in shared memory, but it requires a byte size that is a multiple of 16 B, 16 B-aligned source and destination addresses, and a strictly remote target CTA; PTX's peer-SMEM reduction red.async likewise forbids targeting the executing CTA itself and supports integer operations only (see Chapter 9, Section 3 and Appendix B, Quick Reference 3). Across both cluster-merge families in this chapter, every CTA that merges rows also pushes its own assigned rows to itself (bulk copy forbids self-writes while st.async allows them, and Chapter 9's 4 B floating-point exchange likewise includes 1 self-write): the 1-request 3-in-1 merge sums 264 B floating-point rows in registers (so bulk copy would first have to stage them into shared memory and add fence.proxy.async.shared::cta), while the sliding-window wgmma merge already stages 16 B-aligned row partials and lse values in shared memory, though whether remote bulk copy plus that proxy fence would beat st.async for its remote peers was not measured.

Concretely, we declare the split-segment CTAs of the same request as a cluster. In both cluster-kernel families, the grid dimension spanned by the cluster equals the cluster width, so that block index is already the intra-cluster rank (blockIdx.x in the 1-request sliding-window clusters and blockIdx.z in the sliding-window wgmma merge, whereas general grids read the special register %cluster_ctarank for the cross-dimensional CTA rank within the cluster; see Chapter 9, Section 3). The sender uses mapa.shared::cluster.u32 ra, la, r to map a local shared-memory address la to the address ra of the same variable in CTA r — mapping the receiver's mbarrier address the same way — and passes them to st.async to push each row's partial result into the shared memory of the CTA responsible for that row (each merging CTA in the cluster owns a subset of rows). On 1-request sliding window, the prologue was already fused into the split-KV kernel. Fusing the split-KV main loop and the cluster merge into that same kernel gives a single 3-in-1 kernel (prologue, split-KV, and cluster merge), turns 2 launches into 1, and saves about 0.6 µs on verify 1-request sliding window (see the chart below). We measured this 3-in-1 kernel in the standalone attention benchmark of this chapter. In the full-layer chain of Chapter 9, verify 1-request sliding window likewise merges inside the cluster; there the QKV projection kernel handles the prologue, so it is a 2-in-1 split-KV and merge kernel. Decode 1- and 16-request sliding window there still use a separate merge kernel.

Verify 16- and 32-request sliding window use the sliding-window single-KV-head wgmma kernel (Section 5) and declare the segments of the same request as a cluster (unlike the 3–4-CTA-per-SM mma.sync split kernel in Section 4). This kernel uses 72 registers per thread and 256 threads per CTA, so each SM holds at most 3 CTAs. Look at verify 16-request sliding window: 16 requests × 2\times\ 2× 2 KV heads =32= 32=32 clusters, each containing NS split-KV CTAs. Under the sliding window, each request sees 2,055 keys, or 33 tiles; when NS = 8, assigning ⌈33/8⌉=5\lceil 33/8 \rceil = 5⌈33/8⌉=5 tiles per segment means the first 7 segments already cover all 33 tiles, leaving the 8th segment with 0 tiles while still occupying a CTA slot.

At 3 CTAs per SM, the full chip can hold at most 132×3/8≈49132 \times 3 / 8 \approx 49132×3/8≈49 clusters of 8 CTAs; because a cluster cannot span GPC boundaries, 49 is only an upper bound, and how many 8-CTA clusters the chip can actually hold is neither publicly documented nor measured here. Those 32 clusters total 256 CTAs, which fit in one wave. When NS = 8, measured runs place 3 CTAs on 16 of the SMs, and those SMs finish last and drag out the tail. Changing to NS = 7 drops the empty segment and shrinks each cluster to 7 CTAs, for 32×7=22432 \times 7 = 22432×7=224 CTAs in total. Each cluster fits inside a single GPC more easily, no SM has to hold a 3rd CTA in measured runs, and latency drops by about 1.3 µs (measured when the sliding-window wgmma cluster merge still used its earlier pull form, before switching to st.async direct-write push saved about another 0.49 and 0.25 µs on verify 16- and 32-request sliding window; see the chart below); the trade-off is that with 7 segments, merging must partition 64 output rows across 7 segments, which no longer divides evenly.

Applying in-kernel merge in the wrong regime causes a loss (see the chart below). On single-request full attention, the in-kernel merge tail is more than twice as slow as a standalone merge kernel, making decode 1-request full attention about 3.0 µs slower — inferred from same-address atomic adds serializing one by one in L2 when all 256 segment CTAs target the exact same output row (the second path above spreads writes across 8 workspace copies, whose standalone gain was not measured). On verify 32-request sliding window (64 clusters of 4 CTAs, totaling 256 CTAs), each SM originally holds up to 3 CTAs, fitting all 64 clusters in 1 wave. Expanding each CTA to 2 consumer warpgroups or increasing shared memory drops residency to at most 2 CTAs per SM; querying cluster occupancy shows that at 2 CTAs per SM the GPU co-resides at most 62 clusters of 4 CTAs (with 2 SMs per TPC, even per-GPC SM counts still sum to 132÷2=66132 \div 2 = 66132÷2=66 rather than 62, so which hardware or scheduling limit caps this at 62 was not determined), pushing the last 2 clusters into a 2nd wave and stretching the tail. In addition, inlining the epilogue reduction code directly into the function containing the main loop disrupts compiler scheduling of the main loop and slows execution down.

By this point, both the head and the tail have been pulled into the main kernel. In the final standalone operator of this chapter, each shape runs its corresponding kernel:

  • decode 1/16-request sliding window and verify 1-request sliding window: the 3-in-1 mma.sync cluster kernel. Prologue, split-KV main loop, and intra-cluster DSMEM merge share one kernel, so there is no separate merge kernel. Decode 1-request uses one 16-CTA cluster per KV head with 32 segments; decode 16-request uses one 8-CTA cluster per request and KV head; verify 1-request uses two 16-CTA clusters per KV head, each covering 4 new tokens.
  • verify 16/32-request sliding window: sliding-window single-KV-head wgmma cluster kernel (up to 3 CTAs per SM, with intra-cluster DSMEM direct-write merge).
  • verify 16/32-request full attention: two-KV-head fusion wgmma kernel (2 CTAs per SM, with in-kernel L2 atomic-add merge).
  • decode 16/32-request full attention and decode 32-request sliding window: prologue fused into each split-KV CTA, followed by a separate merge kernel in the standalone operator of this chapter; the single-layer pipeline in Chapter 9 switches these shapes to the second path (last-arriver merge).
  • decode 1-request full attention and verify 1-request full attention: prologue fused into each split-KV CTA, followed by a separate merge kernel (in the single-layer pipeline of Chapter 9, decode 1-request full attention also switches to the second path).
  • prefill: a 1-CTA-per-token prologue kernel, followed by the 1-CTA-per-SM, 3-consumer-warpgroup main kernel. Full-attention layers add a staging kernel that copies paged FP8 KV entries into contiguous 128-key tiles: historical keys are staged on a side stream in parallel with the Stage 1 projection, and tiles that contain new keys are staged after the prologue. The 40 light prefill tiles are each split into 4 segments and merged inside the main kernel by whichever of the 4 CTAs finishes last (via ticket numbers, the second path in Section 12).

Stage 2 Paged Attention Evolution Chain (a0 → a6)

Across this chapter, a0 → a6 groups our optimizations by the bottleneck each mechanism removes. The three charts below follow the chronological order in which versions were developed; because a single version often bundles several steps together, the a labels in the second chart interleave. In same-session paired ABBA runs against original SGLang, the final version runs about 2.7–2.8× as fast as the baseline (with the final step inside the noise band; see the second chart).

  • a0 (Sections 2–3): launch a separate prologue kernel, stack 8 query heads as matrix rows, and run Q⋅K⊤Q \cdot K^{\top}Q⋅K⊤ in FP8, with fixed-split Split-KV followed by a separate merge kernel (corresponding to Bar 1 of the first chart).
