  • a1 (Section 4): tune split count to the concurrent request count, balance segments by key and tile count, and look up configurations per shape, cutting the 6-workload geometric mean by about 8% (corresponding to Bar 2 of the first chart and Bars 1–4 of the second chart).
  • a2 (Sections 5–6): reshape how the two halves of the same K row are read, preload page-table tiles before the loop and prefetch 2 iterations ahead with even/odd register pairs to hide the three-hop wait in the pipeline, and issue sequence-length and page-table loads concurrently at batch size 1; bundled with other changes, these land in Bars 2, 3, 4, and 10 of the second chart (Bar 2 cuts time by about 33% across its bundle, while Bar 10's whole-version gain stays within cross-session run-to-run variation).
  • a3 (Section 7): size residency by register allocation, apply verify full-attention split scheduling and insert virtual tiles to balance 264 CTAs evenly by tile count, make the producer the default partition to split out the unmasked loop at zero spills, and stagger the two consumer warpgroups via named barriers (landing in Bars 3, 4, 5, and 8 of the second chart).
  • a4 (Section 8): skip per-tile rescaling altogether for BF16 P using the score upper bound, and offload row sums onto the Tensor Core when it has spare capacity. Single-KV-head Tensor Core row sum already shipped inside Bar 2 of the second chart, whereas Bar 4 ships BF16 skip-rescaling along with rewriting the main kernels to emit inline PTX inside CUDA C++ (for explicit control over registers, barriers, and instruction scheduling), removes row sum from the single-KV-head kernels, and bundles sliding-window cluster merges to cut time by about 17% (individual shares cannot be separated).
  • a5 (Sections 9–10): compress P to FP8 with lazy rescaling, move exponential encoding onto the FMA/ALU pipelines, overlap FP8 P⋅VP \cdot VP⋅V with the transpose, and use half-precision accumulation in prefill; this cuts prefill kernel time by about 19% in the third chart and lands in Bars 5–7 and 9–10 of the second chart.
  • a6 (Sections 11–12): fold the prologue and the gating epilogue into neighboring kernels, and for some shapes fold the segment merge into the main kernel (landing in Bars 2, 4, 5, 8, and 10 of the second chart).

Takeaway: The bottleneck of paged attention is governed by how many query rows share each KV row (nq=8Ln_q = 8Lnq​=8L). When nqn_qnq​ is small, the job is filling all 132 SMs and hiding the page-table round trip; when nqn_qnq​ is large, the challenge shifts inside each CTA to registers, the SFU, and issue slots. Each step of a0 → a6 removes only whichever bottleneck is slowest at that point.

Next chapter's question: After passing through the o projection in Stage 3 and the fork of Stages 4 and 5, the attention output arrives at Stage 6, the stage with the largest byte volume in a single layer: 32 local NVFP4 experts per GPU under 8-GPU expert parallelism. Why is the expert-by-expert dequantizing starter implementation slow, and how do we move the bottleneck onto the Tensor Core during prefill?

Position in the 8-stage single-layer pipeline: Stage 1 qkv_gate → Stage 2 paged attention → Stage 3 o and gated residual → Stage 4 router ∥ Stage 5 pooler → [Stage 6: Routed Experts] → Stage 7 unpooler → Stage 8 second gated residual

Stage 6's 32 local NVFP4 experts hold the largest share of weights in a single layer. Why is the starter implementation that dequantizes one expert at a time so slow? And as the total token count TTT grows from 1 to 16,384, why does Stage 6 ultimately split into three distinct kernels by TTT, and how does each generation evolve from the last?

1What Five Steps Does Stage 6 Compute for Each Hit Pair, and How Does MeM_eMe​ Split Stage 6 into Two Regimes?

When the token count MeM_eMe​ routed to an expert is less than about 58, reading weights is slower than matrix multiplication: decode, verify, and T=753T = 753T=753 prefill fall below this threshold, whereas T≥3,012T \ge 3{,}012T≥3,012 prefill lies above it.

Stage 6 takes p :  [T,  4096]  BF16\shape{p}{T,\;4096}{BF16}p:[T,4096]BF16 from Stage 5, along with the routing indices topk_ids :  [T,  8]  int32\shape{\mathrm{topk\_ids}}{T,\;8}{int32}topk_ids:[T,8]int32 and routing weights topk_weights :  [T,  8]  FP32\shape{\mathrm{topk\_weights}}{T,\;8}{FP32}topk_weights:[T,8]FP32 from Stage 4. In each row, the 8 routing weights sum to 1 (see Primer 2, Section 2). All 256 experts in the model are split across 8 GPUs, and this GPU's 32 local experts stay resident in HBM (see Primer 1, Section 2). Once Stage 6 finishes, it outputs m :  [T,  4096]  BF16\shape{m}{T,\;4096}{BF16}m:[T,4096]BF16 to Stage 7. A token toktoktok has 8 slots slotslotslot, and only a slot that lands on a local expert eee on this GPU counts as a hit pair (tok,slot,e)(tok, slot, e)(tok,slot,e); if all 8 slots miss this GPU, that token's output row is all zeros.

For the MeM_eMe​ tokens that hit local expert eee on this GPU (one row per hit pair (tok,slot,e)(tok, slot, e)(tok,slot,e)), Stage 6 runs five steps in order:

  1. gate/up projection (W13): [ gugate∣guup ]=ptok dequant(W13[e])⊤[\,gu_{gate} \mid gu_{up}\,] = p_{tok}\, \mathrm{dequant}(W_{13}[e])^{\top}[gugate​∣guup​]=ptok​dequant(W13​[e])⊤, producing the gate and up halves gu :  [Me,  8192]  FP32\shape{\mathrm{gu}}{M_e,\;8192}{FP32}gu:[Me​,8192]FP32. The first 4096 columns are the gate gugategu_{gate}gugate​, and the last 4096 columns are the up projection guupgu_{up}guup​. These are the FP32 accumulator values of the matrix multiply; the kernels below usually keep them in registers and pass them straight to Step 2.
  2. SwiGLU: inter=silu(gugate)⊙guupinter = \mathrm{silu}(gu_{gate}) \odot gu_{up}inter=silu(gugate​)⊙guup​, producing inter :  [Me,  4096]  BF16\shape{\mathrm{inter}}{M_e,\;4096}{BF16}inter:[Me​,4096]BF16 (see Primer 2, Section 2).
  3. down projection (W2): y=inter dequant(W2[e])⊤y = inter\, \mathrm{dequant}(W_{2}[e])^{\top}y=interdequant(W2​[e])⊤, producing y :  [Me,  4096]  BF16\shape{y}{M_e,\;4096}{BF16}y:[Me​,4096]BF16.
  4. post-expert RMSNorm: ynorm=rmsnorm(y⊙(1+wpost))y_{norm} = \mathrm{rmsnorm}\big(y \odot (1 + w_{post})\big)ynorm​=rmsnorm(y⊙(1+wpost​)), producing ynorm :  [Me,  4096]  FP32\shape{y_{norm}}{M_e,\;4096}{FP32}ynorm​:[Me​,4096]FP32. Here wpost :  [4096]  BF16\shape{w_{post}}{4096}{BF16}wpost​:[4096]BF16 (written as wpost_expertw_{post\_expert}wpost_expert​ in Primer 2, Section 2) is the post-expert RMSNorm weight shared across all experts, and a tiny constant ϵ\epsilonϵ sits inside the root mean square to prevent division by zero.
  5. weighted accumulation by routing weights: mtok+=topk_weights[tok,slot]⋅ynormm_{tok} \mathrel{+}= \texttt{topk\_weights}[tok, slot] \cdot y_{norm}mtok​+=topk_weights[tok,slot]⋅ynorm​, writing out m :  [T,  4096]  BF16\shape{m}{T,\;4096}{BF16}m:[T,4096]BF16.

H200 Tensor Cores do not accept 4-bit floating-point (E2M1) inputs. After NVFP4 codewords are loaded onto the chip, the kernel must decode them to BF16 before feeding them into the matrix multiply. Each weight is w=c⋅sblock⋅stensorw = c \cdot s_{block} \cdot s_{tensor}w=c⋅sblock​⋅stensor​: a 4-bit codeword ccc multiplied by a block scale and then by a tensor scale (see Chapter 6, Section 3 for the bit layout and decoding instructions). Counting the bytes, each codeword takes 0.5 B0.5\text{ B}0.5 B, every 16 weights share a 1 B1\text{ B}1 B block scale (0.0625 B0.0625\text{ B}0.0625 B per weight), and each projection matrix (W13W_{13}W13​, W2W_2W2​) of each expert carries one FP32 tensor scale, totaling 0.5625 B0.5625\text{ B}0.5625 B per weight. Within each expert, the gate half and the up-projection half share a single FP32 tensor scale (Section 13 explains why storing one scale is enough).

When we report Stage 6 latency below, we are measuring Stage 6 in isolation: within the same benchmark run, we alternate A/B paired comparisons before and after a change (see Chapter 7, Section 1 for the paired protocol and Chapter 4, Section 6 for the variation criterion). Single-layer latency, by contrast, covers all eight stages of a full layer in Chapter 9. Take the geometric mean of Stage 6 latency across the 6 decode (T=1,16,32T = 1, 16, 32T=1,16,32, with 1 new token per request) and verify (T=8,128,256T = 8, 128, 256T=8,128,256, with 8 new tokens per request) workloads and multiply by 60 (the middle 60 layers use 4-bit experts; see Primer 1, Section 2): that gives the 60-layer total. We compare that total against the baseline SGLang implementation, which invokes a 4-bit grouped-GEMM library routine once per projection (see the first chart at the end of the chapter); the prefill workloads at T=753,3,012,16,384T = 753, 3{,}012, 16{,}384T=753,3,012,16,384 are treated separately in Sections 14–16.

Along the evolution chain, decode and verify start out sharing two kernel generations (m1 and m2), before the final deployment splits into three branches by TTT: m3 for T≤32T \le 32T≤32, m4 for T=128..256T = 128..256T=128..256, and m5 for prefill.

Why split by TTT at all? Because the row count of an expert's matrix multiplication is simply the number of tokens MeM_eMe​ routed to that expert. At 3.56 FLOP/B3.56\text{ FLOP/B}3.56 FLOP/B per token against the H200 ridge point of 206 FLOP/B206\text{ FLOP/B}206 FLOP/B, an expert needs Me≈58M_e \approx 58Me​≈58 tokens before matrix-multiply compute time catches up with the time to read its weights once from HBM (Primer 2, Section 5). Which 8 experts each token picks is the routing distribution: spreading tokens evenly across experts is uniform routing, clustering them onto a few experts is skewed routing, and our single-operator benchmarks generate multiple random routing distributions. That Me≈58M_e \approx 58Me​≈58 line splits the workload into two regimes:

  • decode and verify (T=1..256T = 1..256T=1..256): Under uniform routing at T=256T = 256T=256, almost all 32 local experts on this GPU get hit, leaving each expert with an average of only 8 tokens. Under skewed routing, tokens pile onto fewer experts, so fewer experts get hit than under uniform routing. In this chapter's single-operator benchmark, at T=256T = 256T=256 the busiest GPU receives about 390 hit pairs and hits about 24 local experts on average, leaving each hit expert with an average of about 16 tokens—still far below 58. Only a few hot experts at T=128..256T = 128..256T=128..256 receive several dozen to over a hundred tokens, which we handle in Section 9. Throughout this regime, weight reads set the physical lower bound: the starter implementation m0 is slowed down by its per-expert loop (Section 2), while the first four kernel generations (m1 → m4) strip away on-chip decoding instructions, tail waves, and synchronization overhead step by step to approach that weight-read lower bound.
  • prefill (T=753,3,012,16,384T = 753, 3{,}012, 16{,}384T=753,3,012,16,384): Under uniform routing, each local expert receives an average of 8T/256=T/328T / 256 = T / 328T/256=T/32 tokens—about 24, 94, and 512 tokens across the three points. T=753T = 753T=753 still sits below the ridge point, but T≥3,012T \ge 3{,}012T≥3,012 crosses 58, shifting the bottleneck of our fifth-generation kernel (m5) onto the Tensor Cores and instruction pipelines.

Put the two physical lower bounds side by side, and this crossover is obvious. For prefill under the mean-GPU uniform-routing convention, all 32 local experts on this GPU get hit (906 MB906\text{ MB}906 MB in total), so reading their weights once at 4.8 TB/s4.8\text{ TB/s}4.8 TB/s takes at least 188.7 μs188.7\ \mu\text{s}188.7 μs; counting TTT hit pairs per GPU against the 989 TFLOP/s989\text{ TFLOP/s}989 TFLOP/s BF16 dense peak (without 2:4 sparsity, since 4-bit weights unpack to BF16 on chip before the multiply), the dense compute lower bounds across T=753,3,012,16,384T = 753, 3{,}012, 16{,}384T=753,3,012,16,384 are about 777777, 307307307, and 1,668 μs1{,}668\ \mu\text{s}1,668 μs (at T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384, 16,384×2×3×40962≈1,649 GFLOP16{,}384 \times 2 \times 3 \times 4096^2 \approx 1{,}649\text{ GFLOP}16,384×2×3×40962≈1,649 GFLOP, nearly 9× the weight-read lower bound; under skewed routing on the busiest GPU, the dense compute lower bound in the end-of-chapter chart is 3,096 μs3{,}096\ \mu\text{s}3,096 μs). In decode and verify, by contrast, we read only the hit experts, so the weight-read lower bound stays much smaller than 188.7 μs188.7\ \mu\text{s}188.7 μs. At T=256T = 256T=256 under the busiest-GPU skewed-routing mean (about 24.824.824.8 hit local experts and about 393.6393.6393.6 hit pairs, Me≈16M_e \approx 16Me​≈16), the unscaled physical weight-plus-activation read bound is 147.2 μs147.2\ \mu\text{s}147.2 μs and the dense compute bound is 40.1 μs40.1\ \mu\text{s}40.1 μs; the single-operator benchmark scorer scales mean hit experts and hit pairs by 75%75\%75% (a 0.750.750.75 routing share), setting its task lower bound at 108.9 μs108.9\ \mu\text{s}108.9 μs and the corresponding compute lower bound at about 29.7 μs29.7\ \mu\text{s}29.7 μs. A full 8-GPU deployment also has to wait for the slowest GPU and run a cross-GPU reduction; this chapter measures single-GPU latency under the routing load of the busiest GPU, excluding that cross-GPU reduction.

2Why Does the Starter m0 Take Tens of Milliseconds, and Why Is the First Grouped-GEMM Step m1a ~80× Faster?

m0 loops over experts one by one, launching small kernels and decompressing weights to FP32 in HBM; m1 switches to a single grouped-GEMM launch per projection with on-the-fly in-register decompression.

m0 is the plain-PyTorch starter implementation, not the kernel that baseline SGLang runs in production. On every call, it steps through all 32 local experts one by one in a Python loop—whether hit or not, running every token through each expert with routing weight 0 where not routed: for each expert, it decompresses that expert's entire weight set into a 201.3 MB201.3\text{ MB}201.3 MB FP32 dense matrix in HBM, converts it to BF16, and runs the matrix multiplies. Look at the HBM byte accounting for a single expert: the useful weights are only 28.3 MB28.3\text{ MB}28.3 MB, yet even counting only reading the 4-bit weights, writing out the dense FP32 matrix, and reading it back moves at least 28.3+201.3+201.3=431.0 MB28.3 + 201.3 + 201.3 = 431.0\text{ MB}28.3+201.3+201.3=431.0 MB—about 15× the useful bytes.

Across the 6 benchmark cases, the measured geometric-mean Stage 6 latency is about 37.8 ms37.8\text{ ms}37.8 ms. Across all 32 local experts, that HBM round trip alone costs at least about 2.9 ms2.9\text{ ms}2.9 ms even at full HBM bandwidth; its actual share was not measured separately (see the chart below). Beyond that round trip, each expert in the per-expert loop also runs two dequantizations (producing temporary FP32 and BF16 tensors), two BF16 matrix multiplications, SwiGLU, normalization, and a small launch that adds the weighted result across all output rows. The share of each item was not measured. m1a drops the HBM round trip, the per-expert loop, the temporary tensors, and the repeated small launches all at once, running about 80× faster than m0.

m1 removes that extra round trip in two steps. First (m1a in the first chart at the end of the chapter), we run token bucketing (grouping tokens that hit the same expert together) and then launch a single grouped GEMM grid per projection instead of launching once per expert. A grouped GEMM is a single launch where each CTA processes one token tile for one expert. Stage 6 now runs in four parts: "token bucketing → gate/up grouped GEMM (with SwiGLU) → down-projection grouped GEMM → post-expert RMSNorm and weighted accumulation." Once an expert's 4-bit codewords and block scales arrive on chip, we decode them to BF16 right in registers and feed them straight into the matrix multiply without writing back any dense weights; HBM reads the 4-bit weights only once. This step is faster on all 6 benchmark cases (see the first chart at the end of the chapter).

Second (m1 in the first chart at the end of the chapter), we interleave the gate and up projections in 32+3232 + 3232+32 rows so the gate and up outputs for the same row land in the same tile and can run SwiGLU directly. At the same time, we switch weight decoding to branchless bitwise unpacking (see Chapter 6, Section 3) and turn on Programmatic Dependent Launch (PDL; see Chapter 1, Section 4) so the next kernel launches early to prefetch static weights. Even with those improvements, m1 still takes about 1.6× the latency of baseline SGLang, and only overtakes the baseline with m2 in the next section. What we pay for m1 is maintaining a fixed-shape token-bucketing index table ahead of the matrix multiplications; the overhead of that table and the individual shares of the three items in Step 2 were not measured separately.

3When MeM_eMe​ Is Only a Handful to a Dozen Tokens, How Do We Pipeline Weight Loads?

m2 switches to a pipelined wgmma tiled kernel, splitting along K at small batch sizes to fill SMs and using a multi-slot weight ring buffer to hide weight loads behind compute.

Step 1 replaces the kernel: m2 switches to Hopper's asynchronous wgmma instruction, placing the in-register decoded weights in operand A and the tokens on the operand-B side (swap-AB; see Chapter 5, Sections 3–5). m2 selects the matrix-multiply instruction according to tile height: 8-row tiles use warp-level mma.sync (for reasons explained in Section 4), while taller tiles use wgmma. Running wgmma with operand A in registers (RS mode; Chapter 5, Section 3) comes with a catch: weight decoding consumes ALU cycles and registers. If ALU decoding cycles exceed Tensor Core cycles, operand supply cannot keep up (see Chapter 6, Section 4 for a counterexample). In the Me<58M_e < 58Me​<58 regime, once we compress the decoding instructions tightly enough, the ALU is no longer the bottleneck.

Step 2 raises the tile count. The down projection has only 4096 output columns (64 column tiles), half of the 8192 columns of the gate/up projection: at T=1T = 1T=1 (about 2.6 hit experts on the busiest GPU on average, leaving only 128 column tiles on 2-expert cases) there are sometimes fewer tiles than the 132 SMs, whereas at T=8,16T = 8, 16T=8,16 the grid already exceeds 132 CTAs yet still sits inside a partial residency wave (about 570–760 CTAs at T=16T = 16T=16, below one 924-slot wave at 7 CTAs per SM; T=8T = 8T=8 runs at 9 CTAs per SM, 1,188 slots per wave; T=32T = 32T=32 uses no Split-K on the down projection). Following Split-K from Chapter 2, Section 5, at T=1,8,16T = 1, 8, 16T=1,8,16 the down projection is sliced 2-way or 4-way along K (pushing the grid past one full wave at T=8,16T = 8, 16T=8,16; we infer that keeping more concurrent warps and memory requests per SM outweighs the wave tail, though this was not profiled), storing partial sums into a temporary BF16 matrix that the subsequent post-expert RMSNorm kernel reduces; at T=1T = 1T=1, even the gate/up projection lacks enough tiles and is sliced along K too. What Split-K costs us is writing and reading an extra buffer of partial sums and running the reduction additions, plus the lower precision of BF16 partial sums compared to FP32. Splitting too finely loses performance—cutting the T=16T = 16T=16 down projection into 4 slices makes it slower (see the second chart below).

Step 3 keeps weight loads continuously in flight. Prior to this step, weight unpacking had already moved to paired 4-bit nibble decoding (where each instruction unpacks two 4-bit codes into a packed BF16x2 pair at once; see Chapter 6, Section 3). Next, we build a multi-slot weight ring buffer in shared memory driven by cp.async (Chapter 3, Section 3, rather than TMA), which we infer keeps enough bytes in flight across K-steps to hide HBM latency (Chapter 2, Section 3; Chapter 5, Section 6). Removing that 3-slot cp.async ring buffer slows Stage 6 down by 5–6 µs at T=16T = 16T=16 and T=32T = 32T=32 (that ablation also shifted per-SM occupancy from 8 to 7 CTAs, so the two effects were not separated).

At T=128T = 128T=128 and T=256T = 256T=256, we likewise introduce a weight-only 2-slot cp.async ring buffer: at T=128T = 128T=128, per-SM occupancy stays unchanged at 7 CTAs, cleanly isolating a 4.64 μs4.64\ \mu\text{s}4.64 μs saving from the 2-slot ring; at T=256T = 256T=256, Stage 6 latency drops by about 19 μs19\ \mu\text{s}19 μs alongside fewer registers lifting occupancy from 5 to 6 CTAs per SM (see the chart and note below). Opening too many ring slots consumes extra shared memory and drops occupancy (see Section 4; for the TMA ring counterexample where too few slots leave insufficient bytes in flight, see Section 9). We also tried refilling ring slots early inside the loop, where the compiler inserted a CTA barrier between refilling and dequantization and made the kernel slower (see the second chart below).

Step 4 offloads the decoding left shift onto the FMA pipeline (left-shift FMA offloading; see Chapter 5, Section 1). Five of the six benchmark workloads speed up—saving up to about 9.4 μs9.4\ \mu\text{s}9.4 μs in Stage 6 at T=128T = 128T=128—with only T=8T = 8T=8 coming out slightly slower.

4Why Does the Same Occupancy Change Turn from Faster to Slower Under a Different Routing Distribution?

As the number of active experts varies with routing, the total tile count varies too; changing per-SM occupancy alters the wave count only for routing distributions that cross a full-wave capacity step.

Back in Chapter 2, Section 1, we calculated wave counts: when each SM holds kkk resident CTAs at once, a single wave fits 132k132k132k CTAs, and total runtime is approximately ⌈Ac/(132k)⌉×\lceil A c / (132 k) \rceil \times⌈Ac/(132k)⌉× the duration of one wave. The expert kernel adds a moving variable: the number of active experts AAA is not constant, because different routing distributions hit different numbers of local experts, so the device-wide tile count AcA cAc (where ccc is the CTAs per expert) fluctuates with the routing distribution. Any change that alters kkk shifts the capacity step 132k132k132k. Routing distributions whose tile counts land between the old and new steps run one wave more or one wave fewer, shifting latency by several to over ten microseconds; distributions that do not cross a step see only the small intrinsic cost or benefit of the change itself.

We have a direct measured example at T=8T = 8T=8. We replace mma.sync with wgmma (see Chapter 5, Section 3); each expert launches c=128c = 128c=128 CTAs (gate/up projection 8,192 columns÷64 columns/CTA8{,}192\text{ columns} \div 64\text{ columns/CTA}8,192 columns÷64 columns/CTA), per-SM occupancy drops from k=9k = 9k=9 to k=8k = 8k=8, and a single wave shrinks from 1,1881{,}1881,188 CTAs to 1,0561{,}0561,056. The two routing distributions with A=9A = 9A=9 have 9×128=1,1529 \times 128 = 1{,}1529×128=1,152 CTAs, so they drop right across the boundary from 1 wave into 2 waves and slow Stage 6 down by over 10 μs10\ \mu\text{s}10 μs. The other three routing distributions (A=8A = 8A=8, still within 1 wave) run slightly faster instead (see the chart below). The same thing happens at T=16T = 16T=16 and T=32T = 32T=32 when we expand the weight ring buffer from the previous section from 3 slots to 4 slots and per-SM occupancy drops from 8 to 7: across multiple routing distributions it averages about 1.9 μs1.9\ \mu\text{s}1.9 μs faster, yet under each of the two workloads one routing distribution regresses.

That directly sets a rule: every occupancy or register change to an expert kernel must be benchmarked across multiple routing distributions simultaneously; a change that wins on only one distribution is rejected. To stop a change from moving the wave step 132k132k132k, we pin each CTA's register and shared-memory usage to the exact quota that fits kkk CTAs per SM (Chapter 3, Section 1), isolating the change's own gain or loss. For instance, pinning the T=16T = 16T=16 down projection at 7 CTAs per SM turns its new weight-only 2-slot ring buffer from a loss of about 2.1 μs2.1\ \mu\text{s}2.1 μs into a gain of about 1.8 μs1.8\ \mu\text{s}1.8 μs.

The cost of pinning occupancy is a tighter per-thread register cap. Push the compiler attribute __maxnreg__(N) too low and the compiler spills excess values to local memory (see Chapter 3, Section 1). Switching to wgmma at T=8T = 8T=8 and capping registers at 56 spills 8 registers per thread and slows Stage 6 by about 62 μs62\ \mu\text{s}62 μs; capping at 80 or 72 registers at T=256T = 256T=256 also causes slowdowns from register spilling (see the chart below).

5How Do Narrower Shapes Skip Blank Padding Rows in the Tail Tiles of Light Experts?

At tile entry, compare offset +16 of sorted_pair_ids with the padding sentinel RRR (loading +8 only when +16 is ≥R\ge R≥R) to step the MMA row height down through 32→16→832 \to 16 \to 832→16→8, shrinking only tail tiles with at most 16 valid rows to 16 or 8 rows.

Because token bucketing in Section 2 requires all tokens in a tile to belong to the same expert, we have to pad each expert's token count up to a multiple of the tile height BMBMBM (BMBMBM is the number of tokens per tile, which maps to nnn of wgmma after swap-AB). Under skewed routing, many light experts receive only a few tokens, and the last tile of a heavy expert (its tail tile, a partially filled M-tile) often holds only a few valid rows as well; the extra rows padded at the bottom are called padding rows. If we do nothing, every matrix multiplication issues at the full tile height.

Tail-tile M-dimension trimming never reads or computes a tile's valid row count vvv. Bucketing places valid entries (<R< R<R) first in the index table sorted_pair_ids and fills the trailing padding rows with the sentinel RRR; at tile entry (for M-tile blk), the kernel compares sorted_pair_ids[blk * 32 + 16] with RRR and loads +8 only when +16 is ≥R\ge R≥R, learning only whether vvv falls in v≤8v \le 8v≤8, 9..169..169..16, or ≥17\ge 17≥17: a tail tile with 17..3117..3117..31 valid rows keeps height 32, and only v≤16v \le 16v≤16 gets the narrower 16- or 8-row shape. Because swap-AB puts tokens on the nnn side of wgmma (see Chapter 5, Section 4), and the instruction shape m64nNk16 fixes m=64m = 64m=64 while letting nnn take any multiple of 8 (see Chapter 5, Section 3), tile height can step down through 32→16→832 \to 16 \to 832→16→8 across 3 heights.

How much tail-tile trimming saves varies with MeM_eMe​. On verify workloads (MeM_eMe​ around a dozen), tail tiles make up a large share of all tiles: clipping tail tiles down to 16 rows at T=256T = 256T=256 cuts Stage 6 time by about 26 μs26\ \mu\text{s}26 μs in one step (pure Tensor Core issue cycles account for only part of that saving, and the runtime split across activation loads, MMA, and the epilogue was not profiled with NCU), and introducing the 8-row tier saves even more. As MeM_eMe​ grows larger, on the other hand, the tail tile is only a small fraction at the end of a long queue, so the gain from trimming shrinks (the prefill kernel applies the same trimming; see Section 15).

What you pay for tail-tile trimming is generating extra narrow-tile code branches in the kernel, and having every CTA of every M-tile execute the +16 load at entry (adding 1 load when v≥17v \ge 17v≥17 and 2 dependent loads when v≤16v \le 16v≤16); at what workload size it loses performance was not measured.

6At T = 1..32, How Are Multi-Launch Round Trips Folded into a Persistent Kernel?

Fold bucketing, gate/up projection, and down projection into a persistent kernel with 132 resident CTAs; for T=8..32T = 8..32T=8..32, split back into two PDL-chained kernels to avoid the grid barrier.

In Stage 6, m2 launches token bucketing, the gate/up projection, the down projection, and post-expert RMSNorm one after another, paying a tail wave on every launch.

In the third generation (m3), Stage 6 moves to a persistent kernel (see Chapter 3, Section 1): 132 CTAs stay resident on the SMs (1 CTA of 8 warps per SM). At entry, each CTA works out which tiles it owns; it then steps through them one after another without exiting between tiles. Inside the kernel, Phase 0 runs token bucketing, followed by the gate/up projection with SwiGLU and then the down projection, streaming weights through a TMA ring buffer (see Chapter 3, Sections 3 and 4). Matrix multiplication inside m3 uses warp-level mma.sync (see Chapter 5, Section 3) rather than wgmma. Because m3 keeps 132 CTAs resident, it has no wave capacity steps (the Section 4 example, where occupancy dropped from 9 to 8 and crossed a wave step, was measured on m2's non-persistent grid); why mma.sync was still chosen was not determined. On m3's 1-CTA-per-SM persistent grid, adding warps per CTA does not necessarily pay off either: expanding each CTA from 8 warps to 16 warps at T=32T = 32T=32 (from 2 to 4 warps per SMSP) saves only about 0.85 μs0.85\ \mu\text{s}0.85 μs, sitting inside the control variation envelope (about 0.78 μs0.78\ \mu\text{s}0.78 μs) with no clear gain while costing an extra 8 warps of registers per CTA. One mma.sync tile holds at most 8 tokens; experts with more than 8 tokens are handled below.

Inside m3, Phase 0 token bucketing was also parallelized in a follow-up update (an early build first entered m3 at T=8T = 8T=8, and the next entered m3 at T=16T = 16T=16 saving 13.71 μs13.71\ \mu\text{s}13.71 μs; the following update replaced the single-thread serial scan over 256 slots at T=8..32T = 8..32T=8..32—for example, 32 tokens×8 slots32\text{ tokens} \times 8\text{ slots}32 tokens×8 slots at T=32T = 32T=32—with 8 warps scanning 32 slots each in parallel, bundled in the same build with 8-token virtual passes and 8-warp epilogue rotation to save another 20.29 μs20.29\ \mu\text{s}20.29 μs inside m3 at T=16T = 16T=16 and 7.70 μs7.70\ \mu\text{s}7.70 μs when switching T=32T = 32T=32 to m3, while T=1T = 1T=1 uses 1 warp). __ballot_sync collects a yes/no predicate from each of a warp's 32 lanes into a 32-bit integer where bit iii holds lane iii's answer, and __popc counts the set bits in that integer to tell us how many lanes in this warp hit. Each warp writes its hit count n to shared memory; after an intra-CTA barrier, summing n across the preceding warps gives this warp's write offset base (the snippet below shows that build's parallel-ballot step, still used for active-expert compaction and Section 10's LPT sort, whereas the frozen final build upgrades per-expert lane grouping to a single __match_any_sync instruction—SASS MATCH.ANY, returning in one step the mask of lanes in the warp holding the same expert ID—paired with __popc):

hit  = (topk_id[slot] == e);              // each lane tests whether its slot hits expert e
mask = __ballot_sync(FULL, hit);          // FULL = 0xffffffff (all 32 lanes participate)
n    = __popc(mask);                      // number of hits in this warp
pos  = base + __popc(mask & lanes_below); // lanes_below = (1u << lane) - 1 (mask of lower-numbered lanes)

Now consider hot experts where tokens pile up. Because a single mma.sync tile holds up to 8 tokens, that parallel-ballot build still split experts with more than 8 tokens into multiple 8-token passes that re-read weights; a later m3 version merges 9–16 tokens routed to one expert into a 16-token segment that feeds two 8-token tiles from the same decoded weight registers so weights are read once, while an expert routed 17–32 tokens is broken into two segments. Once T≥128T \ge 128T≥128, hot experts accumulate still more tokens, prompting the switch to a new kernel in Section 9.

Once the gate/up projection and the down projection are merged into a single persistent kernel, the down projection has to wait until the entire GPU finishes writing inter. Because CUDA guarantees full-grid co-residency only under cooperative launch (see Chapter 2, Section 6; see Chapter 7, Section 12 for the grid-barrier conditions required without cooperative launch), the T=1T = 1T=1 persistent kernel uses cooperative launch; synchronizing all 132 resident CTAs across the grid barrier once costs about 1.4 μs1.4\ \mu\text{s}1.4 μs in a microbenchmark. In this chapter's single-operator benchmark, T=1T = 1T=1 retains this single cooperatively launched persistent kernel.

For T=8..32T = 8..32T=8..32 in this chapter's single-operator benchmark, splitting the gate/up projection and the down projection into two kernels chained back-to-back with PDL pays off (Chapter 9's single-layer pipeline instead shares a single persistent expert kernel with an internal grid barrier across T=1T = 1T=1 and T=8T = 8T=8, and replaces cooperative launch with PDL in Chapter 9, Section 4). Because each kernel uses at least 115 KiB115\text{ KiB}115 KiB of shared memory (about 115 KiB115\text{ KiB}115 KiB at T=8T = 8T=8 and about 129 KiB129\text{ KiB}129 KiB at T=16,32T = 16, 32T=16,32), the two kernels do not fit together inside the 228 KiB228\text{ KiB}228 KiB per SM. Still, as soon as a gate/up CTA exits an SM, that SM immediately accepts a down-projection CTA, preloads its weight ring buffer into shared memory while the other SMs are finishing, and then pauses at the synchronization point (the cooperative build likewise preloads the first 3 down-projection weight slots before the full-grid barrier). Splitting into two kernels costs one extra PDL edge of about 0.64 μs0.64\ \mu\text{s}0.64 μs (see Chapter 1, Section 4) and nets under 1 μs1\ \mu\text{s}1 μs in Stage 6 (which factor produces the gain was not measured separately; see the chart below).

Can we stay in a single kernel and avoid the grid barrier? We tested fine-grained tile counters (where each finished inter tile increments its own counter so the down projection waits only for the tiles it needs) and in-band payload readiness flags (encoding the readiness flag and the inter payload in the same word). Every fine-grained counter handoff requires a device-wide memory barrier—the device-scope acq_rel memory fence from Chapter 2, Section 6: the issuing warp stalls until all prior writes reach L2, while other warps and SMs keep running. That slowed down several benchmark cases, and in-band payload readiness flags also slowed T=1T = 1T=1 by about 1 μs1\ \mu\text{s}1 μs (the exact causes of the slowdown in both approaches were not measured separately).

The post-expert RMSNorm kernel reads back y, skips non-local slots, and completes Steps 4 and 5 of Section 1; it already overlaps with the main kernel via PDL, and fusing it into the tail of the main kernel ran slower in single-operator tests.

7At Persistent Kernel Startup, Why Does Activation p Wait in Line Behind Weights?

At kernel entry, all 132 SMs issuing 3 weight slots simultaneously send about 14 MB of requests into the memory path; the first MMA waits on both shared-memory Slot 0 (full[0]) and p in registers (via the scoreboard), so issuing p and Slot 0 first while delaying Slots 1–2 by a few hundred nanoseconds is intended to reduce contention from Slots 1–2 against Slot 0 and p (arrival order after staggering was not measured).

On the T=1T = 1T=1 cooperative persistent kernel, activation p is only a few kilobytes and loads via LDG (through LSU → L1 → the on-chip crossbar XBAR) directly into registers, whereas weights load via TMA (bypassing L1) into shared-memory Slots 0–2, sharing the path from the L2 slices to HBM (see Chapter 3, Section 3). Entry timestamps taken with the GPU's 64-bit global nanosecond timer register %globaltimer (see Chapter 10, Section 5 for the stamping method; here elapsed time is measured within a single CTA) show that after Slot 0 weights (full[0]) arrive, warp 0—which issued all 3 weight TMA commands for its SM—still waits about 0.96 μs0.96\ \mu\text{s}0.96 μs on p's register scoreboard, whereas warps 1–7 (which issued no TMA) wait about 0.06 μs0.06\ \mu\text{s}0.06 μs. A likely reason is that normal global loads (LDG) and TMA requests contend for queues along the memory path (queueing could sit at the SM exit port, XBAR, L2 slice, or memory controller—the exact site was not measured, and other causes are not ruled out). That is queueing delay (see Chapter 7, Section 6): a small request of a few kilobytes gets stuck in line behind the bulk weight requests.

To fix it, we flip the issue order: issue the load of p and Slot 0 weights first, spin-wait on %globaltimer within the same CTA for a few hundred nanoseconds, and only then issue Slots 1 and 2. We do not call __nanosleep(500) here: the PTX specification guarantees only that nanosleep.u32 t sleeps for an interval in [0,2t][0, 2t][0,2t], so holding a fixed delay requires spinning on %globaltimer. Using a fixed delay without checking whether data has arrived is called open-loop staggering (intended to reduce contention from Slots 1–2 against Slot 0 and p; arrival order after staggering was not measured). At T=1T = 1T=1 (a single cooperative kernel), the shipped build also preloads the tensor scales into shared memory during Phase 0 (saving 0.41 μs0.41\ \mu\text{s}0.41 μs on its own, and 0.82,0.40,0.48 μs0.82, 0.40, 0.48\ \mu\text{s}0.82,0.40,0.48 μs at T=8,16,32T = 8, 16, 32T=8,16,32), saving 1.05 μs1.05\ \mu\text{s}1.05 μs in total at T=1T = 1T=1 when bundled with hoisting p and the 500 ns500\text{ ns}500 ns stagger. After splitting T=8..32T = 8..32T=8..32 into two PDL kernels (with tensor-scale preload already active; per-warp timestamps were not retaken at T=8T = 8T=8, so the queueing mechanism there is inferred from T=1T = 1T=1), the gate/up kernel isolates hoisting p plus the delay: T=8T = 8T=8 waits 600 ns600\text{ ns}600 ns, while T=16T = 16T=16 and 323232 simply issue p first with the delay set to 0 ns0\text{ ns}0 ns.

Because this is an open-loop wait, we cannot stretch the delay too far—waiting too long just artificially delays the weights. Sweeping the delay at T=8T = 8T=8 (see the chart below) shows the tradeoff: 0 ns0\text{ ns}0 ns (only issuing p first) captures only about half the gain, the three settings across 300–800 ns300\text{–}800\text{ ns}300–800 ns perform similarly (with 600 ns600\text{ ns}600 ns chosen in the end), and by 1,200 ns1{,}200\text{ ns}1,200 ns the saving drops back again.

The catch with open-loop staggering is that the best delay shifts with TTT, so each TTT needs its own sweep; a closed-loop alternative ("wait until p arrives, then issue Slots 1 and 2") was not measured. On the T=128..256T = 128..256T=128..256 kernel (Section 9), delaying Weight Slots 1 and 2 moves the first MMA instruction earlier by only about 0.4 μs0.4\ \mu\text{s}0.4 μs, and the upper bound on remaining savings at kernel entry is less than 1 μs1\ \mu\text{s}1 μs, so we stopped here.

8In the SASS of the Post-Expert RMSNorm Kernel, What Did the Compiler Schedule Poorly, and What Can Be Loaded Before Waiting?

An empty asm volatile statement blocks rematerialization, and issuing loads via asm volatile blocks instruction sinking; both are only effects observed with the current compiler, not guarantees of the specification.

The first compiler rewrite we run into is rematerialization: instead of keeping a value that has already been computed, the compiler throws it away and recomputes it every time it is needed. Take this 4-line example: outside the loop, the kernel unpacks 16 BF16 weights w[i] to FP32 (Chapter 6, Section 1), adds 1.0f, and stores them into nw[i], then reuses nw[i] repeatedly inside the loop:

float nw[16];
for (int i = 0; i < 16; ++i) nw[i] = 1.0f + float(w[i]);
for (int step = 0; step < steps; ++step)
    for (int i = 0; i < 16; ++i) acc[i] += x[step][i] * nw[i];

To save those 16 registers, ptxas may throw nw[i] away and unpack the BF16 w[i] to FP32 and add 1.0f again on every loop iteration. The numerical result stays identical, but every iteration runs 16 extra unpacks and 16 extra additions.

To stop ptxas from doing that, we place an empty inline-assembly barrier (asm volatile) asm volatile("" : "+f"(nw[i])); right after the precomputation:

for (int i = 0; i < 16; ++i) {
    nw[i] = 1.0f + float(w[i]);
    asm volatile("" : "+f"(nw[i]));
}

Because this empty assembly statement declares that it "reads and writes nw[i]," the compiler must treat nw[i] as the output of an opaque instruction that cannot be rematerialized from w[i]. At runtime it emits 0 instructions, at the cost of holding 16 FP32 registers (64 B per thread) live throughout the loop; after merging this barrier, the small-batch post-norm variant grew from 110 to 114 registers per thread (30,720 allocated registers per CTA), pushing its sum with the 144-register T=1T = 1T=1 cooperative main kernel (36,864 registers) past 65,536 and ending co-residency on the same SM at T=1T = 1T=1 (the cost of losing that co-residency was not measured separately).

The second compiler rewrite is instruction sinking (code sinking), where the compiler moves instructions to a later point in the schedule. In Chapter 1, Section 4, the call cudaGridDependencySynchronize() that waits for the predecessor kernel compiles to griddepcontrol.wait in PTX and ACQBULK in SASS. Before that wait, the kernel can issue loads for data that the predecessor kernel does not write (such as this kernel's own static weights), overlapping those loads with the wait:

uint4 w0 = w_ptr[idx];              // load issued early
cudaGridDependencySynchronize();    // PTX: griddepcontrol.wait / SASS: ACQBULK
use(w0);                            // consumed only after the wait

griddepcontrol.wait acts like an acquire barrier (Chapter 2, Section 6). The PTX specification promises only one thing: it waits until all prerequisite grids have completed and their memory operations are visible to the current grid. So accesses after the wait cannot move ahead of it. But nothing in the specification stops normal loads that sit before the wait from moving down past it. Once those loads sink past ACQBULK, the overlap between loading and waiting is gone. When we issue those loads with asm volatile, the SASS from our build shows that the loads stay ahead of the wait. Still, the PTX specification makes no such promise, so you need to inspect the SASS again after changing compiler versions.

There is a strict correctness boundary here: data written by the predecessor kernel (its output tensors and the routing results it computed) is guaranteed to be visible only after griddepcontrol.wait. Loading predecessor outputs early is valid only when both grids belong to the same memory synchronization domain (the CUDA grouping that determines which kernels share fence synchronization; all kernels share the default domain unless configured otherwise) and the predecessor kernel finishes writing and executes a GPU-scope release fence before triggering the successor (see Chapter 9, Section 5 for the complete rules and measured data-race violations). Instruction sinking itself affects only speed, not correctness.

Stage 6's post-expert RMSNorm kernel ran into both compiler rewrites at once. The first was instruction sinking. In the single-operator benchmark, the kernel entry originally issued 4 pre-wait 16 B16\text{ B}16 B loads (w_post and topk_weights, 2 each) with ld.global.nc, which routes loads through the SM's read-only cache path. ptxas sank them past ACQBULK. We made two changes: we issued normal global loads via asm volatile, and we replaced the post-wait local[] loads with pre-wait topk_ids loads (2 each; local[] is the per-slot local expert index written by the main kernel, with −1 for a slot that is not on this GPU). Now all 6 LDG.E.128 instructions stay ahead of ACQBULK. The PDL overlap window comes from two sources: co-residency where the register budget fits (at T=1T = 1T=1 and 888 in the 110-register build measured here; in the later 114-register final build only T=8T = 8T=8 co-resides, and this prefetch delta was not re-measured at T=1T = 1T=1 on the final build), or entering SMs freed as early-finishing primary CTAs exit while remaining primary CTAs finish (at T=16,32,128T = 16, 32, 128T=16,32,128, and at T=1T = 1T=1 in the final build; primary CTA exit-time spread was not measured). Across T=1..32T = 1..32T=1..32 every point speeds up, saving up to 0.67 μs0.67\ \mu\text{s}0.67 μs (about 0.7 μs0.7\ \mu\text{s}0.7 μs) in Stage 6 at T=16T = 16T=16 (see the chart below). On an earlier ungated prefetch arm before the T≤32T \le 32T≤32 gate was added (inferred to be the immediately preceding ungated build, rather than the T≤32T \le 32T≤32-gated build measured for the other bars), T=128T = 128T=128 instead slowed down by 0.45 μs0.45\ \mu\text{s}0.45 μs: we infer that reading topk_ids adds a cold HBM trip where post-wait local[] hits in L2, outweighing any overlap across m4's unmeasured CTA exit-time spread. The final single-operator version therefore enables this prefetch only for T≤32T \le 32T≤32.

Keep one caveat in mind: issuing all 6 prefetches is safe only in the standalone operator benchmark, where none of the 3 inputs is produced by a preceding kernel. Inside Chapter 9's full-layer pipeline, the Stage 4 kernel writes both topk_weights and topk_ids; without a preceding release fence, reading them ahead of the wait triggers the data race explained under the correctness boundary above. Consequently, the standalone post-expert RMSNorm kernel in the final full-layer build issues no loads ahead of the wait, deferring w_post, topk_weights, and the per-slot local expert index (which the Stage 4 kernel also writes in the full layer) until after the wait returns (Chapter 9, Section 5 states the rule for what may be read before wait).

Second was rematerialization: the 16 values nwi=1+wpost,inw_i = 1 + w_{post,i}nwi​=1+wpost,i​ that the post-expert RMSNorm kernel precomputed outside the loop were pulled back into the inner loop and recomputed, adding 321 FADD instructions alone. Adding the empty inline-assembly barrier cut static SASS on the small-batch variant (T≤32T \le 32T≤32) from 1,615 instructions down to 1,133 (482 fewer; the T>32T > 32T>32 variant drops from 1,603 to 1,120, or 483 fewer); in a 1,000-block paired run across T=1,16,32T = 1, 16, 32T=1,16,32, Stage 6 saves 0.21–0.30 μs0.21\text{–}0.30\ \mu\text{s}0.21–0.30 μs with all 95% confidence intervals strictly above 0 (see the chart below).

9At T = 128..256, Why Switch to a Persistent wgmma Kernel?

A persistent wgmma kernel with 132 resident CTAs lets up to 64 tokens routed to a hot expert share a single tile so weights are read only once, while eliminating full-kernel handoff waits between bucketing, gate/up projection, and down projection.

m3 suffices for T≤32T \le 32T≤32, but by T=128,256T = 128, 256T=128,256, hot experts receive several dozen tokens each. In the design space, continuing with 8 tokens per pass in m3 would re-read a hot expert's weights on every pass (m3 was not measured at T≥128T \ge 128T≥128), while staying on m2's 4-kernel tiled scheme pays 4 tail waves and forces the down projection to wait for the entire gate/up kernel to finish before reading inter.

The fourth generation (m4) switches to a single persistent kernel (see Chapter 3, Section 1), completing in-kernel bucketing, the gate/up projection with SwiGLU, and the down projection in one launch. All 132 CTAs take work in the order of one shared subtask table: during in-kernel bucketing, each CTA builds an identical copy of that table in its own shared memory. At first, work is assigned statically across the CTAs; in the next section, CTAs claim it by atomic increments of one global counter. One subtask covers at most 64 token rows × 256 output columns of one expert. An expert with at most 64 tokens fits into a single tile, so its weights are read from HBM only once. A hot expert with more than 64 tokens splits into several 64-row token tiles; its first tile tags the weight loads with the L2 residency hint (evict_last; see Chapter 2, Section 4), so later tiles hit in the 60 MiB L2 cache as much as possible. After SwiGLU, the output inter goes to a global intermediate matrix, and the down-projection phase reads it directly (Section 11 explains how the down projection knows that the inter tiles it needs are written). Meanwhile, the instruction family switches back from mma.sync in m3 to wgmma: once token counts reach several dozen rows, only wgmma, issued collectively by 4 warps, can keep the Tensor Cores fed (see Chapter 5, Sections 3 and 5). At T=256T = 256T=256, replacing m2's 4-kernel tiled scheme with this persistent wgmma kernel for the first time cuts Stage 6 latency by 22.54 μs22.54\ \mu\text{s}22.54 μs (about 22 μs22\ \mu\text{s}22 μs). Its costs are three: only 96 registers per thread, 2 extra producer warps per CTA, and building that subtask table redundantly in every CTA.

In the initial version, each CTA has 18 warps (576 threads). During the kernel entry phase, 4 consumer warpgroups (512 threads) gather the activations of tokens hitting this GPU and write them into a global buffer; once the main loop begins, they dedicate themselves to matrix multiplication, while the other 2 warps serve exclusively as producers. Warp 16 uses TMA to feed the 3-slot shared-memory weight ring buffer. Warp 17 uses TMA to feed activations from the global buffer into the shared-memory activation ring buffer: the gate/up projection reads the gathered p, and the down projection reads the inter written by the gate/up projection. Slots in both ring buffers synchronize via full and empty mbarrier signals (see Chapter 3, Sections 3–5).

Only 96 registers per thread: in the Chapter 3, Section 6 example (1 CTA per SM, 2 consumer warpgroups), each consumer thread got 232 registers; here we have 4 consumer warpgroups, and 4×128×232=118,784>65,5364 \times 128 \times 232 = 118{,}784 > 65{,}5364×128×232=118,784>65,536 does not fit. As Chapter 4, Section 3 explained, an SM's 65,536 registers are partitioned equally across its 4 SMSPs at 16,384 registers per SMSP: spreading 18 warps across 4 SMSPs places ⌈18/4⌉=5\lceil 18 / 4 \rceil = 5⌈18/4⌉=5 warps (160 threads, billed as 4×160=6404 \times 160 = 6404×160=640 threads across the 4 SMSPs) on two SMSPs, capping every thread at 16,384/160=65,536/640=102.416{,}384 / 160 = 65{,}536 / 640 = 102.416,384/160=65,536/640=102.4, rounded down to a multiple of 8 to land on 96. That differs from dividing the whole-SM pool in Chapter 3, Section 1 by 576 threads alone, which would give 112 registers.

Profiling the initial build of this kernel turned up two problems. First, a runtime branch inside the wgmma pipeline region caused ptxas to serialize wgmma (placing a wait after every HGMMA; see Chapter 6, Section 6 for the mechanism), which we fixed by hoisting that branch out of the region. Second, the entry activation gather originally used scalar writes before we switched it to 16 B16\text{ B}16 B coalesced wide stores (see Chapter 3, Section 2). Prior to those two fixes, the kernel lagged behind the 4-kernel tiled scheme.

Now look at the byte budget of the weight ring buffer. Each slot holds 256 columns×inner dimension 256 elements256\text{ columns} \times \text{inner dimension } 256\text{ elements}256 columns×inner dimension 256 elements: 32 KiB32\text{ KiB}32 KiB of codewords plus 3 KiB3\text{ KiB}3 KiB of block scales packed to 6 bits, for 35 KiB35\text{ KiB}35 KiB in total. By the rule in Chapter 3, Section 4, while 1 slot is being computed, the remaining N−1N - 1N−1 slots are in flight: a 3-slot ring keeps 2 slots (70 KiB70\text{ KiB}70 KiB) in flight, whereas shrinking to 2 slots leaves only 1 slot (35 KiB35\text{ KiB}35 KiB) in flight—below the roughly 36–40 KiB36\text{–}40\text{ KiB}36–40 KiB per SM 95%95\%95% knee of Chapter 3, Section 4's streaming TMA curve (40 KiB40\text{ KiB}40 KiB at 1 CTA per SM, with 48 KiB48\text{ KiB}48 KiB as the 3-slot plateau step at about 98%–99%98\%\text{–}99\%98%–99%; though 35 KiB35\text{ KiB}35 KiB already sits above that curve's 32 KiB32\text{ KiB}32 KiB point at about 92%–95%92\%\text{–}95\%92%–95%, and here it also overlaps consumer decode/MMA and warp 17's activation TMA; how much each masks the bandwidth dip was not measured). Shrinking the ring to 2 slots alone therefore slows Stage 6 by about 1.2–1.3 μs1.2\text{–}1.3\ \mu\text{s}1.2–1.3 μs at T=128T = 128T=128 and T=256T = 256T=256 (see the chart below).

10How Do All 132 Resident CTAs Finish Together?

All four optimizations target tail latency: longest-processing-time-first ordering, atomic producer work claiming, reverse-order down-projection assignment, and tail K-halves splitting.

The duration of a persistent kernel equals the duration of its last-exiting CTA. When full heavy subtasks and light 8-row tail tiles (which still read an entire weight tile, taking about 17 μs17\ \mu\text{s}17 μs) are mixed together, whichever CTA lands a heavy task near the end stalls the entire GPU. Each of the four changes below pays off only when there is a tail skew to trim:

First is LPT (Longest Processing Time first scheduling), which we already used in prefill attention in Chapter 7, Section 4: we sort subtasks in descending order of padded token count so heavy subtasks run first and short 8-row subtasks fill the remaining gaps across SMs at the end. The cost is that every CTA runs the sort at entry; by T=3,012T = 3{,}012T=3,012 and 16,38416{,}38416,384, the speedup disappears (at T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384, nearly every tile is already a full tile, so there are no short tail tiles left to pack; see the fourth chart below).

Second is dynamic work claiming (atomic ticket) (this chapter's standalone Stage 6 m4 enables LPT, dynamic atomic claiming, and tail K-halves below at both T=128T = 128T=128 and T=256T = 256T=256, whereas Chapter 9's full-layer m4 splits into two variants, using dynamic claiming at T=128T = 128T=128 and keeping static back-and-forth dealing paired with reverse load-rank assignment below at T=256T = 256T=256). Take a T=128T = 128T=128 routing distribution from the full-layer benchmark: 16 token tiles, each with 32 gate/up subtasks and 16 down-projection subtasks, for 768 subtasks in total. With static assignment, 108 CTAs get 6 subtasks and 24 CTAs get 5. That one-subtask gap comes from integer division and cannot be eliminated. The real saving comes from uneven subtask durations: gate/up and down-projection subtasks take different amounts of time, and so do full tiles versus short 8-row tail tiles. Under static assignment, a CTA that happens to be assigned several slow subtasks in a row drags out the tail, while SMs assigned only 5 subtasks finish early and sit idle. Instead, while the current subtask is running, each CTA's weight-producer warp uses a single atomic add on a global counter to claim the next subtask from its own shared-memory LPT subtask table. Dynamic work claiming pays off only when single-subtask duration far exceeds claiming overhead and claiming introduces no extra intra-CTA barrier: here a single subtask runs for over ten microseconds, and the claimed subtask is handed to consumers through shared memory without adding a barrier. In Chapter 7, Section 4, by contrast, every claimed 64-key attention tile adds a metadata handoff and a 128-thread intra-CTA barrier, raising per-tile cost by about 10% while breaking the page-table prefetch pipeline, which loses performance.

Third is reverse load-rank assignment, used on Chapter 9's full-layer T=256T = 256T=256 static back-and-forth variant (not used in the standalone Stage 6 m4). Under static dealing, the gate/up projection and the down projection originally claimed subtasks in the same alternating sweep order, so the heaviest down-projection subtasks landed on the exact CTAs that had just finished the heaviest gate/up subtasks, stacking two heavy phases onto the same SMs. Recording each CTA's load rank in Phase 0 (which itself adds 1.6–1.8 μs1.6\text{–}1.8\ \mu\text{s}1.6–1.8 μs to Phase 0; its initial version lost slightly on T=128T = 128T=128 sliding-window at 0.995×0.995\times0.995×) lets the down projection assign work in reverse order: the CTAs with the lightest gate/up load claim the heaviest down-projection subtasks first. Per-CTA exit timestamps at T=256T = 256T=256 compress the latest CTA exit from 189.4 μs189.4\ \mu\text{s}189.4 μs to 176.3 μs176.3\ \mu\text{s}176.3 μs on sliding-window layers (and from 215.0 μs215.0\ \mu\text{s}215.0 μs to 195.0 μs195.0\ \mu\text{s}195.0 μs on full-attention layers), with the project changelog recording single-layer speedups of 4.2%4.2\%4.2% (about 4%4\%4%) and 0.82%0.82\%0.82% (see the third chart and note below).

Fourth is tail K-halves splitting, used in the standalone cooperative m4 at T=128,256T = 128, 256T=128,256 (see Chapter 2, Section 5 for the K-halves mechanism). Two conditions trigger it. First, the final wave of the subtask table has at most 66 subtasks left (no more than half of 132). Second, after sorting by row count in descending order, the fifth-from-last token tile has only 8 rows. Because each token tile produces 16 down-projection subtasks, the last 5 token tiles cover 80 subtasks, which guarantees that all 66 split subtasks at the end of the table are short 8-row tiles. When both conditions hold, we split each of the last 66 subtasks in the table in half along K, creating 2 × 66 half-K tasks that divide evenly across all 132 SMs. Chapter 2, Section 5 splits only the subtasks left over in the final wave; here we also split subtasks from the end of the second-to-last wave to fill out a full set of 66. The first half writes out an FP32 partial sum and sets a readiness flag (release), and the second half waits on that flag (acquire) and adds its half in (see Chapter 2, Section 6 for the ordering rules of cross-SM partial-sum merging). That wait always finishes, for three reasons: all 132 CTAs are resident at once (the single-operator version guarantees this with cooperative launch; see Section 6), every first half sits ahead of its second half in the table, and the CTAs claim subtasks in table order. So the earliest unfinished subtask in the table only ever waits on subtasks that have already finished, never on a later subtask. With the split, the other half of the SMs, which would otherwise sit idle, get work too. The cost is an extra partial-sum matrix and a set of flags; on routing distributions where the guard keeps splitting off, Stage 6 still slows down by 0.75 μs0.75\ \mu\text{s}0.75 μs and 0.52 μs0.52\ \mu\text{s}0.52 μs (exact cause not measured; see the second chart below), so we enable splitting only when both conditions above hold.

11Why Do Consumers Stall on Synchronization, and How Do We Move GPU-Scope Releases Off the Critical Path?

When every consumer thread pays its own GPU-scope release, Stage 6 is measured about 93 µs slower; the fix has only one thread per warp issue the release once, and then hands the GPU-scope release to a dedicated warp.

In the persistent wgmma kernel, every time the consumer warpgroups finish a gate/up subtask, they set a completion flag to tell the down-projection phase that this inter tile has been written. In development-stage diagnostic runs, the first bottleneck came from per-thread releases: having all 512 consumer threads fire red.release.gpu at the same L2 counter queued atomic requests at one L2 address and ran 93.3 μs93.3\ \mu\text{s}93.3 μs (about 93 μs93\ \mu\text{s}93 μs) slower than aligning each warp with __syncwarp (see Chapter 4, Section 4) so lane 0 alone issued 1 immediate release per warp (16 in total). Still before m4 was promoted in Section 9, development builds first deferred that per-warp release into group 3 of the next subtask's first stage (standalone delta not measured) and then switched to 1 leader thread per warpgroup (4 in total) releasing later, saving another about 20–23.6 μs20\text{–}23.6\ \mu\text{s}20–23.6 μs relative to the group-3 position (source records differ slightly, and the 16-to-4 count reduction alone was not measured; the initial m4 promotion in Section 9 already included this step). In the subsequent frozen builds retained on disk (after an unrecorded shift in release site), on consecutive gate/up subtasks the 4 warpgroup leaders wt == 0 issue red.release.gpu right after stage 0's 8 wg_wait<1>() groups with no wg_wait<0>() and no intra-warpgroup barrier (whose cross-thread causality is not determined under the PTX specification; the warpgroup barrier runs only on the flush path before each down-projection subtask and at kernel exit). Below, we show how a dedicated release thread removes even those 4 GPU-scope releases from the consumers.

The remaining problem is that even with just 4 warpgroup leaders issuing releases, every GPU-scope release still executes a device-wide memory barrier inside the consumers (fence.acq_rel.gpu or red.release.gpu compiles to an instruction sequence containing MEMBAR.ALL.GPU). L1 caches across SMs are not automatically coherent. On the writer side, each device-wide memory barrier waits for prior global writes to drain to L2: per-CTA timestamps on Chapter 9's full-layer expert kernel measured 0.6–1.3 μs0.6\text{–}1.3\ \mu\text{s}0.6–1.3 μs per barrier under load (inside standalone m4, the per-subtask stall was not stamped, and design notes estimated about 400–700 cycles). On the reader side, once a thread reads the flag with acquire.gpu, subsequent normal loads from that same thread see all prior writes published by the release (Chapter 2, Section 6). To publish completion flags and activation readiness, m4 makes three changes:

Step 1: publishing activation-gather readiness at kernel entry switches to a cross-proxy fence. Normal thread loads and stores travel through the generic proxy, whereas asynchronous TMA and wgmma reads travel through the async proxy; bridging the two takes fence.proxy.async (see Chapter 3, Section 3). On the reader side, the thread issuing TMA executes fence.proxy.async.global after ld.acquire.gpu and before issuing TMA (both when the gate/up projection reads gathered activations and when the down projection reads inter). On the writer side, 16 consumer warps write gathered activations into the global buffer at kernel entry, where previously every thread executed fence.acq_rel.gpu (5 SASS instructions). Now each thread executes only a single-instruction fence.proxy.async.global, and after a CTA barrier, thread 0 issues a single red.release.gpu; by cumulativity (Chapter 2, Section 6), this suffices (see the chart below for the speedup). For safety, we placed this cross-proxy fence on both the writer and reader sides; what happens if the writer-side fence is removed was not measured.

Step 2: consumers perform only an on-chip CTA-scope release and delegate the GPU-scope release to a dedicated release thread. Why did just 4 warpgroup leaders wt == 0 issuing MEMBAR.ALL.GPU still stall all 512 consumers? Because wgmma is warpgroup-wide (sync.aligned; see Chapter 5, Section 3) and all 4 warpgroups step through the shared weight ring together: stalling wt == 0's warp on MEMBAR.ALL.GPU stalls its entire 128-thread warpgroup and holds back the CTA's Tensor Core pipeline. Instead, each time a consumer thread finishes a subtask, it issues only an on-chip red.release.cta on its warpgroup's shared-memory counter. A dedicated thread waits with ld.acquire.cta until all 4 warpgroup counters reach the target, and then issues a single red.release.gpu on behalf of the CTA for each subtask that needs a flag, in subtask order. Every gate/up subtask needs this flag; among down-projection subtasks, only the first half of a K-halves split from Section 10 needs a readiness flag (which this dedicated thread also publishes), while the remaining down-projection subtasks publish none. When the dedicated thread observes the counters via acquire, it also observes all writes performed by the consumers before their release. When it then issues a GPU-scope release, it publishes all writes it has observed—cumulativity holds across scopes as well (see Chapter 2, Section 6). After warp 17 in the down projection observes the flag via ld.acquire.gpu, it likewise executes a reader-side fence.proxy.async.global before issuing TMA (see Step 1; inter has no writer-side proxy fence). Because all gate/up subtasks precede all down-projection subtasks in the subtask table, by the ordering invariant of Section 10 this wait cannot deadlock either.

Step 3: give the dedicated release thread its own dedicated release warp. Initially, the release thread lived on lane 1 of weight-producer warp 16. Although lane 0 and lane 1 of warp 16 each have their own program counter, the warp issues instructions for only one of their paths at a time (see Chapter 4, Section 4). While lane 1 polls and issues releases, lane 0's path waits for the warp to switch back, so lane 0 cannot issue the next round of weight TMA loads on time (how long each switch takes was not measured separately). We therefore add 1 extra warp per CTA (warp 18, expanding the CTA from 576 to 608 threads) and move the release thread there. At T=256T = 256T=256, deleting MEMBAR in place without moving the thread to a separate warp saves much less time (see the chart below), showing that most of the gain comes from no longer blocking lane 0. The cost is 32 extra threads per CTA (608 threads are still billed as 640 threads at the same 96-register per-thread cap from Section 9). Conversely, having this dedicated thread also emit per-phase signals to wake the post-expert RMSNorm kernel early does not pay off: the upper bound of tail latency that could be hidden is only 1.06–2.21 μs1.06\text{–}2.21\ \mu\text{s}1.06–2.21 μs, while emitting the signal itself costs 2.2–3.2 μs2.2\text{–}3.2\ \mu\text{s}2.2–3.2 μs, so every signaling variant tested ran slower.

There is also a correctness fix, measured across two distinct builds in the standalone operator benchmark and Chapter 9's full-layer benchmark. Consumers must not arrive on the weight ring's empty barrier before the shared-memory loads from the slot have returned to registers; otherwise the producer's next TMA transfer can overwrite a slot that is still being read (see Chapter 3, Section 5 for the arrival rule). In the code, mbarrier.arrive.shared::cta uses the default .release.cta semantics. By the PTX specification, that orders prior shared-memory reads before the arrival only within the generic proxy; it does not cover the next round's TMA write, which goes through the async proxy (Chapter 3, Section 5). On top of that, the compiled arrival instruction did not wait for the scoreboard of preceding shared-memory reads (see Chapter 4, Section 2 for scoreboards). In the isolated standalone Stage 6 build, moving only the weight-ring empty-barrier arrival after the wait on the activation ring's full barrier (Section 9)—with no intra-CTA fence and no change to activation-ring arrivals—reduced observed corruptions from 551 events in about 4.58 million calls down to 0 events in about 4.40 million calls, at a measured cost of slowing Stage 6 by 0.4–1.6 μs0.4\text{–}1.6\ \mu\text{s}0.4–1.6 μs (this is a correctness requirement, not an optional optimization).

Waiting on the activation ring's full barrier, however, has no data dependency on the weight reads. In the compiled T=256T = 256T=256 full-layer version of Chapter 9, even when the source code placed the decoding instructions that consume the weight registers before the arrival instruction, the compiler still sank them past it. Reordering the source alone was no longer enough at T=256T = 256T=256, so Chapter 9's full-layer fix bundled three changes: deferring the weight-ring empty arrival, adding an explicit fence.acq_rel.cta before that arrival at T=256T = 256T=256 (omitted at T=128T = 128T=128 under the benchmark compiler, where deferring the arrival alone clears unreturned shared-memory loads at arrival sites from 16 of 34 down to 0 of 34), and having lane 0 of each consumer warp arrive once on the activation ring's empty barrier. In the T=256T = 256T=256 SASS, that fence lowers to an instruction that waits until pending shared-memory loads land in registers, pairing with the deferred arrival to clear unreturned shared-memory loads at arrival sites from 24 of 50 down to 0 of 50; the 3-part bundle slows the 12-case full-layer geometric mean by 0.55%0.55\%0.55% (2.0%2.0\%2.0% and 1.1%1.1\%1.1% on T=256T = 256T=256 sliding-window and full-attention layers). Why the default release did not emit that wait instruction was not determined; this is only what the current compiler does (Section 8). Neither the latency delta of the fence alone nor the race count of this merged full-layer build was measured separately.

12Before Each CUDA Graph Replay, Who Zeros the Completion Counters?

Maintain even and odd counter arrays alternated by launch index; once a launch gets its ledger index, idle producer threads zero the opposite array for the next launch.

The completion flags in Section 11 are an array of global counters; on every CUDA Graph replay (see Chapter 1, Section 2), the next launch has to see all zeros. Previously, before each launch finished, every CTA ran an exit sequence (one device-wide memory barrier, two CTA barriers, one atomic increment, and several zeroing stores) so the last-exiting CTA could zero the counters. That exit sequence sat right on the critical path of the last-exiting CTA.

To get that cleanup off the tail, we switch to an even-odd ledger (ping-pong counter array): the counter buffer in device memory is doubled and split into an even ledger and an odd ledger (see Figure 8-11 for indices and buffer sizes). At kernel entry, thread 0 of each CTA runs atom.inc on a global counter to claim a ticket ttt (see Chapter 2, Section 7 for atomic ticket numbers). Because that instruction carries the upper limit 2G−12G - 12G−1 (where GGG is the number of CTAs per launch), hardware wraps the counter back to 0 once it hits the limit, keeping every ticket ttt between 000 and 2G−12G - 12G−1. Taking ⌊t/G⌋\lfloor t / G \rfloor⌊t/G⌋ gives 0 or 1 to pick which ledger this launch uses: each launch claims GGG tickets that all land on the same ledger, and the next launch switches to the opposite ledger. Lanes 1–31 of the weight-producer warp are otherwise idle; once Phase 0 bucketing ends and the CTA barrier hands them this launch's ledger index, they zero the inactive ledger for the next launch. The K-halves readiness flags and dynamic work-claiming counter from Section 10 are zeroed together inside the same even-odd ledger.

Why do tickets from two consecutive launches not interleave, and why does zeroing the opposite ledger never collide with the previous or next launch? Two preconditions guarantee this. First, every launch uses the same GGG, and all launches execute in order on the same CUDA stream. Second, every expert kernel launch is followed by the post-expert RMSNorm kernel; when that kernel's griddepcontrol.wait returns (see Chapter 1, Section 4; Section 8 of this chapter), the expert kernel before it has finished. The single-operator final expert kernel launches without PDL, so it enters only after the preceding post-expert RMSNorm kernel finishes. By the time it enters, claims tickets, and zeroes the idle ledger, the prior expert kernel launch has exited completely and will not claim another ticket or touch that ledger. Likewise, the next expert kernel launch enters only after the current launch's post-expert RMSNorm kernel finishes, by which time the current launch (zeroing stores included) has already finished.

Deleting the exit sequence from the tail of the kernel removes one device-wide memory barrier and two CTA barriers on the tail path, saving about 0.3 μs0.3\ \mu\text{s}0.3 μs in Stage 6 at T=256T = 256T=256 (see the chart below). The cost of the even-odd ledger is 4 KiB4\text{ KiB}4 KiB of extra device memory while shifting the zeroing stores onto the idle threads of the producer warp; whether any workload loses performance was not measured.

13What Bottlenecks the Gap Between Subtasks, and Why Does Folding the Scale into the Exponent Save Instructions?

Inside the gate/up subtask-switch gap, the SwiGLU epilogue is issue-slot bound (the down-projection switch has no SwiGLU and its cause was not determined); folding the tensor scale into the exponent argument and denominator cuts instructions from 9 to 7 per element, and the final version switches to a tanh⁡\tanhtanh form to cut them to 6.

Per-CTA timestamps split subtask switches (including the tile epilogue; see Chapter 1, Section 3) into about 1.26 μs1.26\ \mu\text{s}1.26 μs (about 1.3 μs1.3\ \mu\text{s}1.3 μs) per gate/up switch and 1.75 μs1.75\ \mu\text{s}1.75 μs (about 1.8 μs1.8\ \mu\text{s}1.8 μs) per down-projection switch, totaling about 12.7 μs12.7\ \mu\text{s}12.7 μs per CTA (6.1%6.1\%6.1% of total kernel runtime). The down projection has no SwiGLU, timestamps show neither stores nor stage-0 data are exposed, and expanding m4's main loop from 2 decoded-weight register buffers (operand A) to a third (wait_group<2>; see Chapter 5, Section 5) moves warpgroup_arrive stalls only from 14.6%14.6\%14.6% to 14.3%14.3\%14.3% for zero gain—data supply is not the bottleneck, and the cause of the 1.75 μs1.75\ \mu\text{s}1.75 μs down-projection switch gap was not determined. Focusing on the gate/up (1.26 μs1.26\ \mu\text{s}1.26 μs) pre-fold 9-instruction (ex2 plus reciprocal) SwiGLU epilogue: a derived SMSP cycle tally gives 932 issue cycles across the 4 consumer warps versus 768 SFU (MUFU) cycles, and recompiled source-edit variants on this 9-instruction form that traded the 2 MUFU ops for roughly 14 extra issue slots per element were all flat or slower. That confirms the gate/up epilogue is bottlenecked by the issue slot, which issues at most one instruction per cycle (see Chapter 4, Section 1), rather than by SFU throughput (see Chapter 5, Section 1).

Here we also answer the question left open in Section 1: why do the gate half and the up-projection half of each expert share a single tensor scale sss? In the original model, the two halves have separate tensor scales sgs_gsg​ and sus_usu​; let r=su/sgr = s_u / s_gr=su​/sg​. Because SwiGLU is linear in the up projection uuu, changing uuu's scale from sus_usu​ to the gate scale sgs_gsg​ only multiplies the down-projection output yyy by a positive constant 1/r=sg/su1/r = s_g / s_u1/r=sg​/su​. And in Step 4 of Section 1, each expert runs its own RMSNorm right after the down projection and before the weighted accumulation across experts. Because RMSNorm divides a vector by its own root mean square, any positive constant c>0c > 0c>0 cancels out between numerator and denominator: ignoring the tiny constant ϵ\epsilonϵ, rmsnorm(c z)=rmsnorm(z)\mathrm{rmsnorm}(c\,z) = \mathrm{rmsnorm}(z)rmsnorm(cz)=rmsnorm(z). Each expert's gate/up projection therefore stores only a single tensor scale s=sgs = s_gs=sg​.

Because instruction count is the bottleneck, we use that shared scale sss to fold instructions algebraically. Let dg,dud_g, d_udg​,du​ be the unscaled accumulator values in registers before multiplying by sss (g=s dgg = s\,d_gg=sdg​, u=s duu = s\,d_uu=sdu​), and substitute them into SwiGLU:

silu(g) u=s dg1+e−s dg s du=dg duk+k⋅2 dg⋅(−slog⁡2e),k=1/s2.\mathrm{silu}(g)\,u = \frac{s\,d_g}{1 + e^{-s\,d_g}}\, s\,d_u = \frac{d_g\, d_u}{k + k \cdot 2^{\,d_g \cdot (-s \log_2 e)}},\qquad k = 1/s^2 .silu(g)u=1+e−sdg​sdg​​sdu​=k+k⋅2dg​⋅(−slog2​e)dg​du​​,k=1/s2.

Here both −slog⁡2e-s \log_2 e−slog2​e and kkk are constants per expert: multiplying once when computing the exponent argument and evaluating the denominator with a single FFMA(e, k, k) absorbs both multiplications by sss. That cuts the gate/up epilogue from 9 instructions per element down to 7; the build introducing this fold saves about 0.6 μs0.6\ \mu\text{s}0.6 μs in Stage 6 at T=256T = 256T=256 (see the chart below). The final version goes one step further and rewrites SwiGLU as silu(g)=g2(1+tanh⁡(g/2))\mathrm{silu}(g) = \frac{g}{2}(1 + \tanh(g/2))silu(g)=2g​(1+tanh(g/2)). With K=s2/2K = s^2/2K=s2/2 and A=KdgA = K d_gA=Kdg​, each element computes A(1+tanh⁡(dg⋅s/2))⋅duA(1 + \tanh(d_g \cdot s/2)) \cdot d_uA(1+tanh(dg​⋅s/2))⋅du​. A single tanh.approx (MUFU.TANH) replaces ex2 plus the reciprocal, dropping the gate/up epilogue to 6 instructions, with only 1 of them on the SFU. This chapter does not list the standalone gain of this step (Chapter 10, Section 8 separately reports recompiled source-edit checks on this later 6-instruction tanh⁡\tanhtanh form: removing MUFU.TANH changed whole-kernel latency by 0.0%0.0\%0.0%—with exact build, cell, and replacement unrecorded, which does not by itself separate SFU from issue slots, cause not determined—whereas replacing it with a longer polynomial slowed the kernel by 0.4%0.4\%0.4%).

What epilogue scale folding costs is computing two scale constants before each subtask's epilogue (−slog⁡2e-s\log_2 e−slog2​e and kkk, or s/2s/2s/2 and K=s2/2K = s^2/2K=s2/2 in the tanh⁡\tanhtanh form), and relying on the gate and up projections sharing a single scale. This folding pays off only when the epilogue is issue-slot bound: porting it to Chapter 9's full-layer expert kernels (m3 and m4) trims 22%–41%22\%\text{–}41\%22%–41% of the epilogue instructions yet leaves single-layer latency unchanged (0.999×0.999\times0.999×), from which we infer that the epilogue inside the full layer is not issue-slot bound.

14When All 32 Experts Are Busy in Prefill, How Large Should the Grid Be and Who Dispatches Tiles to SMs?

m5 caps the main grid at twice the per-GPU average hit-pair count (~TTT) plus alignment padding (with 2 separate overflow kernels in the measured builds, later folded into the main kernels' tail loops), while launching 9,216 ordinary CTAs for the down projection under the hardware block distributor.

Across the workloads in the earlier sections, the mean token count per expert remains under 58; in prefill, T=3,012T = 3{,}012T=3,012 and 16,38416{,}38416,384 step past 58 (while T=753T = 753T=753 stays below the threshold). The fifth generation (m5) is the grouped GEMM built for prefill, and every optimization below is measured in paired ABBA runs against the immediately preceding version of m5 itself (m4 and m5 were not benchmarked against each other on the same shape). Three names appear throughout this section. The route-alignment kernel reorders hit pairs by expert, pads each expert up to a multiple of the tile height BMBMBM, and outputs the reordered token table and per-tile expert IDs. gemm1 is the gate and up projection (Step 1 of Section 1, computing SwiGLU in its epilogue). gemm2 is the down projection (Step 3 of Section 1).

Step 1 keeps only tiles belonging to this GPU: the route-alignment kernel outputs tiles only for the 32 local experts on this GPU, filtering out non-local slots at the source. The cost is pre-allocating a fixed-size worst-case buffer in device memory that CUDA Graph reuses on every replay (Chapter 1, Section 2). How much extra memory that buffer takes and when it would lose performance were not measured separately.

Step 2 sets the grid size. Each CUDA Graph replay uses the grid size fixed at capture (or at the last graph update; see Chapter 1, Section 2), while the actual number of local hits is only computed on the GPU during that replay. Originally, the grid was sized for the worst case: all 8 slots of every token landing on this GPU, plus one padding tile for each of the 32 local experts (1,056 tiles in total at T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384). Counted under the busiest-GPU benchmark workload at T=16,384T = 16{,}384T=16,384, 77% of the CTAs find no work upon entry and exit immediately, implying that only about 1,056×0.23≈2431{,}056 \times 0.23 \approx 2431,056×0.23≈243 tiles have actual work (see Figure 8-13).
