Chapters 1–9 open up only the hardware units directly hit by this book's kernel evolution chains; Appendix B covers the machine instructions discussed across the main text, figures, and this appendix; and Appendix C indexes terms that recur across the book alphabetically. When you read NVIDIA architecture whitepapers, the PTX and CUDA manuals, or Nsight Compute (NCU) panels, you also run into single-GPU inference hardware units and modes that our Muse Spark Open workload either never expands on or mentions only once in passing—this appendix organizes them into four quick-reference tables, moving from off-chip to intra-SM and from arithmetic to data movement.

Scope and epistemic labels: This appendix covers model-inference hardware on a single Hopper (sm_90a, H200 SXM) GPU only; graphics rasterization and ray tracing, texture sampling and filtering, video and image codecs (NVDEC / NVENC / OFA / NVJPG), confidential computing and virtualization administration (TEE / MIG setup / SR-IOV), power/thermal governors and ECC scrubbing, double-precision-only (FP64) pipelines, dynamic-programming DPX instructions, and multi-GPU or host interconnects (NVLink / NVSwitch / PCIe / GPUDirect RDMA / multimem) lie outside this book's scope. Every entry distinguishes what is Documented in official NVIDIA manuals/datasheets, what is Measured via device attribute on H200 or on sibling GH100 GPUs in public papers, what is Derived from documented or measured constants, what is Inferred, and what remains Unknown (not published / not measured / not disassembled) in public documentation and in this book.

1Chip Physical Topology and Global Memory Path

On the compute side, the chip groups hardware across four levels—Die → GPC → TPC → SM—while on the global-memory side traffic travels from SMs through the partitioned crossbar (XBAR) and the L2 Request Coalescer (LRC) into two-partition L2 slices (LTS) and out through FrameBuffer Partitions (FBPA) to HBM3e; internal arbitration orders, exact attachment points of the MMU and LRC, and H200's active slice and controller counts are not published.

Unit / NCU Name Location on Chip What It Does, Limits, and Epistemic Status Book kernel and Chapter Pointer
Die → GPC → TPC → SM hierarchy (tpc, launch__tpc_count) Full GH100 die → GPC → TPC (2 SMs plus 1 shared ICC per TPC; 1 IDC inside each SM) Documented (H100 whitepaper p18, p29; NCU §2.3.4, §2.4.2): a GPC is a group of physically close SMs; TPCs sit inside a GPC, with 1 Instruction Constant Cache (ICC) per TPC servicing all SM sub-partitions in that TPC, whereas the Indexed Constant Cache (IDC, accessed by LDC) is a per-SM cache; full GH100 has 8 GPC × 9 TPC × 2 SM = 144 SM (72 TPCs) and H100 SXM5 has 8 GPC / 66 TPC / 132 SM (the H200 datasheet prints no SM count). Measured via device attribute on H200: querying multi_processor_count on our H200 returns 132 SMs. Derived: combining full GH100's 2 SMs per TPC and at most 9 TPCs (18 SMs) per GPC with 132 active SMs shows that H200 enables 132 ÷ 2 = 66 TPCs, and because 132 > 7 × 18 = 126, all 8 GPCs are active. Unknown: how many TPCs / SMs each individual GPC enables on H200 is not published (even TPC pairs also do not explain the measured 4-CTA cluster residency cap at 2 CTAs per SM in Chapter 7, Section 12, whose cause is not determined); instruction and constant cache byte capacities, and whether NCU's ICC is the same unit as the whitepaper's L1 instruction cache, are not published. Every kernel in this book runs across these 132 SMs (Primer 3, Section 1; Chapter 2, Section 1); CTAs of the same thread block cluster co-reside inside one GPC (Chapter 7, Section 12; Chapter 9, Section 3)
Virtual-to-physical address translation (GPU MMU) Along the memory path between the SM and physical-address L2 (exact hardware site of translation not published) Documented (PTX §8.2; CUDA Guide §4.18; NCU §2.3.1): kernel pointers and tensor descriptors hold virtual addresses that the OS/driver and hardware Memory Management Unit (MMU) translate into physical device addresses during memory access, and L2 operates in physical-address space. Unknown: where between the SM and L2 translation physically happens, how many on-chip TLB levels exist and their capacities, the miss penalty, and the default allocation page size are not published by NVIDIA and not measured in this book. Every global access and TMA transfer passes virtual addresses; buffer allocation order shifting the physical-page and partition placement of later tensors is inferred (Chapter 10, Section 5)
Partitioned crossbar (XBAR; L1-to-XBAR / XBAR-to-L1) Between the 132 SMs (GPCs) and the two L2 partitions Documented (H100 whitepaper p37, p43; NCU §2.3.5, §2.11.2): the partitioned crossbar carries packets from source units to destination units; NCU's L1/TEX table separately reports peak-utilization percentages for the L1-to-XBAR request interface and the XBAR-to-L1 return path. Measured on other GPUs in public papers (MICRO 2024 abstract): core-to-partition on-chip latency can differ by about 70% depending on core position. Unknown: whether TMA and L1TEX share one per-SM XBAR injection port, along with XBAR peak bandwidth and internal arbitration order, is not published and not measured in this book. Every global load, store, atomic, and TMA transfer crossing L2 / HBM traverses it (Chapter 2, Section 2); also one candidate queueing site at kernel startup in Chapter 8, Section 7 (exact queueing site not measured)
L2 Request Coalescer (LRC / VIDLRC) Inferred to sit in front of L2 (VIDLRC for global device memory; which side of XBAR it sits on and unit count not published) Documented (NCU §2.3.4, §2.3.5): LRC receives incoming requests headed for L2, tries to coalesce read requests before forwarding them to L2, serves programmatic multicast requests from SMs, and supports write compression (the Inline Compressor ILC is part of LRC, compressing writes before L2 when possible and decompressing read responses). Inferred: sits on the L2 ingress side from that functional description, and "programmatic multicast requests" corresponds to thread-block-cluster TMA .multicast::cluster (PTX §9.7.10.28.4.1 / .5.3). Unknown: whether it sits before or after XBAR, how many LRC units exist across the chip, its coalescing window, and its service order are not published, and not measured in isolation in this book. No standalone step in this book isolates LRC (vector x reuse in Chapter 2, Section 2 is explained by L1/L2 cache hits; the cluster merges unpacked in the main text—Chapter 7, Section 12 and Chapter 9, Section 3—use distributed shared memory st.async rather than TMA multicast, whereas the shipped prefill pooler [T = 753, see Chapter 9, Section 7, and 3,012] and router use 2-CTA cluster .multicast::cluster, not unpacked in the text, with LRC effect not measured)
Per-allocation inline compression (ILC, GXC, XCOMP; scope note) GPC-to-L2 write path (GXC), inside LRC (ILC), and L2 / HBM (XCOMP hardware position not published) Documented (Hopper Tuning Guide §1.4.2.3; CUDA Guide §4.18.5.2; H100 whitepaper p37; NCU §2.3.4–§2.3.5): explicitly opted into per allocation via the CUDA Driver virtual-memory API with CU_MEM_ALLOCATION_COMP_GENERIC (GXC attempts to compress fully covered 128 B writes coming from GPCs to L2, the Inline Compressor ILC lives inside LRC, and XCOMP is the crossbar compressor); depending on the data, it saves DRAM bandwidth, L2 read bandwidth and L2 capacity (CUDA Guide §4.18.5.2), while the allocated memory footprint does not shrink. Inferred: off by default on ordinary cudaMalloc allocations. Unknown: the exact hardware position of XCOMP is not published; how many bytes it would save if enabled on BF16 or quantized weights was not measured. None of this book's kernels allocates compressible memory; weight and KV byte reductions use explicit narrow formats instead (C12 / NVFP4 in Chapter 6, Sections 1–3; FP8 in Chapter 7, Section 1)
Shared L2 cache and two-partition interconnect (LTC, ltcfabric) Central cache layer between on-chip memory clients and FBPA Documented (NCU §2.3.1, §2.3.4, §2.11.3; H100 whitepaper p18, p37): LTC is the chip-wide physical-address Level 2 cache, physically split into two L2 partitions connected by the partition communication fabric LTC Fabric (ltcfabric) (documented as 60 MB on full GH100 and 50 MB on H100 SXM5; the H200 datasheet states no L2 size). Measured via device attribute on H200: querying cudaDevAttrL2CacheSize (and NCU device attributes) on our H200 gives 60 MiB (62,914,560 B). Unknown: H200's hardware peak L2 read bandwidth is not published. Unloaded round-trip latency and the two partitions are in Chapter 2, Section 2, residency policy hints in Chapter 2, Section 4, and read-only versus write-flush comparison in Chapter 10, Section 2
L2 cache slices and three-stage pipeline (LTS: lts__t / lts__m / lts__d) Parallel sub-partitions inside the two L2 partitions Documented (NCU §2.3.4; H100 whitepaper p43): each L2 Cache Slice (LTS) is a sub-partition of L2, and counter prefixes lts__t, lts__m, and lts__d denote its Tag, Miss, and Data stages. Measured on sibling GH100 H20 (preprint) (arXiv:2611.13860): 96 slices grouped into 12 FBPs across the two partitions, selected by a physical-address XOR hash. Unknown: H200's active slice count, address hash function, and intra-slice hit/miss service order are not published and not measured in this book. Encountered when inspecting low-level NCU L2 counters (Chapter 10, Section 6); serialization when many CTAs atomically add into the same L2 address is inferred and does not depend on total slice count (Chapter 7, Section 12)
Memory controllers / FrameBuffer Partitions (FBPA; i.e., HBM partitions) Between L2 (LTC) and the 6 off-chip HBM3e stacks Documented (NCU §2.3.4; H100 whitepaper p18; H200 datasheet): FBPAs are the memory controllers sitting between LTC (L2) and off-chip DRAM, and their count varies by GPU; full GH100 pairs 6 stacks with 12 512-bit controllers, H100 SXM5 pairs 5 stacks with 10 512-bit controllers, and H200's nominal total bandwidth is 4.8 TB/s. Derived / Inferred: combining full GH100's 6 stacks with the 6,016-bit (> 5 × 1,024-bit) memory bus listed in the H200 NVL brief gives 6 HBM3e stacks. Unknown: H200 SXM's exact active FBPA count, address hash, and DRAM row-scheduling policy are not published and not measured in this book; mcc in NCU §2.3.4 belongs to the SoC Memory Subsystem (MSS), and whether data-center H200 has such a unit is unknown. Every HBM weight, activation, and KV stream in this book enters and leaves device memory through it (Chapter 2, Sections 2–3; startup queueing candidates and the "HBM partition" mapping-shift inference are in Chapter 8, Section 7 and Chapter 10, Section 5)

2Intra-SM Cache Sub-Stages, Shared Data Ports, Address Generation, and Warp-Stall Index

NCU breaks each SM's unified L1TEX unit into an input stage plus Tag, Miss, and Data stages, and explains how a shared bidirectional unit data port can saturate before any single directional link hits its own peak; warp-stall reasons and the on-chip hardware warp sampler are consolidated in Chapter 10, Section 7.

Sub-Stage / NCU Name Location on Chip What It Does, Limits, and Epistemic Status Book kernel and Chapter Pointer
L1TEX input and three internal stages (lsuin, l1tex__t, l1tex__m, l1tex__d) Each SM's unified L1 data cache / texture / shared-memory unit (L1TEX, managing 256 KiB of on-chip SRAM) Documented (NCU §2.3.4, §2.3.5, §2.11.2): lsuin is the Load/Store input stage; l1tex__t, l1tex__m, and l1tex__d denote the Tag, Miss, and Data stages of L1TEX; requests, serialized cycle-by-cycle wavefronts, and 32 B sectors are defined in NCU §2.11.2 (note that the global-load pipeline diagram in that section is drawn for Ampere GA100, not GH100). Measured on sibling GH100 H800 PCIe (paper) (arXiv:2501.12084): TMA transfers bypass the L1 cache. Unknown: internal queue depths, detailed stage division of labor, and per-stage peak bandwidths on GH100 are not published, and not measured in isolation in this book. Ordinary global loads/stores, cp.async, shared-memory accesses (including ldmatrix / stmatrix), and SHFL all pass through L1TEX (Chapter 3, Sections 2 and 7; Appendix B, Section 6); consult this row when reading raw l1tex__* metrics in NCU (Chapter 10, Section 6, Step 3)
Shared bidirectional unit data ports (NCU Memory Chart Ports) Ports on cache and memory unit boundaries in NCU's Memory Chart Documented (NCU §2.10.1 Ports): incoming and outgoing traffic of a memory or cache unit often share a single common data port; even when every individual directional link sharing that port operates well below its own peak, the unit's shared data port can already reach saturation. Unknown: which specific hardware units on GH100 share one bidirectional port versus split separate ports is not itemized by NVIDIA and not measured in isolation in this book. Encountered when opening NCU's Memory Workload Analysis panel to inspect the memory chart (Chapter 10, Section 6, Step 3)
Address Generation Unit and interleaved .local layout (AGU) Along the SM memory path (specific parent hardware block not published) Documented (NCU §2.3.1 Memory): thread-private local memory (.local, backed by global device memory) has its addresses translated into global virtual addresses by the AGU; local memory is interleaved so consecutive thread IDs access consecutive 32-bit words, making accesses to the same relative offset across a warp fully coalesced. Unknown: which hardware block inside GH100 houses the AGU, and whether it also computes shared-memory or ordinary register-offset addresses, is not published by NVIDIA. Touched only when register spills, uninlined function stack frames (STACK), or dynamically indexed local arrays land in .local (Chapter 3, Section 1; Chapter 7, Section 7; Chapter 8, Section 4; Chapter 10, Section 6, Step 1; Appendix B, Item 26); compare multi-dimensional tile hardware address generation in TMA (Chapter 3, Section 3)
Warp-stall reasons and hardware warp sampler (lg_throttle, no_instructions, sleeping, drain, etc.) Per SMSP (smsp__pcsamp_* stall counters; L0 instruction cache: H100 whitepaper p21 Fig. 7 (figure label only)), per SM (hardware warp sampler), per TPC (ICC); exact hardware location of the LG queue not published The four stalls lg_throttle, no_instructions, sleeping, and drain, together with each SM's hardware warp sampler (alongside long_scoreboard, mio_throttle / short_scoreboard, barrier, and wait), are not defined a second time in this table (per-TPC ICC containment is in Section 1, Row 1 above; queue depths and instruction-cache byte capacities are not published). See Chapter 10, Section 7

3Tensor Core and Integer Datapath Quick Reference

Beyond the BF16 / FP16 and FP8 paths used directly in our operators, Hopper Tensor Cores also support TF32, INT8, and 2:4 structured sparsity; 4-bit integers remain only in single-warp mma.sync and are absent from wgmma, while CUDA-core integer dot product dp4a runs on the heavy half of the FMA pipeline.

Datapath / Feature On-Chip Execution Unit Shapes, Precision Rules, Nominal Peaks, and Epistemic Status Book kernel and Chapter Pointer
FP16 / BF16 Tensor Core (mma.sync, wgmma) 4 Tensor Cores per SM (1 per SMSP) Primary 16-bit floating-point matrix-multiply path in this book (instruction shapes, SS / RS operand modes, dense compute peak, and SASS mnemonics are not restated here). See Primer 2, Section 4; Chapter 5, Section 3; and Appendix B, Quick Reference 3 (Items 40 and 42)
FP8 (E4M3 / E5M2) Tensor Core and accumulator precision 4 Tensor Cores per SM (single-warp mma.sync expands on sm_90a into unpack plus HMMA) Primary 8-bit floating-point matrix-multiply path in this book (2× throughput at k = 32, direct .f16 f16x2 or .f32 accumulators, PTX's documented .f32 accumulation "at higher than half precision but lower than single precision" alongside about 13–14 mantissa bits measured in external papers, and single-warp expansion are not restated here). See Chapter 5, Section 3; Chapter 7, Section 10 (.f32 and f16x2 accumulators); and Appendix B, Quick Reference 3 (Items 41 and 43)
TF32 Tensor Core path (mma.sync m16n8k4/k8, wgmma m64nNk8) 4 Tensor Cores per SM Documented (PTX §5.2.3, §9.7.17.2, §9.7.17.5.2; H100 whitepaper Table 1 p20, Table 3 p39; H200 datasheet Footnote 2): same dynamic range as .f32 with >= 10-bit precision (internal bit layout implementation-defined; wgmma truncates the lower 13 bits of 32-bit inputs before multiplying), accumulates into .f32 with dense k = 8; nominal peak 494.7 / 989.4 TFLOP/s (dense / sparse). Derived from documented constants: about 7.4× the datasheet FP32 FMA peak (66.9 TFLOP/s) at rated boost clocks, and 8× per clock at equal frequency (2,048 vs 256 FLOP/cycle/SM). Unknown: sm_90a SASS mnemonics and modifiers are not disassembled; accuracy impact on Muse Spark Open was not measured. Unused in this book's kernels; in the baseline inference code, Stage 4 router runs in FP32 at T <= 8 and splits weights into high/low BF16 halves summed in FP32 at T > 8 (see Primer 2, Section 2), whereas this book's shipped kernels use FP32 CUDA cores at T = 1 and split high/low BF16 halves into FP32 on Tensor Cores at T >= 8
Transformer Engine (hardware FP8 vs software amax scaling) Hardware half in Tensor Cores and conversion pipelines; software half in host framework libraries Documented (H100 whitepaper p11, p23, p46; Transformer Engine 2.0 User Guide FP8 Primer; PTX §5.2.3, §9.7.17.5.2): the hardware half supplies dual-format FP8 Tensor Core inputs—E4M3 (4 exponent + 3 mantissa bits, finite range ±448, finer precision) and E5M2 (5 exponent + 2 mantissa bits, finite range ±57,344 plus ±inf, wider dynamic range, with mixed E4M3 × E5M2 operands supported in wgmma)—plus saturating conversion instructions; the software half tracks historical maximum absolute values (amax, delayed scaling) across steps to compute per-tensor scale factors. Unknown: which execution pipeline runs FP8 pack/unpack F2FP on H200 was not measured (see Appendix B, Items 19 and 41). This book uses only the hardware half: the Stage 2 prologue divides by the supplied input scale factor (1 on benchmark shapes) and saturates into ±448 E4M3 (Chapter 7, Section 1; native FP8 attention MMA is in Chapter 7, Sections 9–10)
INT8 Tensor Core path (.s8 / .u8 → .s32, opcodes IMMA / IGMMA) 4 Tensor Cores per SM Documented (H100 whitepaper Table 1 p20, Table 3 p39; H200 datasheet Footnote 2; PTX 9.5 §9.7.16.5.14, §9.7.17.5.2, §13.11; Binary Utilities §4.3 Table 8): inner dimension k = 32, accumulating into .s32 (optional .satfinite clamping, wrapping otherwise); both single-warp mma.sync (m16n8k32) and sm_90a wgmma (m64nNk32, from PTX 8.4 onward) let A and B choose .s8 or .u8 independently (supporting mixed .s8 × .u8 and .u8 × .s8; the stale same-signedness summary line in PTX §9.7.17.3 is superseded by the instruction section and §13.11 release notes); nominal peak 1,978.9 / 3,957.8 TOPS (dense / 2:4 sparse); Hopper instruction-set opcodes are IMMA and IGMMA. Unknown: full sm_90a shape suffixes and whether single-warp integer mma.sync expands into multiple instructions on sm_90a are not disassembled in this book (compare single-warp FP8 expansion in Appendix B, Item 41). Unused in this book's model (used in W8A8 integer quantized inference; for the k = 32 FP8 Tensor Core path, see Chapter 5, Section 3 and Appendix B, Quick Reference 3, Items 42–43)
Sub-byte INT4 single-warp MMA (mma.sync .s4 / .u4 → .s32; absent from wgmma) Single-warp mma.sync target ISA (sm_90a lowering unknown) Documented (PTX §9.7.16.2, §9.7.16.5.4, §9.7.16.5.14, §9.7.17.3; H100 whitepaper and H200 datasheet): PTX single-warp mma.sync accepts m8n8k32 (sm_75+) and m16n8k32 / m16n8k64 (sm_80+), but requires both A and B to be 4-bit integers (.u4 or .s4, mixed .u4 × .s4 allowed per §9.7.16.5.14 example) accumulating into .s32; Hopper wgmma has no .s4 / .u4 type at all, and NVIDIA publishes no INT4 Tensor Core peak on H100 or H200. Unknown: what SASS sm_90a emits for this mma.sync and its actual throughput are not disassembled and not measured in this book. Unused in this book, and directly explains why Hopper NVFP4 must unpack weights in registers with 8 integer instructions: expert weights are block-scaled E2M1 floats, activations are BF16, and large batches require wgmma (Chapter 6, Section 3; Chapter 8, Section 1; Appendix A, Section 3)
Tensor Core 2:4 structured sparsity (mma.sp, wgmma.mma_async.sp) 4 Tensor Cores per SM (left-operand A path) Documented (PTX §9.7.16.6.1, §9.7.17.6; H100 whitepaper p20 Table 1, p22; H200 datasheet Footnote 2): sparsity applies only to left matrix A; 16-bit and 8-bit types store at most 2 nonzeros per 4 consecutive elements at 2:4 granularity (1:2 granularity for .tf32) alongside a .b32 metadata operand holding 2-bit nonzero indices, doubling the instruction k dimension (BF16/FP16 16→32, TF32 8→16, FP8/INT8 32→64) and doubling nominal peak throughput (e.g., BF16 989 → 1,979, FP8 1,979 → 3,958 TFLOP/s). Unknown: Hopper's internal zero-skipping mux hardware details are not published; our model weights are unpruned, and sparse accuracy and speedup were not measured. Unused because our model weights are dense; explains how the datasheet's 2× "with sparsity" footnote numbers relate to this book's dense lower bounds (989 / 1,979 TFLOP/s) (Primer 2, Section 4; Chapter 5, Section 3; Chapter 7, Section 1)
CUDA-core 4-way byte integer dot product (dp4a / dp2a, opcodes IDP / IDP4A) Heavy half of the FMA pipeline (FMA Heavy) in each SMSP Documented (PTX §9.7.1.24–25; Binary Utilities §4.3 Table 8; NCU §2.3.6 Pipelines): dp4a computes a per-thread dot product of 4 pairs of packed 8-bit integers (.s8 / .u8) from two 32-bit registers and accumulates into a 32-bit integer register (dp2a is the 2-way form), mapping to Hopper SASS opcodes IDP / IDP4A; per the NCU manual, integer dot products run on the FMA Heavy half of the FMA pipeline alongside IMAD, not on the ALU pipeline. Unknown: full SASS modifiers and H200 issue intervals are not published, and not disassembled or measured in this book. Unused in this book's model (single-token gemv uses floating-point FFMA; for the FMA pipeline and its IMAD half, see Chapter 5, Section 1 and Appendix B, Item 12a)

4Extended TMA Modes, Descriptor Updates, and Cluster Bulk Copy

Beyond the rectangular .tile loads/reductions and static host descriptors used in the main text, Hopper's TMA also supports convolution im2col, narrow-channel interleaved global layouts, in-kernel descriptor updates through the tensormap proxy, and intra-cluster peer-CTA shared-memory bulk copies.

TMA Mode / Mechanism On-Chip Unit and Proxy Syntax Rules, Hardware Limits, and Epistemic Status Book kernel and Chapter Pointer
TMA im2col convolution unrolling mode (.im2col) Each SM's TMA unit (async proxy) Documented (PTX §5.5.2, §5.5.4, §5.5.5, §9.7.10.28.5.3): supports 3D (NWC), 4D (NHWC), and 5D (NDHWC) tensors, extracting elements from a convolution window bounding box plus offsets in DHW space and rearranging them directly into columns in shared memory; H200 (sm_90a) supports only plain .im2col, while .im2col::w, .im2col::w::128, and .im2col_no_offs::w require sm_100 or higher. Because it still steps across regular sliding-window geometry, it cannot accept an arbitrary page-table row-index array. Unknown: .im2col throughput and SASS modifiers on H200 were not measured in this book. Unused in this book's kernels; explains why neither multi-dimensional TMA mode on Hopper can gather scattered KV rows from a page table in one command (Chapter 10, Section 10; Appendix C, TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator) entry; for Blackwell's .tile::gather4, see Appendix A, Section 4)
Tensor-descriptor channel interleave and allocation class (.alloc_class) Fields in the 128 B CUtensorMap descriptor, parsed in hardware by TMA Documented (PTX §5.5.3.3, §5.5.6, §9.7.10.29 Table 36, §9.7.10.30; CUDA Guide §4.13.2.2): interleave applies only to 3D–5D tensors and groups channel dimension C in global memory into 16 B (NC/8DHWC8) or 32 B (NC/16HWC16) interleaved slices to speed up loads of elements narrower than 4 B—it alters global-memory layout, unlike on-chip bank-conflict XOR swizzle; .alloc_class (.alloc_small / .alloc_large / .alloc_same, introduced in PTX 9.5 and supported on sm_90a) tags the underlying tensor allocation size class to bound out-of-bounds access safety. Unknown: latency differences from either attribute on H200 were not measured in this book. Every kernel in this book uses INTERLEAVE_NONE and never sets .alloc_class; for the tiled descriptor fields built on the host, see Chapter 3, Section 3
In-kernel descriptor updates and the tensormap proxy (tensormap.replace, tensormap.cp_fenceproxy, fence.proxy.tensormap::generic) SMEM → global memory → TMA tensormap proxy Documented (PTX §8.6, §9.7.10.29, §9.7.15.4, §9.7.15.17; CUDA Guide §4.13.2.2.2–§4.13.2.2.3): TMA reads tensor descriptors through a separate tensormap proxy; when patching a 128 B (1024-bit) descriptor on the device, in tensormap.replace (requires sm_90a) the .ss operand may be .global or .shared::cta; the shared-memory path is recommended (CUDA Guide §4.13.2.2.2): the modifying thread edits fields in shared memory first and then copies back to global memory with release via tensormap.cp_fenceproxy.global.shared::cta.tensormap::generic.release (sm_90+) (or releases with fence.proxy.tensormap::generic.release if editing directly in global memory); before using the descriptor, one thread in the same CTA must also run fence.proxy.tensormap::generic.acquire, after which it or other threads in that CTA following a block sync can issue TMA (read-only const __grid_constant__ descriptors built on the host—and prefetch.tensormap on them—require none of these proxy fences). Unknown: which cache level holds descriptors in hardware, the SASS lowering, and device-side update latency are not published by NVIDIA, and not disassembled or measured in this book. Every TMA kernel in this book builds static descriptors on the host ahead of launch, avoiding device-side proxy fences (see Chapter 3, Section 3 and Appendix B, Item 30a)
Intra-cluster peer-CTA shared-memory bulk copy (cp.async.bulk.shared::cluster.shared::cta) Source SM's TMA unit writing directly into peer CTA shared memory over the intra-GPC SM-to-SM interconnect Documented (PTX §9.7.10.28.4.1; Hopper Tuning Guide §1.4.1.2; CUDA Guide §4.13.2; H100 whitepaper p11, p22): issued by a single thread without staging payload through registers, copying contiguous bytes from local shared memory (.shared::cta) directly into another CTA's distributed shared memory (.shared::cluster) in the same cluster and decrementing the receiver CTA's mbarrier expected-byte count on arrival (if generic shared-memory stores just wrote the source buffer, fence.proxy.async.shared::cta is required before issuing). PTX imposes three hard rules: (1) byte count size must be a multiple of 16 B; (2) both source and destination addresses must be 16 B-aligned; and (3) the destination must lie in the shared memory of a different CTA in the cluster (self-copy is forbidden). Unknown: its speed crossover byte size against st.async on H200 was not measured, and cluster-direction SASS modifiers are not disassembled in this book. Both cluster merges in this book use st.async instead: in Chapter 7, Section 12, both cluster kernel families write their own CTA's slice (forbidden by the no-self-copy rule; the 3-in-1 mma.sync kernel also holds partial sums in registers and would need shared-memory staging plus a proxy fence, while the sliding-window wgmma kernel already stages output rows and LSE in two separate 16 B-aligned/sized shared-memory arrays but would still need a proxy fence and a separate self-write path, with which is faster not measured); in Chapter 9, Section 3, each partial sum of squares is only 4 B (one FP32, under 16 B) and likewise includes 1 self-write. For global → SMEM TMA forms, see Appendix B, Quick Reference 2, Items 30 and 33

Takeaway: Whenever an unfamiliar single-GPU Hopper hardware name shows up in whitepapers, PTX manuals, or NCU panels, check first which chip level it lives at, what specification rules bind it, and which details even official documentation leaves unpublished—then follow the rightmost column back to the operator step in this book.
